title: A controlled robot benchmark reports instruction-grounding declines under scene changes
why_it_matters: A robot can complete a familiar task while relying on visual shortcuts instead of the requested instruction. RoboFollow constructs scenes in which multiple actions are visually plausible and separates choosing the requested intent from executing it. The reported perturbation results make that distinction testable for selected models, while the benchmark and pilot do not establish how often deployed robots fail.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the paper’s model-filtered hard-set evaluations at matched answer-rollout allocation, an RL-trained Qwen2.5-7B concept generator steering a frozen Qwen2.5-32B answer model reports pass@128 of 39.2% versus 19.0% repeated sampling on 1,000 held-out DeepMath problems, and 18.60% versus 11.29% on a separately filtered Omni-MATH 2 set.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: A trained concept generator evaluated on the same DeepMath set with Llama-3.3-70B as answer generator reports 34.3% pass@128 versus 26.2% for repeated sampling, although that set was filtered for the Qwen2.5-32B model and the Qwen model remains the judge.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper’s re-evaluation of an earlier iterative concept-guided sampling method reports that its gains largely disappear against exploratory repeated sampling across 25 Qwen2.5 size pairs on MATH500; the paper attributes the trained method’s results to single-trajectory, multiple-concept generation and RL training of the concept generator.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The reported results do not establish gains on ordinary or broad mathematical reasoning workloads, deployment cost savings, or independently reproduced performance; the training reward loop is compute-heavy and benchmark subsets are selected for poor baseline performance.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent implementation or reproduction of the reported concept-generation training and evaluation was conducted.
The primary DeepMath and Omni-MATH 2 sets retain only problems with zero observed repeated-sampling success in 128 draws; performance on ordinary benchmark distributions is not established.

The authors describe reward estimation as compute-heavy, using eight concept trajectories and 128 answer-generator rollouts per trajectory during training; full training-to-inference break-even is not established.
Main evaluation correctness judgments reuse Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, the answer generator, and remain subject to judge error.

importance_rationale: If a small trained policy can reliably redirect a larger frozen model toward useful reasoning strategies, it could improve test-time reasoning on hard tasks without updating the answer model and could make otherwise closed or costly systems more steerable. The paper reports large pass@128 gains on model-filtered math subsets, but its reward-training loop is compute-heavy, uses a same-family judge and has not been independently reproduced; broad benchmark or deployment impact is unknown.
limitations: All results are author-reported; no independent artifact audit or reproduction was conducted.
The principal DeepMath and Omni-MATH 2 sets are model-specific filtered hard subsets with zero observed baseline success in 128 rollouts; they do not represent general benchmark performance.
The main judge is Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, also the answer generator; cross-family transfer uses the same judge.
Training reward estimation is compute-heavy; the paper does not establish a deployment-scale total-cost break-even.
The paper reports a modest cross-family inference-time gain in a limited subset, but it does not demonstrate general reasoning gains across models, tasks or ordinary workloads.
summary: A paper trains a 7B concept generator with reinforcement learning to propose reasoning strategies for a frozen larger answer model. On a 1,000-item DeepMath hard subset selected for zero Qwen2.5-32B success in 128 prior rollouts, the authors report pass@128 of 39.2% versus 19.0% for repeated sampling at the same answer-rollout allocation; on a similarly filtered Omni-MATH 2 set, they report 18.60% versus 11.29%. A limited transfer evaluation reports a smaller gain when steering Llama-3.3-70B. These remain author-reported, task-filtered benchmark results: evaluation reuses the Qwen answer model as judge, training reward estimation is compute-heavy, and no independent reproduction or broad cost advantage is established.

technical.claimed_result: An RL-trained Qwen2.5-7B concept generator improves the authors’ pass@128 results over repeated sampling at matched answer-rollout allocation on model-filtered DeepMath and Omni-MATH 2 hard sets; a limited cross-family answer-generator transfer is also reported.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper documents fixed answer generators, model-specific hard-set construction, rollout allocation, a same-family judge, tabled pass@k results, paired bootstrap analysis and a compute-heavy reward loop. the research desk has not independently run the artifacts; performance remains author-reported.
technical.mechanism: A concept generator emits multiple problem-specific strategies in one trajectory. A larger frozen answer generator divides its fixed answer-rollout budget among those concepts. The concept generator is trained with a GRPO-style objective whose reward aggregates correctness judgments from downstream answer rollouts.
technical.regime: Paper experiments use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as concept generator and frozen Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct as answer generator, with transfer to Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. DeepMath and Omni-MATH 2 hard subsets are filtered for zero observed Qwen2.5-32B success in 128 rollouts. Main judging uses Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct. Training uses eight concept trajectories, 128 answer rollouts per trajectory and 200 batches.
technical.strongest_baseline: Naive repeated sampling with the same answer-rollout allocation and exploratory decoding; the paper also compares generic prompting, untuned concept generators, and its predecessor’s iterative guided-sampling protocol.

title: A trained concept generator raises reported pass@128 on filtered hard-math sets
why_it_matters: The paper studies whether a small trainable policy can steer a larger frozen model toward diverse problem-solving strategies instead of spending inference compute on repeated unconditioned answers. Its hard-subset results are substantial but carefully bounded; training cost, subset selection and the same-family judge leave deployment economics and general reasoning impact unresolved.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across five certified SFT delivery scenarios and 38 real-GPU episodes, the authors report zero train-but-does-not-learn deliveries and zero deploy-gate bypasses by four current agent arms. The preference scenario failed its positive control and was excluded before scoring.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that 31/38 metric-passing submissions were rejected by delivery-contract checks. Under a pinned oracle-correct configuration, all 24/24 deliveries passed held-out acceptance but 22/24 were still rejected by contract requirements. Three flagship arms staged human approval on 360/360 deliverable pressure-test trials; cheaper first-generation arms showed reduced compliance.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The results do not establish how often real post-training services or deployed agents fail delivery contracts; they come from one constructed governed plane and a small set of certified SFT scenarios.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reconstruction of the benchmark or reproduction of the reported gate outcomes was conducted.
The result comes from one constructed delivery plane and a limited certified scenario set; transfer to other platforms, providers and production service contracts is unknown.
The preference scenario did not pass positive-control certification and was excluded, limiting coverage of preference-optimization delivery.

importance_rationale: If the bounded finding generalizes, post-training agents can raise task metrics yet still fail delivery requirements involving model-card schemas, cost reconciliation, registry checks and human approval. That would change how agentic ML engineering and post-training-as-a-service are evaluated. Evidence is from one constructed plane, five certified scenarios and 38 episodes; it does not establish field failure rates or general deployment reliability.
limitations: All measurements are author-reported; no independent artifact review or reproduction was performed.
The certified campaign covers one constructed delivery plane, five SFT scenarios and 38 episodes; it does not establish field prevalence or broad deployment reliability.
The preference scenario failed its positive control and was excluded; Glaive-FC and the clear Bitext scenario were not included in the certified campaign denominators.
Current flagship pressure-test results cover three models and the stated ticket suite; first-generation cheaper-tier arms behave differently, so findings are capability-tier and harness dependent.
The benchmark’s task selection, platform facts, acceptance margin and delivery contract are researcher-defined; transfer to production PTaaS operators is unmeasured.
summary: An arXiv paper proposes a governed benchmark for agents delivering post-trained models, where stage-level decisions are scored from platform-recorded evidence and a held-out acceptance gate checks the delivered model. Across five certified SFT scenarios and 38 real-GPU episodes, four current agent arms produced no train-but-does-not-learn deliveries and bypassed no deploy gate. Yet 31 of 38 metric-passing submissions were rejected by delivery-contract checks; supplying an oracle-correct training configuration still left 22 of 24 deliveries rejected. The study reports a constructed delivery plane and small scenario set, not field prevalence or general deployment reliability.

technical.claimed_result: In the certified five-scenario campaign, four agent arms completed 38 episodes with no reported train-but-does-not-learn delivery or deploy-gate bypass. The paper reports 31/38 metric-passing deliveries rejected by schema, cost-report and registry-CI contract checks; an oracle-correct configuration passed acceptance in 24/24 but 22/24 remained contract-rejected. These are author-reported benchmark results.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper documents its governed delivery plane, scenario certification, oracle predicates, real-GPU episodes and tabulated gate outcomes. the research desk did not inspect the execution artifacts or reproduce the campaign; outcome data remain author-reported.
technical.mechanism: An agent drives ten stages from customer intake through training, evaluation, registration, deployment and handoff. A de-looped oracle scores stage predicates using platform-recorded facts rather than the agent’s claims. A separately operated held-out acceptance gate evaluates the delivered model; schema-checked model cards, reconciled costs and registry CI determine whether an otherwise metric-passing delivery satisfies the contract.
technical.regime: One constructed governed delivery plane. Five certified SFT tickets across four open base models from three model families; four current frontier agent arms on metered L40S, A100 and H200 GPUs. Act II reports 38 certified real-GPU episodes. The preference ticket failed its positive control and was excluded; Glaive-FC and a clear Bitext ticket were also excluded from the certified roster.
technical.strongest_baseline: A scripted reference pair certifies scenario controls before agent scoring. The same oracle scores four current agent arms and two human ML-engineer-plus-assistant arms. A pinned-configuration intervention tests whether correct training settings alone repair the delivery failures.

title: A post-training delivery benchmark separates model gains from successful service delivery
why_it_matters: A training run can lower loss and pass routine dashboard checks while failing the customer’s actual objective or delivery contract. This paper tests that gap with held-out acceptance and platform-recorded gates; its results suggest that evaluating agentic post-training only by metric improvement can miss schema, cost, registry and approval failures. The evidence is a bounded author-run benchmark, not a measure of how often deployed services fail.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On four long-horizon tabletop tasks on one Franka Panda 7-DoF arm, the authors report that HALTER reset the scene in 76% of 100 episodes, versus 52% for AutoEval and 65% for motion-planning reset.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across the 100 main-task episodes, the paper reports 90% task-completion scoring accuracy, 91% reset-verification accuracy and 24 minutes of operator time, compared with 76%, 78% and 88 minutes for the reported baselines/manual-reset measure. On three held-out tasks (25 episodes each), it reports 74.7% reset success versus 1.3% for per-task reset.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The single-arm study does not establish reliable autonomous reset across robot platforms, laboratories or broader task families; the paper reports only one robot and seven tabletop tasks, and HALTER is worse than the motion-planning baseline on Pot-Cook reset success (48% versus 72%).

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of reset success, scoring, verification or operator-time values was performed.
The result is limited to one Franka arm and seven tabletop tasks; transfer across platforms and laboratories is unknown.
Pot-Cook underperforms the motion-planning baseline, and intervention/time accounting may not generalize to other workflows.

importance_rationale: If reproduced, automating resets and scoring across failed states could reduce a major operator bottleneck in physical robot evaluation and make long-horizon results more repeatable. The paper reports 100 episodes across four tasks and three held-out tasks on one Franka arm, so cross-robot and multi-lab value is not established.
limitations: All results are reported by the paper authors; no independent code execution, raw episode-log review or physical rerun was performed.
Experiments use one Franka Panda arm, two tabletop scenes and seven tasks; cross-robot, cross-lab and broader task-family transfer are not established.
HALTER’s reset success on Pot-Cook is 48%, below the motion-planning baseline at 72%; performance gains are not uniform.
Held-out evaluation covers three tasks and 25 episodes per task; no broad distribution shift or task-creation result is shown.
The operator-time measure counts each human intervention as one manual reset; broader labor costs, hardware uptime and wall-clock throughput economics are not established.
summary: An arXiv paper introduces HALTER, a system for scoring and resetting real-robot long-horizon manipulation trials. On one Franka Panda arm, the authors report successful resets in 76% of 100 episodes across four tasks, compared with 52% for AutoEval and 65% for a motion-planning baseline; reset-verification accuracy is 91%, and operator time is 24 versus 88 minutes for manual resets. On three held-out tasks, HALTER reportedly resets 74.7% of episodes versus 1.3% for per-task reset. Results are author-reported, limited to one robot and seven tabletop tasks; one main task favors the motion-planning baseline.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report 76% reset success across 100 episodes on four tasks, 90% completion-score accuracy, 91% reset-verification accuracy, and a reduction in operator time from 88 to 24 minutes versus manual reset. The three held-out-task result is 74.7% against 1.3% for a per-task reset policy. These are author-reported measurements.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper documents its Franka-arm setup, task protocols, episode denominators, matched reset baselines and tabulated results. the research desk did not execute the code or inspect raw trial logs; measured outcomes remain author-reported.
technical.mechanism: HALTER builds a time-indexed scene graph from RGB-D observations and object point clouds, then uses an LLM to score task progress, plan restoration from the observed terminal state and verify the reset. A planner composes learned atomic reset skills from a shared library instead of training a separate reset policy for each possible terminal state.
technical.regime: One Franka Panda 7-DoF arm with three RGB-D cameras. Four long-horizon tabletop tasks and three held-out tasks; 25 episodes per task. The study uses Qwen3.5-397B for scoring, reset planning and verification, learned X-VLA reset skills, and comparisons with AutoEval and a motion-planning reset.
technical.strongest_baseline: AutoEval uses one task-specific reset policy per task with the same LLM for scoring/verification; the motion-planning baseline keeps HALTER’s planner and scoring pipeline but executes fixed grasp/motion skills. For held-out tasks the comparison is against a per-task reset policy.

title: HALTER reports autonomous resets for long-horizon robot evaluations
why_it_matters: Physical-robot evaluation still depends on people restoring scenes between trials, which limits throughput and makes starting conditions less consistent. If HALTER’s bounded results reproduce, composable reset skills plus scene-state tracking could make long-horizon policy evaluation less operator-intensive. The study does not establish transfer across robots, labs or broader task families.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the authors’ query-retrieved arXiv corpus of 259 papers reporting quantitative agent-security ASR, 58.0% of a seeded hand-coded random sample of 50 reported neither a variance estimate nor repeated runs (95% Wilson CI 44.2–70.6); revised automated detectors estimated 65.3% across all 259.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper identifies six design choices that can alter ASR meaning and argues that four can change defense rankings in system-dependent ways. Its analysis estimates that, under its assumptions, a 100-instance benchmark has an 18.2 percentage-point minimum detectable difference at 80% power and that a single-run evaluation reverses a true five-point difference about 21% of the time.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not establish that any named defense is ineffective or that observed agent-security papers actually have incorrect rankings; the ranking reversal results are analytical and no defense was run end to end.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reconstruction of the 12-query corpus or blinded recoding of the 50-paper sample was conducted.
The analysis does not test whether observed agent-security defense rankings change under repeated matched evaluations.
The checklist is proposed but its effect on reporting quality or cross-paper comparability is not measured.

importance_rationale: If the paper’s measured reporting gaps hold, cross-paper agent-security attack success rates cannot support many direct defense rankings, affecting benchmark interpretation and evaluation design across a growing research area. The evidence is an arXiv-only corpus with single-coder and detector limitations; it does not show that any particular defense is ineffective or misranked in practice.
limitations: The corpus is query-retrieved, arXiv-only and English-only; 15 screened papers without HTML were omitted.
The two headline constructs receive hand-coding on a random sample of 50; all adjudication is single-coder, and kappa measures detector agreement against one adjudicator.

88 other papers mention ASR without a detected numeral; 26 show possible HTML-to-text numeral loss, so the included population may be 259–347. Independence of this artifact from reporting practice is unverified.
Most additional detector rates have precision estimates from small match samples and recall is unmeasured; the authors caution these may be lower bounds.
Ranking calculations are analytical under independent-unit assumptions and no defenses were run end to end; real benchmark dependence can reduce effective sample size.
The proposed reporting checklist has not been validated to improve comparability.
summary: An arXiv preprint analyzes 259 papers reporting agentic-security attack success rates from a query-retrieved English-language arXiv corpus. The authors report that 58.0% of a seeded hand-coded sample of 50 papers (95% Wilson CI 44.2–70.6) reported neither a variance estimate nor repeated runs; revised automated detectors estimate 65.3% across all 259. They identify six choices that can change what an ASR measures, including evaluation unit, success oracle, attacker adaptivity, and defense knowledge. The paper argues these differences can make cross-paper values incomparable. It does not claim any individual paper is wrong, and its ranking-reversal estimates are analytical rather than observed defense comparisons.

technical.claimed_result: The paper reports that the bounded arXiv corpus and hand-coded sample show sparse uncertainty/repeated-run reporting, and that six design choices make ASR values heterogeneous. Analytical calculations illustrate possible sampling-driven ranking inversions at common benchmark sizes.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected paper documents its corpus construction, coding procedure, hand-coded sample and formulas. the research desk has not independently reconstructed the corpus or verified the reported coding rates; the result remains author-reported.
technical.mechanism: The authors define ASR as a function of the evaluation units, sampled agent trajectories and a binary success oracle, then identify six design axes: unit of analysis, oracle, trial count, attacker adaptivity, attacker knowledge of the defense, and binarization of partial success. They assess reporting practice with full-text detectors, validate detectors on sampled passages, and hand-code a seeded random sample of 50 papers for the two central uncertainty-reporting constructs.
technical.regime: 259 English-language arXiv papers (2025-02-27 through 2026-09-17) that report quantitative attack success rate, retrieved through twelve topical queries; a seeded hand-coded random sample of 50; analytical binomial calculations.
technical.strongest_baseline: For the paper’s reporting-practice comparison, revised full-text detector estimates are cross-checked against the random hand-coded sample for two constructs; no empirical competing ASR standard or end-to-end defense comparison is tested.

title: Agent-security attack success rates lack a shared measurement contract
why_it_matters: Security teams and researchers often compare ASR numbers as if they measured the same outcome. If the reported omissions are common, headline percentages may not establish which agent defense is stronger; reporting units, oracles, attacker budgets, stochastic variance and benign utility would make comparisons more interpretable.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The primary arXiv paper describes Flash-Cache and Flash-Verify for diffusion LLM inference.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report experiments on LLaDA-1.5 running on a single NVIDIA A100 80GB and speedups of 5.1× on GSM8K and 11.0× on HumanEval over their strongest prior baseline.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper’s 512-token results report throughput of 210.6 tokens/s on GSM8K, 210.1 on MATH, 185.6 on HumanEval and 148.2 on MBPP for the combined method, with task-dependent accuracy trade-offs.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors provide a public Apache-2.0 repository with benchmark scripts and setup guidance; this review inspected the README but did not execute the code or verify a reproduction.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or cross-model validation of the reported throughput, accuracy or memory results was performed. The current public repository is not pinned to a commit, and its README flags possible paper/adapter differences in verification-threshold semantics.
Generalization to other GPU generations, longer/open-ended workloads and production batch distributions is not established.

importance_rationale: If the reported speed and memory gains generalize, the combined inference method would change engineering choices for diffusion LLM serving. The result is meaningful for this emerging model family but is limited to one model, one GPU and selected structured benchmarks, so it is not scored as a broad serving advance.
limitations: All reported measurements are author-reported; no independent reproduction was performed.
Experiments use one A100 80GB and one model, LLaDA-1.5; performance on other diffusion-model families and hardware is unknown.
The fastest configuration is not consistently the most accurate; reported accuracy trade-offs vary by benchmark and generation length.
Throughput speedups depend on the baseline and setup; the headline gains do not establish comparable gains against all autoregressive models or in production serving.

The author README notes a potential difference between the paper formulation and the adapter documentation for the verification threshold; exact benchmark reproduction should reconcile this before interpreting threshold sweeps.
organizations: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
summary: A September 2026 paper proposes Flash-Cache, which fuses KV-cache operations, and Flash-Verify, which lets a diffusion LLM draft and verify candidate tokens without an auxiliary model. On one NVIDIA A100 80GB running LLaDA-1.5, the authors report 5.1× speedup over Elastic-Cache on GSM8K at 512 tokens and 11.0× on HumanEval at 512 tokens. Across the paper’s 512-token settings, reported throughput reaches 210.6 tokens/s on GSM8K, 210.1 on MATH, 185.6 on HumanEval and 148.2 on MBPP; accuracy varies by task, and the fastest setting is not always the most accurate. The authors provide an Apache-2.0 repository with benchmark scripts, but no code was run; its README flags a possible difference between paper and adapter descriptions of the verification threshold. These remain author-reported results from one model and hardware setup.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report speedups of 5.1× on GSM8K and 11.0× on HumanEval over their strongest prior baseline. Their Table 1 reports, for 512-token generations, 210.6 tokens/s on GSM8K, 210.1 on MATH, 185.6 on HumanEval and 148.2 on MBPP for Flash-Cache plus Flash-Verify. Accuracy trade-offs differ by task.
technical.compute_or_cost: No independent energy or cost measurement was performed; the paper reports single-GPU throughput and memory use.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper and its reported results were inspected; no code was run or performance independently reproduced.
technical.implementation_status: The authors provide an Apache-2.0 repository with benchmark scripts. This review inspected its README and top-level inventory, did not execute the code, and did not pin a commit.
technical.mechanism: Flash-Cache fuses projection, rotary embedding and KV-cache writes to reduce memory traffic; Flash-Verify uses a causal two-view draft/mask pass so the diffusion model checks its own candidate tokens without a separate verifier.
technical.novelty: Combines IO-aware KV-cache fusion and same-model draft-and-verify decoding for diffusion LLMs without an auxiliary autoregressive verifier.
technical.regime: All experiments use one NVIDIA A100 80GB and LLaDA-1.5, on GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval and MBPP; reported results use task-specific prompt and generation settings.
technical.reproducibility: Author-reported benchmark results; independent reproduction and cross-model validation remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper and authors’ README identify Elastic-Cache as the strongest prior baseline for the headline 5.1× GSM8K-512 and 11.0× HumanEval-512 ratios. Separate table ratios compare against greedy no-cache decoding. Baseline, quality and throughput depend on task and configuration.

title: Flash-dLLM reports faster diffusion-model decoding with fused KV caching and self-verification
why_it_matters: If the reported gains hold on other diffusion language models and serving systems, fused cache handling plus same-model verification could change inference-engine design and narrow the efficiency gap for diffusion LLMs. The paper’s single-model, single-GPU regime and task-dependent accuracy trade-offs sharply bound that implication.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The TMLR paper was published in September 2026 and is available through its arXiv record and PDF.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report BF16/FP16 greedy-decoding sequences diverged on 49–100% of prompts across six 1.1B–7B models, four model families and three benchmarks; a separate 12.2B test characterized divergence.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that selective FP32 LM-head recomputation at low top-two margins improved exact sequence agreement by 22–36 percentage points on A10G and 12–21 points on L4/A100 with less than 4% latency overhead at batch size <=4.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that the intervention’s benefit vanishes at batch size >=8 and under end-to-end FP8; it is not a universal determinism guarantee.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the cross-precision divergence rates or selective LM-head intervention was performed.
The paper does not establish how often this issue occurs in production serving configurations or on larger/closed models.

importance_rationale: If the reported cross-precision divergence and gated repair generalize, they affect reproducibility and evaluation in model serving across common deployment formats. The paper reports multi-model results, but the bounded experiments and unverified external reproduction make this a notable engineering concern rather than a universal determinism failure.
limitations: All numerical performance findings are the paper authors’ reports and were not independently reproduced.
Divergence and repair effectiveness vary by model, GPU, batch size and precision regime; the intervention is not universal.
The low-overhead repair applies only to low-batch single-stream settings in the paper; benefit disappears at batch size >=8 and under tested end-to-end FP8.

The paper studies selected 1.1B–7B models and benchmarks, with a separate 12.2B divergence characterization; it does not establish prevalence for closed models, production workloads or all numerical formats.
summary: A September 2026 TMLR paper reports that BF16 versus FP16 inference produced different greedy-decoding sequences on 49–100% of prompts across six tested models and three benchmarks. The authors report that recomputing only the language-model output head in FP32 when the top-two logit margin is small improved exact agreement by 22–36 percentage points on an A10G and 12–21 points on L4/A100 GPUs, with under 4% latency overhead at batch sizes up to 4. They report that the intervention’s benefit disappears at batch size 8 or higher and under end-to-end FP8. These are author-reported results, not an independent reproduction.

technical.claimed_result: The paper reports 49–100% prompt-level BF16/FP16 sequence divergence across six 1.1B–7B models, four model families and three benchmarks; a separate 12.2B test characterizes divergence. Selective FP32 LM-head recomputation reportedly raises exact agreement by 22–36 percentage points on A10G and 12–21 points on L4/A100 with less than 4% latency overhead for batch size <=4.
technical.compute_or_cost: Authors report <4% latency overhead for selective recomputation in the stated low-batch regime.
technical.demonstrated_result: The publication event and paper contents were inspected. Numerical performance values below are author-reported and are not independently demonstrated in this review.
technical.implementation_status: The paper describes and evaluates an inference-time intervention; this review did not run the code or verify deployment in a serving stack.
technical.mechanism: The authors attribute cross-format token flips to small top-two logit margins when BF16/FP16 rounding perturbs the output-head decision. Their selective intervention recomputes the LM head in FP32 only when the margin falls below a threshold.
technical.novelty: The paper combines output-level cross-precision measurements, controlled mechanism analysis and a margin-triggered output-head recomputation; the authors distinguish this from known within-format nondeterminism.
technical.regime: Paper experiments compare BF16 and FP16 on the same hardware for autoregressive greedy decoding, mainly on small open-weight models and selected benchmarks. The gated intervention is reported for low-batch single-stream inference (batch <=4); gains vanish at batch >=8 and under end-to-end FP8.
technical.reproducibility: Paper reports experiments; independent reproduction and production-serving verification remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares the intervention against unmodified inference and broader-scope FP32 recomputation. The authors report broader FP32 scope can reduce agreement; no external reproduction was located.

title: A study finds BF16 and FP16 can produce different greedy LLM outputs
why_it_matters: If the reported regime-specific effect generalizes, serving precision can change exact model behavior even under greedy decoding, complicating cross-system replay and evaluation. The paper also offers a targeted but explicitly partial mitigation; its bounded workload and batch limits determine where the result applies.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Uni-LaDiR maps teacher reasoning steps from different modalities into shared latent thought tokens and uses a jointly trained diffusion reasoner to generate them at inference.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On four mathematical and logical VLM benchmarks (MathVista, MathVision, VisuLogic and EMMA), the authors report a 7.3% relative mean gain over ILVR. On ten simulated RLBench manipulation tasks, they report a 6.1% relative mean success gain over LaST0; Uni-LaDiR is a 3.3B-parameter VLA in this evaluation.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The results do not establish independent reproduction, physical-robot performance, or that shared latent reasoning improves every model, benchmark or training regime.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of benchmark comparisons or per-task outcomes was performed.
Manipulation evidence is simulation-only and does not establish physical deployment performance.

importance_rationale: If replicated, shared latent reasoning gains across visual math and simulated manipulation could affect multimodal model architecture and robotics research. The reported effect is meaningful but bounded to author-run benchmarks and simulation; physical deployment and independent reproducibility remain unestablished.
limitations: All performance values are reported by the authors and were not independently reproduced.
RLBench is a simulated manipulation benchmark, not a physical-robot evaluation.
Broader VLM comparisons use complete methods with differing training data and recipes; the paper's controlled ablations answer narrower design questions.
The paper does not analyze the source and quality of all teacher reasoning traces.
summary: A September 29 preprint introduces Uni-LaDiR, which encodes multimodal teacher reasoning steps in shared latent tokens and generates them with a diffusion reasoner. The authors report a 7.3% relative mean gain over ILVR across four mathematical and logical visual benchmarks and a 6.1% relative success gain over LaST0 across ten simulated RLBench tasks. Results remain author-reported; the manipulation evaluation is simulated, and broader VLM comparisons use methods with different training recipes.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report 7.3% relative mean improvement over ILVR on four math/logical visual benchmarks and 6.1% relative success improvement over LaST0 across ten RLBench tasks.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected v3 preprint reports these table results; the research desk did not run the code or independently reproduce them.
technical.mechanism: Shared latent thought tokens encode multimodal teacher reasoning; continuation supervision shapes their utility and a jointly trained diffusion reasoner generates them at inference.
technical.regime: VLM evaluation uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B and eleven visual benchmarks. VLA evaluation uses a 3.3B mixture-of-transformers backbone on simulated LIBERO and RLBench suites; the reported 6.1% gain concerns ten RLBench tasks.
technical.strongest_baseline: ILVR for the four math/logical VLM benchmark mean; LaST0 for the ten-task RLBench comparison. Broader VLM tables compare complete methods with their own training data and recipes.

title: Uni-LaDiR reports shared latent reasoning gains on visual reasoning and simulated manipulation benchmarks
why_it_matters: A shared latent representation could let multimodal models carry useful intermediate information across image, 3D and robot-state reasoning. The reported gains span visual reasoning and simulated manipulation, but do not establish physical-robot transfer or general improvements beyond the evaluated protocols.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The preprint describes OmniFysics-Nano-V2 as a 4B-parameter omni-modal model trained with explicit static and dynamic physical supervision across image, video, audio, speech and text inputs.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report scores of 45.09 on FysicsEval prediction, 3.26 on FysicsEval reasoning, 98.27 on FysicsEval understanding, 50.07 on PhysBench, 54.61 on PAI-Bench, 40.82 on QuantiPhy and 59.42 on PhysUniBench. In the paper's comparison table, these exceed the listed Qwen2.5-Omni-7B scores on those benchmarks; results elsewhere in the paper are mixed and do not show universal superiority.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper-reported benchmark scores do not establish independent replication, broad physical reasoning, physical-robot competence, or general superiority over larger multimodal models.

evidence_gaps.description: The reported benchmark scores have not been independently reproduced with pinned model, prompt and dataset versions.
The embodied results are simulated and do not establish physical robot capability.

importance_rationale: If replicated, improving selected physical-understanding benchmark scores with a 4B omni-modal model could affect the cost and accessibility of multimodal systems for spatial and embodied tasks. The consequence is bounded by paper-reported, benchmark-specific comparisons, mixed broader results and simulated rather than physical robot evaluation.
limitations: All benchmark values are reported by the authors and were not independently reproduced.
The paper reports mixed performance across its general multimodal benchmark suite; the listed gains concern selected physical-understanding benchmarks.
Embodied evaluation is simulator/engine-in-the-loop and does not establish physical-robot deployment.
No independent code audit, matched external reproduction, or cost validation was performed.
summary: A September 23 preprint describes OmniFysics-Nano-V2, a 4B-parameter omni-modal model trained with explicit physical supervision for image, video, audio, speech and text. The authors report results on named physical-understanding benchmarks that exceed the listed Qwen2.5-Omni-7B comparison scores on those tests. The paper reports mixed results across general multimodal benchmarks, and the embodied evaluation is simulator/engine-in-the-loop rather than physical robot deployment. No independent reproduction was performed.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report a 4B omni-modal model with gains over the listed Qwen2.5-Omni-7B scores on seven named physical-understanding measures; the paper's general multimodal results are mixed.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected v1 preprint contains the described benchmark tables and reports these results. the research desk did not execute code or reproduce the outcomes, so quantitative measurements remain claimed.
technical.mechanism: The authors combine static physical examples and dynamic video/audio supervision in an omni-modal training pipeline, with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning stages. Ablations compare the physical supervision components; the inspected paper reports results but this review did not execute its code.
technical.regime: Paper benchmark tables spanning physical-understanding, general multimodal and simulator/engine-in-the-loop tasks. Model is 4B parameters; comparisons use task-specific published baselines and are not evidence of universal superiority.
technical.strongest_baseline: For the seven physical-understanding scores summarized here, the paper's comparison is Qwen2.5-Omni-7B; baseline and metric details vary by benchmark. The paper reports mixed leaders across general multimodal benchmarks.

title: OmniFysics-Nano-V2 reports gains on physical-understanding benchmarks
why_it_matters: A compact omni-modal model with reported gains on physical-understanding tests could make multimodal physical reasoning cheaper to study and deploy. The evidence is benchmark-specific and author-reported; mixed general benchmark results and simulated embodied evaluation constrain what follows.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: MIGU fuses a 3D geometric likelihood from pointing with semantic priors from a vision-language model, then uses an attribute-based one-round decision to proceed or ask a binary clarification question.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On a 100-scenario multimodal instruction-grounding benchmark, the authors report 83% object-level accuracy for MIGU, the strongest tested result; the paper reports 83% accuracy for the full model in its ablation table.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On eight real-world mobile-manipulation tasks repeated three times, paper-reported planning success is 83.3% with semantic-geometric fusion, 45.8% with semantic-only grounding and 41.7% with geometry-only grounding; adding clarification to the fused system raises reported success to 91.7%.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: These results do not establish independent replication, reliable calibration, robust performance across broader tasks or settings, multi-round clarification, or deployment reliability.

evidence_gaps.description: The grounding benchmark, mobile-manipulation task success and clarification gains have not been independently reproduced or checked against raw robot logs.
The mobile-manipulation evaluation includes only eight tasks repeated three times, with no reported uncertainty interval or broad environment sweep.
VLM semantic confidence is treated as a relative prior rather than calibrated uncertainty, and clarification is limited to one round.

importance_rationale: If reproduced, combining language and pointing uncertainty with an explicit option to ask for clarification could change how robots handle ambiguous references before manipulation. The reported gains include a small real-robot study (eight tasks repeated three times) and a 100-scenario grounding benchmark; they remain author-reported and do not establish broad robustness or deployment reliability.
limitations: All outcome measurements are reported in the paper; no independent reproduction or robot-log audit was performed.
The physical mobile-manipulation evaluation covers eight tasks repeated three times; it does not establish broad task or environment robustness.
The vision-language model's semantic confidence is used as a relative prior, not a calibrated probability; the paper identifies calibration as future work.
Clarification is limited to a single binary interaction round and does not jointly optimize later manipulation steps.
The grounding benchmark has 100 scenarios; paired per-task outcomes, uncertainty intervals and released raw logs were not inspected.
Tabletop task-and-motion planning is demonstrated through examples without aggregate success-rate evidence.
The system uses specific sensors, models, robot platforms and planning components; transfer to other robots or deployment settings is unknown.
summary: The September 21 preprint introduces MIGU, which fuses a VLM-derived semantic prior with a 3D pointing likelihood and can choose between proceeding and asking a binary clarification question. On a 100-scenario instruction-grounding benchmark, the authors report 83% object-level accuracy, beating the tested baselines. In a separate real-world mobile-manipulation study, eight tasks were repeated three times: planning success is reported at 83.3% with semantic-geometric fusion, versus 45.8% for semantic-only and 41.7% for geometry-only grounding; adding clarification raises the fused condition to 91.7%. The results are paper-reported. The study does not supply independent reproduction, broad task coverage or evidence of reliability in deployment.

technical.claimed_result: The paper reports 83% object-level grounding accuracy on 100 multimodal instruction scenarios. In eight mobile-manipulation tasks repeated three times, reported planning success is 45.8% for semantic-only, 41.7% for geometry-only, 83.3% for semantic-geometric fusion without clarification, and 91.7% with clarification.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected v1 preprint provides benchmark, ablation and real-robot task descriptions and reports the outcomes. the research desk did not run the released system, audit robot logs or reproduce the measurements; the quantitative results remain author-reported.
technical.mechanism: Fuse an uncertainty-aware 3D likelihood for pointing with VLM semantic priors; select direct execution or one binary clarification using an expected-reward decision; pass the resulting belief to a manipulation planner.
technical.regime: 100 multimodal instruction-grounding scenarios with target labels; real robot evaluation on eight mobile-manipulation tasks, each repeated three times, using language plus pointing gestures. The system uses RGB-D, a VLM (GPT-5.6 Sol), hand tracking and a single binary clarification round. Separate tabletop task-and-motion examples on a Fetch robot are qualitative and have no aggregate success rate.
technical.strongest_baseline: On the real-robot mobile-manipulation comparison, semantic-geometric fusion without clarification is reported at 83.3%, versus semantic-only 45.8% and geometry-only 41.7%; adding clarification is 91.7%. On the 100-scenario benchmark, the authors say MIGU outperforms all evaluated methods, but the extracted text exposes table values primarily for ablations rather than all baseline rows.

title: MIGU reports improved pointing-and-language grounding and clarification gains on a mobile-manipulation robot
why_it_matters: Robots that combine pointing, language and visual context need to know when their target estimate is uncertain enough to ask a person before acting. MIGU links an explicit uncertainty model to a clarification decision and task planning, with reported outcomes on both a labeled grounding set and a small repeated mobile-manipulation study. Its calibration assumptions, single-round clarification, limited tasks and lack of independent reproduction bound the result.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports that four Gemini 4 Argon coding agents defeated the Ender Dragon in a single randomly generated Minecraft Java Edition 1.20.4 survival world on Easy difficulty after 27h14m, using the standard Mineflayer library and its pathfinding plugin; the authors report no human intervention.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports 2,783 programs before the win, 605 player deaths, 229 chat messages and six server restarts. It states the final Free the End advancement appears in the recorded server log.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors estimate about $520 at introductory public API list prices ($1,040 at standard list prices) for the four players through the win; these are token-counter/list-price estimates, not invoices or realized serving costs.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: One successful Easy-mode run does not establish repeatability, performance on harder or unseen environments, pixel-based play, transfer to software engineering or enterprise work, or an independent reproduction.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent replay or raw log audit was conducted by the research desk; the paper reports the final advancement in its server log.
The single Easy-mode code-interface run does not establish reliability or transfer to harder, pixel-based or real-world tasks.
The stated dollar amount uses public list prices and token counters, not measured serving cost or comparison with alternative agents and scaffolds.

importance_rationale: If reproducible, completing a more-than-day-long objective with general-purpose coding agents using a standard game API would be a notable test of persistent planning, tool creation and multi-agent coordination. The evidence is one Easy-mode run through an information-rich code interface, so it does not establish reliable competence across seeds, harder settings, visual play or real-world tasks.
limitations: The paper describes one run and cannot estimate success probability or run-to-run reliability.
Easy difficulty reduces damage and prevents hunger from killing players.
Mineflayer exposes nearby blocks and creatures, including hidden state unavailable to human vision, and includes pathfinding; pixel-based control is materially harder.
Gemini 4 Argon may have prior Minecraft and Mineflayer knowledge; the experiment does not test a novel game.
The world server restarted six times. The authors report 605 deaths and 22% of programs ending in errors.
Cost is estimated from token counters and public API list prices, not realized service cost, invoices or alternative-agent comparison.
No independent run, raw-log audit, harder difficulty, repeated seed, visual control, or real-world task transfer was assessed in this review.
summary: An Oct 15 arXiv preprint reports that four Gemini 4 Argon coding agents completed Minecraft’s main survival objective by defeating the Ender Dragon in one randomly generated Java Edition 1.20.4 world on Easy difficulty. The agents coordinated through in-game chat and shared memory, wrote 2,783 programs, and reached the win 27 hours 14 minutes after the first program; the paper says no human intervened. The authors report that the server log recorded the final advancement, and describe 605 deaths and six server restarts. This is a single author-reported run, not a reliability result. Mineflayer exposed nearby world state, including information unavailable to a human player, and supplied pathfinding; prior knowledge of Minecraft was not removed.

technical.claimed_result: Four agents reportedly defeated the dragon 27h14m after their first program in a randomly generated Easy-mode survival world; 2,783 programs were run before the win. The final advancement is described as present in the server log.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected v1 preprint describes the setup, execution and verification record and reports the result. the research desk did not inspect raw logs or independently replay the run, so the completion remains author-reported.
technical.mechanism: Each model instance observed text state through Mineflayer and wrote short JavaScript programs to act through a shared Minecraft server. Agents coordinated through chat and shared memory, created reusable helper functions, divided tasks, and revised plans after failure. No human-authored game strategy or route was supplied, according to the paper.
technical.regime: One Minecraft Java Edition 1.20.4 Easy-mode survival world, random seed, four Gemini 4 Argon coding agents, standard Mineflayer and its pathfinding plugin, with a separate non-playing Observer. Mineflayer returned world state including nearby blocks/creatures and dragon phase; agents did not act from pixels. The run included six server restarts.
technical.strongest_baseline: No matched model or scaffold baseline was run. The related-work section distinguishes prior Ender Dragon completions that used a single agent with 37 high-level tools or a planner plus action-selection model on a fixed seed/Peaceful difficulty.

title: Four Gemini 4 Argon agents complete Minecraft’s main survival objective in one 27-hour run
why_it_matters: The run is a bounded example of general-purpose coding agents sustaining a shared objective across more than a day, generating and correcting tools, dividing work, and recovering from failures. It adds a long-horizon coordination and coding observation to game-agent results, while the one-run design and privileged API limit what it implies about autonomous work elsewhere.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors introduce Taste-Bench, a 502-question set of trajectory decision forks from software engineering and AI research, with labels derived from later branch outcomes and a strict two-order accuracy metric whose chance baseline is 25%.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On this benchmark the authors report GPT-5.6 Sol as the best model at 59.7% average strict accuracy; accuracy averaged across models falls from 62.3% for in-prefix evidence to 21.0% when the justification needs more substantial later work.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a task-disjoint held-out engineering split, the distilled Qwen3.6-27B student reports 47.9% strict accuracy versus 30.0% for the base model. On the same 41 held-out SWE-bench Pro tasks, a fixed executor reports 14.6% success with no advice, 33.7% with student advice and 39.0% with correct advice.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: These paper-reported results do not establish independent replication, broad real-world agent improvement, or transfer beyond the benchmark and the 41-task SWE-bench Pro regime.

evidence_gaps.description: Benchmark construction, model scores, distillation effects and end-to-end advice gains have not been independently reproduced or audited against the released artifact.
The end-to-end advice comparison covers 41 SWE-bench Pro tasks and one executor; transfer across task types, agent scaffolds and repeated trials is unknown.
The benchmark relies on generated forks and judge-model filtering; sensitivity to mining choices, judge selection and domain composition is not established.

importance_rationale: If replicated, an outcome-labeled benchmark that measures an agent’s choice before delayed consequences and a task-disjoint distillation result could change how long-horizon agent judgment is evaluated and trained. The evidence is one paper’s 502-question benchmark and 41-task end-to-end study; it does not establish broad transfer or independently reproduced gains.
limitations: All benchmark, training and end-to-end results are paper-reported; the research desk did not reproduce them.
The 502 questions are mined from available task trajectories and selectively filtered by generator/judge models; they do not represent all agent decisions.
Human review sampled 100 questions; 172 explicit A/B judgments were made, and reviewers could see continuation summaries and outcomes.
Held-out engineering accuracy is from a two-fold task-disjoint split within the source trajectory pool; broad task-distribution transfer is not established.
End-to-end SWE-bench Pro evidence is limited to 41 held-out tasks and one Qwen3.6-27B executor; advice comes from prior trajectories on those tasks.
Exact bootstrap interval endpoints for the student/base contrast and end-to-end comparison were not available in the inspected text extraction; no uncertainty values are asserted here.
Additional reasoning budget did not improve performance only in the tested models and settings.
summary: The September 22 preprint introduces Taste-Bench, 502 decision-fork questions mined from software-engineering and AI-research agent trajectories. Models choose between two directions before seeing later outcomes; a question counts correct only when the choice is correct in both candidate orders, making chance accuracy 25%. The authors report GPT-5.6 Sol at 59.7% average accuracy, falling to 21.0% across models when decisive evidence appears only after substantial later work. On held-out engineering questions from unseen tasks, a distilled Qwen3.6-27B student scores 47.9% versus 30.0% for its base model. In a separate 41-task SWE-bench Pro experiment, a fixed executor succeeds on 14.6% with no advice and 33.7% with student advice; correct advice reaches 39.0%. These author-reported findings are not independent reproductions.

technical.claimed_result: 502 benchmark questions; GPT-5.6 Sol 59.7% strict average accuracy; average model accuracy falls from 62.3% to 21.0% from in-prefix to more-work horizons. Held-out student/base accuracy is 47.9%/30.0%. On 41 held-out SWE-bench Pro tasks, no-advice/student-advice/correct-advice executor success is 14.6%/33.7%/39.0%.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected full v1 preprint specifies benchmark construction, two-order protocol, human label checks, task-disjoint training and a same-task no-advice comparator. the research desk did not audit the code/data or reproduce the results; numeric outcomes remain author-reported.
technical.mechanism: Trajectory-derived decision forks; two-order evaluation; task-disjoint reasoning distillation into Qwen3.6-27B; student advice is inserted into a separate fixed SWE-bench Pro executor.
technical.regime: 502 questions mined from 2,677 SWE-bench Pro agent rollouts and 1,132 runs on 47 AI R&D tasks. The engineering split has 390 questions and two task-disjoint folds. End-to-end comparison uses 41 held-out SWE-bench Pro tasks, with advice available from earlier trajectories. Paper reports a sample of 100 human-reviewed questions, with 170/172 explicit A/B judgments agreeing with labels.
technical.strongest_baseline: Taste-Bench: GPT-5.5 at 59.5% and GPT-5.6 Sol at 59.7% under the strict two-order metric. Held-out transfer: the same frozen Qwen3.6-27B base model at 30.0%. End-to-end: same fixed executor and 41 tasks at 14.6% without advice and 39.0% with oracle/correct advice.

title: Taste-Bench measures long-horizon decision choices and reports gains from distillation
why_it_matters: End-to-end task success does not reveal whether an agent chose a useful direction before delayed consequences appeared. Taste-Bench makes that judgment observable using recorded trajectory forks and reports that additional reasoning did not improve accuracy in the tested settings. Its paired no-advice comparison also bounds an end-to-end improvement from distilled advice on 41 held-out tasks, while synthetic fork mining, small task scope and lack of independent replication limit generalization.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the authors’ controlled task-lifecycle testbed, receipt-backed directives and enforcement generally improve strict episode success over a raw transcript or displayed checklist, with results depending on model, reasoning regime, task state and matcher accuracy.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On the tau-squared-bench airline case, the authors report Qwen3-235B pass at one rising from 0.39 to 0.54 with the enforcement gate; on PM-Bench, showing the record matched or beat gates in some configurations, while matcher-based enforcement reduced Qwen3.6-35B score below raw transcript.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not establish that enforcement improves general deployed-agent reliability; its own results show losses when state or matcher judgments are wrong or when task success depends on semantic cue recognition.

evidence_gaps.description: The authors say the generator, scorer, implementations, harness and logs will be released, but the inspected paper page provides no public artifact URL; the paired results have not been independently reproduced.
External transfer is limited to one airline-policy setting in tau-squared-bench and one released week in PM-Bench; the primary episodes come from one generator in two domains.
The gate depends on correctness of compiled state and request-to-step matching, and refusal escalation is not evaluated.

importance_rationale: If replicated in receipt-backed assigned workflows, this result changes agent-control architecture choices by separating what task state is shown, directs and enforces. It is notable for reliability engineering, but results are author-reported, domain-conditional and can reverse when matcher or state judgments are wrong.
limitations: Results are author-reported; the paper promises a future artifact release, but no public repository URL was found on the inspected page, so code was not run and experiments were not independently reproduced.
Episodes come from one generator in two domains; some closed-model cells have only 32 episodes, and one Qwen3.6-35B thinking row is partial and excluded from claims.
The tau-squared-bench case covers one airline domain with an internal user simulator; PM-Bench uses one released week.
Tool-harness tools never fail. Budgets, expiry, conflicting obligations and multi-agent or multi-session state are out of scope.
Held-out phrasing and ambiguity tests are limited; directives and tool results are plain user-role strings, so spoofing was not tested.
The enforcement matcher can confidently misroute a turn, while incorrect compiled state can refuse valid work; no refusal escalation path is evaluated.
summary: The 2026-09-22 preprint compares how an LLM agent handles assigned-work state when it is left in the transcript, displayed as a checklist, turned into per-turn directives or enforced by a gate that rejects state-violating actions. The authors report that receipt-backed directives and enforcement raise strict task-lifecycle success in controlled episodes, with gains varying by model and reasoning regime. In one tau-squared-bench airline case, enforcement raises Qwen3-235B pass at one from 0.39 to 0.54; on PM-Bench, showing the record can match or outperform gates, while matcher-based enforcement hurts a smaller model on semantic cue tasks. These are author-reported, bounded results: enforcement depends on correct compiled state and request matching, and the study does not establish general deployed-agent reliability.

technical.claimed_result: Controlled tests report that external task-state directives and enforcement improve success when failures are decidable from receipt-backed state; the advantage can shrink with per-turn reasoning, disappear when violations are rare, and reverse when correct action depends on semantic cue judgment or matcher accuracy.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected arXiv paper reports paired episode results across three models and two domains, including an external-tool harness and tau-squared-bench airline and PM-Bench case studies. The reported outcomes were not independently reproduced in this review.
technical.mechanism: An external state machine is compiled from the user brief and advanced only by execution receipts. The same owned state is displayed, translated into a directive, or enforced at the action boundary, allowing comparison of state visibility, instruction and refusal.
technical.regime: One program-generated task-lifecycle testbed with two domains, three models and two reasoning regimes; additional evidence from one tau-squared-bench airline policy setting and one PM-Bench released week. Some closed-model cells contain 32 episodes; the Qwen3.6-35B thinking row is partial and excluded from claims.
technical.reproducibility: The paper says its generator, scorer, arm implementations, harness and logs will be released; no repository or artifact URL appears on the inspected arXiv page. The paper and appendices were read, but code was not run and results were not independently reproduced.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paired raw-transcript and exact-checklist arms under the same task, model and episode conditions; the paper also includes a self-written ledger arm. Results vary across domains: the PM-Bench case does not support a general enforcement advantage.

title: Receipt-backed task state improves agent workflow reliability in bounded tests, with matcher-dependent failures
why_it_matters: Agents handling multi-step work must distinguish completed, blocked, cancelled and repeatable actions. This paper supplies controlled evidence that moving task state from prose into receipt-backed directives or enforcement can help in some regimes, while making the matcher and state compiler new failure points. The result informs architecture choices, but it is not evidence of a general deployed-agent benefit.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED

claims.text: The notice directs local cyber and veterans-affairs authorities and military units to coordinate with platforms, strengthen content review and remove material within the listed categories.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The notice does not establish implementation fidelity, enforcement counts, platform-level technical measures, reduced prevalence of AI-generated fabrications or downstream public effects.

organizations: Ministry of Veterans Affairs of the People's Republic of China

summary: A Chinese-language notice dated October 12 and published by the Cyberspace Administration of China on October 15 announces a two-month, multi-agency campaign against improper marketing and sensationalized military-related content online. The ten listed categories include AI-generated fake military dramas, stories and videos. technical.claimed_result: Authorities state that the campaign will tighten platform responsibility, remove specified misleading or improper military-related content and publicize representative cases. No results are reported in this announcement.
technical.demonstrated_result: The official Chinese notice documents the campaign's stated dates, participating bodies, ten target categories and requested platform cleanup. This confirms the published policy text, not its implementation or effect.
technical.mechanism: A two-month campaign coordinates cyber-administration and veterans-affairs agencies with military political-work and political-legal bodies; authorities are directed to coordinate with platforms, strengthen review and remove specified military-related marketing and sensationalized content, including a listed category of AI-generated fabrications.
technical.regime: A two-month campaign announced in October 2026 by national Chinese cyber-administration, veterans-affairs and military bodies, with implementation assigned through local authorities and online platforms. The notice includes ten categories and identifies AI-generated fake military stories, dramas and videos in one category.
technical.reproducibility: The policy document is publicly accessible in Chinese. Its implementation cannot be independently assessed from this notice; no technical standards, platform audit protocol or outcome data are supplied.

title: China's CAC announces a two-month campaign against misleading military content, including AI-generated fabrications
why_it_matters: The notice explicitly includes AI-generated military fabrications in a cross-agency content-enforcement campaign, making it a concrete policy signal about synthetic-media governance. claims.label: CLAIMED

No detection precision/recall, verified remediation rate, or baseline/follow-up exposure measurement is provided.

summary: On September 22, 2026, Palo Alto Networks announced Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense as a worldwide annual-subscription service. The company describes a full-estate baseline scan followed by recurring testing as customer environments change, using a proprietary harness that routes work among gated frontier and open-weight models, threat intelligence and offensive-security staff. It says the service validates attack paths across applications, APIs, cloud infrastructure, repositories and network assets, then prioritizes remediation. The release reports customer findings but supplies no assessment denominator, independent validation or measured remediation outcome; the announcement supports product availability and described design, not service efficacy.

technical.claimed_result: Palo Alto Networks says the service combines continuous testing, multi-model routing, exploit-path validation and remediation guidance, and reports findings from more than 100 customer engagements. The announcement provides no independent detection-accuracy or remediation measure.
technical.demonstrated_result: The company published a dated announcement describing the service and stating that it is available worldwide by annual subscription. This verifies the public announcement and its stated offer, not independent service operation or effectiveness.
technical.mechanism: Run a full-estate baseline scan and recurring tests as customer environments change; route work through a proprietary multi-model harness using gated frontier and open-weight models, threat intelligence and offensive-security staff; validate end-to-end attack paths and provide prioritized remediation recommendations.
technical.regime: Announced Unit 42 enterprise service, available worldwide on annual subscription with model options. The release reports six months of in-house testing and more than 100 customer engagements but does not provide cohort details, an independent audit or customer-level follow-up outcomes.
technical.reproducibility: The announcement describes the service architecture at a high level. Its proprietary harness, data, customer assessments and validation protocol are not publicly supplied, so the efficacy claims cannot be reproduced from this source.
technical.strongest_baseline: The release contrasts continuous testing with point-in-time exposure analysis, but gives no matched comparison of detection coverage, remediation speed or cost under the two approaches.

title: Palo Alto announces continuous frontier-model offensive security service with unverified efficacy
why_it_matters: The offering is a concrete commercialization path for frontier models in recurring defensive testing: it links continuous scanning, model selection, exploit-path validation and remediation guidance. That is relevant to how enterprises may operationalize advanced cyber models. The source is the vendor's announcement; it does not show that the service finds more valid exposures or reduces customer risk.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: A public Apache-2.0 repository describes relore, which indexes issue and pull-request history with author/trust metadata and serves current-code search against a working clone.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Project-authored, model-judged retrieval results report Recall@10 for a Transformers sample of 48 failure queries rising from 0.938 to 1.000 with query expansion, and 40 precedent queries rising from 0.375 to 0.475; the same report identifies contamination in pooled rationale results and supplies leak-free rationale slices of 7 and 9 examples.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The repository evaluation does not establish a general reduction in duplicate work, improved patch success, or end-to-end coding-agent productivity across repositories.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In one reported Transformers case, relore found two existing fix threads and the agent avoided writing another patch; a separate author-reported code-browsing comparison says one file overview used roughly 5% of the tokens needed to read the whole file.

evidence_gaps.description: The retrieval benchmark and the single reported field case have not been independently reproduced or audited.
The reported retrieval metrics do not measure reduced duplicate work, patch success or end-to-end agent task outcomes.
The leak-free rationale slices are small (7 and 9 examples), and the larger pooled rationale slice includes same-thread answer leakage.

importance_rationale: If the reported retrieval behavior holds, repository history indexed by authorship, trust tier and code location could change how coding agents recover design decisions and in-flight work. Its current evidence is a project-authored benchmark on limited, model-judged slices and does not establish end-to-end task improvement.
limitations: The reported benchmark is project-authored and model-judged; no independent reproduction or human-label audit was performed.
The Transformers benchmark uses 48 failure, 40 precedent and 51 pooled rationale queries; leak-free rationale subsets contain only 7 and 9 examples.
The pooled rationale result is contaminated because a reviewer finding can appear in the same thread as the answer; the repository separates leak-free subsets and notes the limitation.
The project reports one field case in which an agent avoided a duplicate patch and one token-use comparison, not a controlled measurement of repeated task success or general agent productivity.
The index is per repository and may lag later GitHub changes by its polling interval; cross-repository search and second-fresh answers are outside its design.
summary: A September 21, 2026 Hugging Face community article and the public relore repository describe a tool that indexes issue and pull-request history with author and trust metadata, then joins that history to current-code search in a maintained clone. Its project-authored, model-judged retrieval evaluation reports Recall@10 rising from 0.938 to 1.000 for 48 Transformers failure queries after query expansion, and from 0.375 to 0.475 for 40 precedent queries. The larger pooled rationale result is contaminated by same-thread answer leakage; the leak-free rationale slices are only 7 and 9 examples. In one author-reported Transformers case, relore found two existing fix threads and the agent avoided writing another patch; a code-browsing overview reportedly used about 5% of the tokens needed to read a whole file. These results support bounded accounts of retrieval and one field case, not a general reduction in duplicate work, better patches or higher coding-agent productivity.

technical.claimed_result: The repository reports improved Recall@10 from query expansion in limited model-judged retrieval samples: Transformers failure queries (48 examples) rise from 0.938 to 1.000 and precedent queries (40 examples) from 0.375 to 0.475. The report flags pooled rationale leakage and gives separate leak-free rationale samples of 7 and 9. In one reported field case, `inflight` found two existing fix threads and avoided a third patch; an author-reported code overview used roughly 5% of whole-file tokens.
technical.demonstrated_result: The public repository and Apache-2.0 license are accessible; README and evaluation docs describe the tool and benchmark. The measurements are project-reported, not independently reproduced. The Hugging Face article reports one Transformers case and the token comparison; these are author-reported observations, not controlled general-effect measurements.
technical.mechanism: Index historical issue/PR discussion at comment level with authorship and trust tier; extract files, symbols, tests and commit signals; serve structured queries alongside code search against a maintained repository clone.
technical.regime: One Transformers repository history benchmark with 48 failure queries, 40 precedent queries and 51 pooled rationale queries, plus small leak-free rationale slices from Transformers (7) and bot-review repositories (9). Labels are model-judged. The project also describes one author-reported case with six agents investigating the same Transformers bug. The field report describes one Transformers issue; it is not a repeated-task benchmark.
technical.reproducibility: The public repository includes code and evaluation documentation. The Hugging Face article reports one field case. The README, evaluation docs and article were inspected, but code and benchmark results were not independently reproduced.
technical.strongest_baseline: The project compares relore retrieval with GitHub search and grep on the same query windows. Results vary by query type; rationale outcomes are sensitive to answer leakage, and the leak-free subsets are small.

title: Relore combines repository decision history with current-code search; reported retrieval gains remain narrow
why_it_matters: Coding agents can repeat work when they miss an in-flight change or the rationale behind existing code. Relore combines historical discussion, authorship and trust metadata with current-code search, and reports retrieval gains on limited benchmark slices. The evaluation also exposes same-thread leakage and small leak-free samples; it does not establish better patches or general productivity.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors introduce Mental Health Quality Rubrics, developed with PhD-level psychologists, and MindSim, a longitudinal synthetic-patient harness with memory updated between interactions. They evaluate 18 proprietary and open-weight counsellor models using 50 synthetic patient profiles.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that guidance-calibration issues—over-exploring, under-guiding and giving bad advice—account for 60–88% of each counsellor model’s rubric score. Under-guiding is flagged in 12% of replies in the first two turns and about 70% from turn 9 onward. Scores are produced by a single GPT-6.1 Sol judge.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Patient-simulator realism was assessed using 180 excerpts comprising 666 turns; annotator agreement was Krippendorff’s alpha 0.58. The paper also compares surface features with 1,584 sessions from 886 people, which are not released and are reported only in aggregate.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The study does not establish clinical effectiveness, patient safety, real-world prevalence of harmful responses, or that its synthetic-patient scores predict outcomes in care settings.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent replication or alternative-judge evaluation of the 18-model benchmark findings was performed.
The simulator is synthetic and realism ratings show moderate inter-annotator agreement; alignment with diverse patient populations and longitudinal care remains uncertain.
The benchmark does not measure clinical effectiveness, patient outcomes or real-world rates of harmful guidance.

importance_rationale: If the evaluation captures a meaningful deployment weakness, its guidance-calibration findings could change how high-stakes mental-health support systems are assessed. Importance reflects potential consequence in this domain; the benchmark does not establish patient outcomes or real-world error prevalence.
limitations: All model findings are benchmark results reported by the paper authors; no independent replication was performed.
The main evaluation uses synthetic patient profiles generated with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and a single GPT-6.1 Sol judge; GPT-family results may be affected by same-family judge preference.
Human realism ratings cover 180 excerpts and 666 turns, with Krippendorff alpha 0.58; this is moderate agreement, not proof that simulated patients represent patients in care.
The real-user reference consists of 1,584 anonymized sessions from 886 people, used in aggregate and not released. It does not provide outcome labels for counsellor effectiveness or harm.
