With Gemini 3.1 Pro, full GRA scores 47.6 versus 50.8 for GRA tools without that guidance, so the orchestration gain is model-dependent.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that specialized geospatial skills and tools account for the largest measured gains: with Gemini 3.8 Flash, GeoExpertQueries rises from 3.3 with basic tools to 52.2 with GRA tools before full orchestration; GRA scores 85.9 on GeoKTools and 86.4 on the modified 44-question CBGB evaluation. UnivEARTH is saturated in this setup: even a standalone model without Earth Engine access scores 86.9–93.6, and the authors say systems can answer from source text without doing the intended geospatial analysis.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports GeoExpertQueries with 101 authored prompts (76 held out) and GeoKTools with 305 queries (220 held out), and says it releases the development splits and evaluation materials. The official benchmark repository at commit c21a6d9 identifies itself as v1.0.0 and reports 25/76 for GeoExpertQueries but 85/210 for GeoKTools (295 total), leaving a 10-query discrepancy with the paper’s 85/220 split.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: This review did not independently reproduce the author-reported results. The paper evaluates Gemini models only; excludes tasks that require unavailable/proprietary data; relies on an LLM autorater for open-ended tasks; modifies CBGB and finds UnivEARTH saturated; and states that its benchmark/tool design favors configurations using GRA tools. Reported inference costs exclude external data and Earth Engine services.

claims.label: DISPUTED
claims.text: The paper’s GeoKTools test split (220) conflicts with the official v1.0.0 repository README and provenance document (210); the repository’s 85 development plus 210 held-out cases total 295, not the paper’s 305. The cause is unresolved. GeoExpertQueries counts agree at 25 development plus 76 held out.

contradictory_evidence: The paper reports 305 GeoKTools queries, including a 220-query test split (arXiv:2610.15750v1, §4.2/Table 2 and §5.3/Table 6); the official v1.0.0 repository README and provenance at commit c21a6d9 state 85 development plus 210 held-out cases (295 total). The cause of this 10-query difference is unresolved; the current official repository is not silently treated as correcting the paper.

evidence_gaps.description: Independent reproduction of the four-configuration results on the released benchmark development materials and an independently held-out geospatial task set.
Whether the agent’s measured benchmark performance transfers to real partner workflows and produces useful, decision-relevant outcomes at known data and service costs.

How much of the reported advantage comes from Google-exclusive models and data versus reusable geospatial tooling and orchestration, and whether the model-dependent orchestration effect persists outside this setup.
The official GeoKTools v1.0.0 repository lists 210 held-out test queries while the arXiv report lists 220; the reported results’ exact test split cannot be reconstructed from the public repository.

importance_rationale: If the reported matched-model comparisons generalize, they show when specialized geospatial tools and planning materially improve an applied agent system and provide reusable evaluation resources. The impact is meaningful for geospatial AI, but bounded to one provider’s stack and a specialized domain; confidence is not part of this score.
limitations: All benchmark outcomes are reported by the paper’s authors; no independent reproduction was performed.
Only two Gemini model versions are evaluated; transfer to other model families is unknown.

Upfront planning/execution guidance is model-dependent: the reported GeoExpertQueries gain is 10.5 points for Gemini 3.8 Flash, while full GRA is 3.2 points below the GRA-tools configuration for Gemini 3.1 Pro.
GeoExpertQueries uses an LLM autorater and expert-crafted workflows; absolute scores depend on workflow and judge validity.
GeoKTools is designed around tool operations GRA supports and therefore favors tool-using configurations.
The modified 44-question CBGB protocol excludes one infeasible item and updates four data-sensitive reference answers; scores are not directly comparable to the original benchmark.
UnivEARTH is saturated in this setup: a standalone model scores highly without performing the intended analysis.
Estimated token inference costs exclude external data and compute services such as Earth Engine; partner testing does not quantify deployment outcomes.

A material count discrepancy remains between the paper and its official benchmark release: GeoKTools is 85 development + 220 held-out (305 total) in the paper, but 85 + 210 (295 total) in the v1.0.0 repository README/provenance. Held-out queries are private, so this review could not resolve which test split produced the reported numbers.
summary: Google Research’s Oct 14 announcement expands experimental access to its Geospatial Reasoning agent and links a technical report that compares four configurations around Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 3.8 Flash. In the paper’s 76 held-out open-ended GeoExpertQueries, GRA with Gemini 3.8 Flash scores 62.7/100, compared with 52.2 for the same model plus GRA’s geospatial tools without full planning and execution guidance, and 3.3 with basic tools. The full orchestration configuration does not improve the same test with Gemini 3.1 Pro (47.6 versus 50.8), making the added benefit model-dependent. The paper reports the largest gains from the specialized geospatial tool suite, introduces two benchmarks and releases their development splits. A material count mismatch remains: the paper reports 220 held-out GeoKTools queries, while the official v1.0.0 repository lists 210. These are author-reported results from one provider’s Gemini stack, not independent replications or field-deployment outcomes.

technical.claimed_result: On the authors’ 76-test GeoExpertQueries split, Gemini 3.8 Flash scores 62.7/100 in full GRA, 52.2 with the same GRA tool suite absent full planning/execution guidance, and 3.3 with basic tools. With Gemini 3.1 Pro, full GRA scores 47.6 versus 50.8 for the GRA-tools configuration. In the three-run mean evaluations, full GRA also scores 85.9 on GeoKTools and 86.4 on modified CBGB with Gemini 3.8 Flash. All metrics and conclusions are paper-reported.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary preprint documents a four-configuration, two-model evaluation across four test benchmarks, the construction of two new benchmark sets, and the authors’ report that development splits were publicly released. This review did not rerun the study or audit the benchmark repository contents.
technical.mechanism: GRA combines Gemini with domain-specific geospatial foundation models, datasets and tools. It exposes modular skills on demand, keeps large intermediate data in an external workspace, plans a multi-step analysis before tool use, and then executes the plan with documented fallbacks and data attribution. The paper’s ablations compare a standalone model, the same model with basic search/maps/code tools, the same model with GRA skills but without upfront planning/execution guidance, and full GRA.
technical.regime: Authors report three-run mean and standard deviation on test sets: 76 GeoExpertQueries held-out open-ended workflows, 220 GeoKTools templated queries, a modified 44-question CBGB subset, and 140 UnivEARTH questions, using Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 3.8 Flash. The paper reports that two new benchmarks’ development splits and evaluation materials were released. Its GeoKTools split is 85/220 (305 total), while the official v1.0.0 repository states 85/210 (295 total); the cause is unresolved. Evaluated performance is not independent replication or deployment evidence.
technical.reproducibility: No independent reproduction or code execution was performed. The official repository contains development materials and scoring runners, while the held-out test sets are withheld. Its v1.0.0 README/provenance reports 210 held-out GeoKTools cases, conflicting with 220 in the paper; this review did not access hidden test data or determine which split generated the published scores.
technical.strongest_baseline: For the added value of full orchestration, the closest matched baseline is the same Gemini model with the GRA geospatial skills/tools but without upfront planning and execution guidance. For the contribution of domain tooling, compare full GRA against the same-backbone basic-tools configuration; that comparison bundles access to unique Google models/data with tool use and is not a general-model-only effect.

title: Google reports controlled evaluation gains from Earth AI geospatial reasoning agent and expands experimental access
why_it_matters: The report tests an important agent-design question with matched backbone models: whether a domain-specific tool layer and a planning/execution harness add more than a general model and basic tools. Its results point to specialized data/tools as the largest contribution, while showing that added orchestration can help one model and slightly hurt another. The benchmarks also expose saturation in a public geospatial test. The released GeoKTools test count also conflicts with the report by 10 queries, limiting exact reconstruction of that result. These findings are relevant to applied agent evaluation, but do not yet establish transfer beyond Google’s geospatial stack or real-world partner workflows.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Vision-RL2 uses region-level reinforcement learning to train a lightweight region proposal predictor with a frozen MLLM reader, then applies sparse visual encoding to emphasize selected evidence.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report gains over base models across six fine-grained benchmarks and four backbones; under a training-aligned protocol, Qwen3.5-4B at a 576-token source limit scores 71.1 average versus 66.6 for SD-RPN, while matching SD-RPN at 4,096 tokens with 4.2× fewer visual tokens.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The paper reports lower MME-RealWorld scores than full-fine-tuning references for the smaller Qwen3.5 configurations, and its main benchmark table and training-aligned efficiency protocol are not directly comparable.

evidence_gaps.description: The linked training code, region predictor, data selection and released weights were not inspected.
No independent replication of the six-benchmark accuracy and token/latency trade-offs was located in this review.
The paper does not establish cost, latency or throughput under a production multimodal serving stack.

importance_rationale: If replicated, learning which coherent image regions deserve resolution could improve fine-grained multimodal perception while reducing visual-token and latency costs. Results span four backbones and several benchmarks, but the efficiency protocol is training-aligned and the reported gains remain author-run measurements with task-specific trade-offs.
limitations: All results are author-reported; no independent reproduction was performed in this activation.
The main 16,384-token comparison uses multiple scoring sources and includes rows quoted from other papers; the efficiency protocol is separate and explicitly not comparable with the main table.
The training-aligned efficiency study uses short-answer prompts, rule-based scoring and an RTX A6000; this does not establish production serving cost or broad deployment benefit.
Qwen3.5-4B and 9B results trail full fine-tuning references on MME-RealWorld splits, consistent with the frozen-reader design trade-off.
The claimed code link and training implementation were not audited.
summary: Vision-RL2 trains a small region proposal network with region-level reinforcement learning to identify evidence regions for a frozen multimodal reader, then encodes those regions sparsely. The authors report improved accuracy over base systems across six fine-grained benchmarks and four backbones. In a separate training-aligned protocol, the Qwen3.5-4B system at a 576-token source limit reports a six-benchmark average of 71.1, versus 66.6 for SD-RPN, and matches SD-RPN at a 4,096-token limit with 4.2 times fewer visual tokens. These remain paper-reported results; the evaluation protocols differ and performance trades off on some MME-RealWorld splits.

technical.claimed_result: Under the main 16,384 source-image-token protocol, the paper reports results across V* Bench, ZoomBench, HR-Bench 4K/8K and MME-RealWorld EN/CN. Under a separate training-aligned protocol, Qwen3.5-4B with region-level RL and sparse encoding scores 71.1 average at 576 source tokens; the authors report matching SD-RPN accuracy at the 4,096-token limit with 4.2× fewer visual tokens.
technical.compute_or_cost: The training-aligned protocol reports visual tokens and latency on one RTX A6000; deployment cost, energy and serving throughput were not established.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv HTML specifies the method, four backbone families, benchmark protocols and author-reported measurements. the research desk did not execute released code or reproduce the results.
technical.implementation_status: The method updates a small attached region predictor while keeping the MLLM reader frozen; code availability is claimed in the preprint but was not checked here.
technical.mechanism: A small predictor proposes coherent image regions. A frozen MLLM reader scores each region by how its removal changes answer likelihood; region-level reinforcement learning trains the predictor without region annotations or reasoning trajectories. Sparse encoding then spends the crop budget on selected evidence.
technical.novelty: Region-level reinforcement learning treats coherent visual regions as actions and scores them by changes in a frozen reader’s answer likelihood, separating evidence proposal from the reader’s reasoning.
technical.regime: Four backbones (Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4) across six fine-grained benchmarks. The main comparison uses a shared 16,384 source-image token limit and a mix of rule-based parsing and LLM judging. The training-aligned efficiency protocol uses a 576-token training limit, token-budget curves, short-answer prompts and rule-based scoring; its efficiency table is explicitly not comparable with the main table.
technical.reproducibility: The paper reports re-evaluation of some released model weights and links code, but this review did not inspect the repository or independently reproduce the experiment.
technical.strongest_baseline: For the training-aligned Qwen3.5-4B ablation, SD-RPN averages 66.6 and the full region-RL plus sparse-encoding system averages 71.1 at the same 576-token source limit. In the main table, the 9B result is compared with multiple published and re-evaluated references; not all rows use the same retraining procedure.

title: Vision-RL2 reports fine-grained visual accuracy gains with a small region predictor
why_it_matters: High-resolution visual reasoning can spend substantial compute on background pixels. Vision-RL2 treats coherent image regions as actions and trains a lightweight predictor to concentrate resolution on evidence while leaving the main reader frozen. The reported token-efficiency gains could matter for multimodal inference, but they come from specific benchmark protocols and do not establish deployment cost or broad visual reasoning improvements.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper describes D-Quant, which entropy-codes quantized KV values and uses a drift assignment to satisfy a fixed per-token storage budget while preserving regular layouts for parallel decoding.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at 2.26 bits per value, the authors report RULER average scores of 86.50 and 88.94, compared with BF16 scores of 87.31 and 89.69; at 128K context, D-Quant reports 70.92 and 74.65 versus strongest listed low-bit baselines of 57.14 and 66.15.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The paper evaluates two 8B models on RULER and English LongBench-E under its stated GPU/configuration setup; it does not establish production serving savings or results on other architectures.

evidence_gaps.description: The code, fused kernels, benchmark scripts and storage-accounting implementation were not inspected.
No independent reproduction of accuracy, memory use or throughput was performed.
The paper does not establish serving impact under production batch sizes, concurrency or different hardware.

importance_rationale: If the reported results generalize, fitting key-value cache state into roughly 2.26 bits per value while retaining near-BF16 long-context benchmark scores could materially reduce the memory burden of long-context inference. The evaluation is limited to two 8B models and author-run benchmarks, so deployment savings and broader model transfer remain unestablished.
limitations: All benchmark and implementation results are author-reported; this activation did not inspect code or independently reproduce them.
Evaluation covers Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, NVIDIA H20 GPUs, RULER and English LongBench-E; transfer to other model architectures and serving stacks is unknown.
Qwen3-8B results at 64K and 128K use static YaRN beyond its native 40K context, which degrades absolute performance even though baselines share the setting.
LongBench-E differences among compressed methods are smaller than the RULER differences.
The paper’s storage result does not alone establish production throughput, concurrency, energy or monetary savings.
summary: The paper proposes D-Quant, which entropy-codes KV-cache values and adjusts a small subset of quantized symbols to keep each token stream within a fixed-size container. On Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, the authors report 2.26 bits per value and RULER averages close to BF16 across 4K–128K contexts; at 128K, reported scores exceed the strongest listed low-bit baselines. The measurements are paper-reported and use NVIDIA H20 GPUs; the research desk did not run the implementation.

technical.claimed_result: For Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, D-Quant at 2.26 bits per value reports RULER averages of 86.50 and 88.94 versus BF16 87.31 and 89.69. At 128K the respective scores are 70.92 and 74.65, versus the strongest listed low-bit baselines at 57.14 and 66.15. LongBench-E differences among compressed methods are smaller.
technical.compute_or_cost: Storage is reported at 2.26 bits per value for the main setting, with GPU throughput/cost not normalized in this review.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv HTML specifies the algorithm and reports results on two models, RULER and English LongBench-E. No code or independent result was executed in this review.
technical.implementation_status: The paper describes CUDA kernel design and reports H20 experiments; this review did not inspect a released implementation or measure a production serving stack.
technical.mechanism: After rotation and normalization, D-Quant entropy-codes quantized KV values using a shared analytic probability model. A length-constrained drift assignment shifts selected values toward lower-cost symbols to fit fixed-size token containers; fused token-oriented kernels decode each stream once and feed the values into attention.
technical.novelty: The method combines entropy-coded variable information with a drift constraint that restores fixed-size per-token storage and regular access for fused attention kernels.
technical.regime: Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; RULER at six context lengths from 4K to 128K and English LongBench-E; 100 RULER samples per task and length. Evaluations use greedy decoding and NVIDIA H20 96GB GPUs. Qwen3-8B uses static YaRN at 64K and 128K. The main D-Quant setting averages 2.26 bits per value with a 128-token BF16 residual window.
technical.reproducibility: The paper reports experiments and names official baselines, but the repository, kernel code and exact run artifacts were not independently inspected or executed.
technical.strongest_baseline: At 128K on RULER, OScaR is the strongest listed quantized baseline: 57.14 for Qwen3-8B and 66.15 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, compared with D-Quant 70.92 and 74.65. The full-precision BF16 reference scores 72.13 and 76.44.

title: D-Quant reports near-BF16 long-context accuracy with about 2.26 bits per KV value
why_it_matters: KV-cache memory can limit the context length and concurrency available for serving large models. D-Quant reports a way to use entropy coding with regular fixed-stride access patterns, and near-BF16 RULER scores at about 2.26 bits per value on two 8B models. If reproduced in real serving stacks, this could improve the memory side of long-context inference, but the paper does not by itself establish production throughput, cost or transfer to other architectures.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The v3 preprint describes EvoHarnessBench, a controlled benchmark of externally expanding tool, skill, and specialist-agent harnesses, built from 17 multi-stage streams and 802 unique tasks drawn from verifier-based benchmarks.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that exposing agents to cumulative expanding harnesses can lower performance on previously solved tasks even when the model and prompt stay fixed; the reported drops differ by tools, skills and specialist agents (12.1%, 13.8% and 46.4%, respectively).

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across the paper's tested self-evolving methods and benchmark settings, gains are inconsistent, and retaining earlier competence can conflict with adapting to newly introduced capabilities.

evidence_gaps.description: The paper links benchmark materials, but the benchmark repository, task data, harness implementations and run configuration were not inspected in this review.
The reported harness-expansion effects and adaptation comparisons have not been independently reproduced.
The paper evaluates constructed streams from two verifier-based benchmark sources; real production harness growth and broader task distributions are not measured.

importance_rationale: If the reported effect generalizes, adding tools, reusable skills or specialist agents can reduce previously available agent competence and alter how systems should be evaluated and deployed. The result is important across agent research, but its evidence remains a paper-reported benchmark built from two task sources, so it does not establish production-scale impact.
limitations: All performance figures are author-reported; no independent reproduction was performed in this activation.
The deployment evaluation holds model and prompt fixed while expanding the exposed harness; it does not establish that every real system will regress as tools or agents are added.
The 17 streams and 802 unique tasks are constructed from EnterpriseOps-Gym and Agents' Last Exam; they are not a representative sample of production workloads.
Skill-to-task association uses heuristic matching between skill content and verifier-checked outcomes, which the authors state may not identify necessary or sufficient skills.
Some tables compare system configurations with distinct underlying harnesses; the authors omit Claude Code from the main controlled comparison and report it separately.
organizations: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
summary: The v3 preprint introduces EvoHarnessBench, which tests how agent performance changes as the externally supplied pool of tools, reusable skills or specialist agents expands. Its 17 constructed streams contain 802 unique tasks derived from two verifier-based agent benchmarks. The authors report that harness expansion alone can reduce performance on previously solved tasks, with reported declines varying across the tool, skill and agent tracks; adaptation gains are also inconsistent and retention can conflict with learning new capabilities. These are paper-reported benchmark results, not independent or production measurements.

technical.claimed_result: In the deployment setting, the paper reports harness-induced performance drops of 12.1% for expanding tools, 13.8% for skills and 46.4% for specialist agents. The paper also reports inconsistent self-evolving adaptation across stages and environments. These measurements are author-reported.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports operating time and token metrics for benchmark runs, but this review did not normalize them into comparable monetary or energy costs.
technical.demonstrated_result: The v3 preprint specifies a benchmark with 17 multi-stage streams and 802 unique tasks instantiated across 1,510 axis-specific examples, 520 tools, 42 reference skills and 62 specialist agents. the research desk did not inspect or execute the linked benchmark artifact.
technical.implementation_status: A project page is linked from the arXiv HTML; the benchmark repository and its runnable artifacts were not inspected in this activation.
technical.mechanism: The benchmark derives cumulative harness stages from verifier-based tasks, progressively exposing additional tools, skills or specialist agents while retaining previously available capabilities. A deployment evaluation isolates the effect of broader exposure; a separate self-evolving setting tests persistent adaptation across stages.
technical.novelty: The study makes externally supplied harness growth itself a controlled source of non-stationarity, separate from changing task streams or capabilities learned by the agent.
technical.regime: The paper constructs 17 streams with three to six stages from EnterpriseOps-Gym and Agents' Last Exam. Controlled tool/skill comparisons use GPT-5-based systems; other multi-agent and adaptation configurations are reported by axis. Skill matching is heuristic. Claude Code is reported separately because it has a different underlying model and harness.
technical.reproducibility: The arXiv v3 HTML gives construction and evaluation details and links a project page, but artifacts were not audited and no independent run was performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: The task-specific harness reference exposes only capabilities annotated as required for each task, compared with the full cumulative harness in deployment evaluation. This is a controlled benchmark reference, not a production baseline.

title: EvoHarnessBench reports competence losses as agent tool, skill and specialist pools expand
why_it_matters: Agent systems increasingly gain tools, reusable procedures and specialist agents over time. This paper tests that growth as an evaluation variable and reports that broader harnesses can impair performance on earlier tasks, even when the underlying model and prompt remain fixed. The result motivates tracking retention separately from adaptation, while remaining limited to author-run benchmark streams rather than measured production systems.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: KATok learns per-token keep/drop decisions jointly with video latents and uses a cascaded mask prior to predict sparse token positions for downstream flow-matching generation.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On approximately 5,000 Panda-70M validation clips, the authors report 366.24 average 64-channel tokens, 31.24 PSNR and 5.12 rFVD at 256²×16; at 512²×32 they report 1,554.24 tokens, 33.23 PSNR and 6.40 rFVD. Listed baselines use 8 channels, and the paper's compression metric accounts for channel count.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For UCF-101 video generation using the same 686.29M-parameter SiT-XL backbone, the authors report gFVD 61.53 for cascaded mask-prior conditioning versus 100.00 for Omni-VAE; 5,000 generated samples are used for gFVD reporting.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not establish independently reproduced performance, hardware-normalized deployment savings, or general video-generation gains outside its tested datasets and model setup.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the Panda-70M reconstruction or UCF-101 generation tables was inspected.
The paper reports token counts and channel-aware compression but does not establish comparative end-to-end memory, latency or energy savings on deployed systems.
High-frequency detail combined with large motion is an identified reconstruction failure regime, and the official repository says weights remain under internal review.

importance_rationale: If replicated in the tested video regimes, content-adaptive latent allocation could change tokenizer and generator design by reducing redundant video representation while preserving or improving reported quality. The result is bounded to author-run datasets and models, and channel-normalized compression is materially less than raw token-count ratios suggest.
limitations: All performance results are author-reported; the research desk did not run code or independently reproduce them.
KATok uses 64 latent channels while listed OmniTokenizer and ElasticTok baselines use 8; raw token-count reduction is not a channel-normalized compression ratio.

The paper reports its principal reconstruction result on about 5,000 Panda-70M validation clips and generation on SkyTimelapse, UCF-101 and Kinetics-600; this does not establish broad video-generation improvement.
The supplement identifies high-frequency detail with large motion as a failure case (about 19–20 PSNR on Panda-70M).
The official repository provides inference code but no training code, and states that weights are under internal review.
summary: Kakao's KATok paper reports a video VAE that learns per-token keep/drop masks and uses a cascaded mask prior to place sparse latents during generation. On about 5,000 Panda-70M validation clips, the authors report 366 average 64-channel tokens with 31.24 PSNR and 5.12 rFVD at 256²×16; at 512²×32 they report 1,554 tokens, 33.23 PSNR and 6.40 rFVD. For UCF-101 generation with the same SiT-XL backbone, cascaded position conditioning reports gFVD 61.53 versus 100.00 for Omni-VAE. The results are paper-reported; token counts alone overstate compression because KATok uses 64 latent channels versus 8 for the listed baselines.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report adaptive video tokenization with improved reconstruction metrics at fewer active tokens and sparse-position-aware generation that improves gFVD against an Omni-VAE tokenizer under the stated benchmarks.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv paper, project page and official repository establish the method, reported setups, metrics, public inference-code status and stated limitations. the research desk did not reproduce model performance.
technical.mechanism: A transformer VAE learns a Gumbel-Softmax keep/drop mask jointly with continuous latent tokens and applies the same mask to decoder attention. A cascaded generator first predicts an occupancy mask, then generates sparse latent content conditioned on selected positions; the joint content-position method is an ablation.
technical.regime: Paper-reported Panda-70M validation reconstruction at 256²×16 and 512²×32; downstream flow-matching generation with a 686.29M SiT-XL backbone at 256²×16 on SkyTimelapse, UCF-101 and Kinetics-600; gFVD from 5,000 generated samples. The main tokenizer is trained on Panda-70M.
technical.strongest_baseline: For reconstruction, ElasticTok-KL and OmniTokenizer-VAE in the same transformer continuous-token family; at 256²×16 KATok reports 366.24 tokens ×64 channels vs 3,845.56 ×8 (ElasticTok) and 5,120 ×8 (OmniTokenizer), with 31.24 PSNR/5.12 rFVD vs 30.52/12.37 and 28.10/7.84. For UCF-101 generation, same-backbone Omni-VAE reports gFVD 100.00 vs KATok cascaded 61.53; author-run comparison only.

title: Kakao reports content-adaptive video latents with sparse-position generation
why_it_matters: Video tokenizers usually spend a fixed latent grid on every clip. KATok tests a content-adaptive alternative and addresses the spatial-layout problem created by dropping tokens. If the reported results hold in independent matched runs, this could change tokenizer and generator design for video workloads. The evidence is limited to author-run benchmarks, and the channel-normalized compression ratio is smaller than the headline token-count reduction.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: DeltaSelect ranks tasks by the fifth-percentile Pearson correlation across 10,000 deterministic resamples, calibrates fractional verifier results to a common full-score scale, and greedily selects tasks within a configured budget. On the DeepSWE snapshot the authors report that 22 of 113 tasks reached a fifth-percentile correlation of at least 0.50.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In 13 eight-task evaluations of one gpt-5.6-luna low-reasoning Agent Layer skills/instructions case study, the authors report a final configuration with a 42.36% calibrated score at $1.75, compared with the initial custom bundle at 36.46% and $4.18. The analysis uses one endpoint run per task and transfers variance estimates from published mini-swe-agent runs.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For the same eight tasks and gpt-5.6-luna settings, paper-reported Codex-harness costs were 1.5 to 3.5 times the corresponding DeepSWE estimates; scores also differed. The paper cautions these comparisons establish a planning mismatch, not a causal estimate of the harness effect.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv paper links a public Agent Layer repository and DeltaSelect implementation page. The repository README identifies itself as an open-source coding-agent orchestration project; this review did not run its code.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent team reproduced the selector, case-study endpoints or reported costs in this review.
The selector was not compared with random, cheapest-first or median-correlation selection at equal cost; ranking and published-data example use the same DeepSWE snapshot.

The case study covers one model family, one custom harness and one skill/instruction bundle; endpoint uncertainty uses transferred published variance and some iterations changed multiple instructions.
The paper links public code, but no repository code or study artifacts were run or independently audited in this review.

importance_rationale: If validated across benchmarks and harnesses, an affordable fixed task set could make coding-agent workflow changes easier to compare repeatedly; this is one author-reported method and case study with untested selector alternatives and limited transfer evidence.
limitations: The task selector and calibration choices are not shown to outperform alternative selectors at matched cost; the paper names those comparisons as future work.
The published-data projection uses the same DeepSWE snapshot to construct and assess selection, so the evidence is in-sample.

The Agent Layer case study has one run per endpoint task, transfers variance from mini-swe-agent, and changes more than one instruction in several evaluations; it does not establish a causal effect of a single edit.
A small fixed task set may omit capabilities, magnify task-quality problems and induce specialization; it is not a broad benchmark or safety evaluation.
The repository was inspected at README level only; no code, data, or evaluation was executed in this review.
summary: A paper introduces DeltaSelect, which ranks tasks using resampled one-run correlations with full-benchmark scores, calibrates fractional verifier results, then selects tasks under a cost budget for repeated baseline-versus-candidate comparisons. In one author-reported Agent Layer case study, 13 eight-task evaluations led to a configuration with a 58.1% lower recorded cost and a higher calibrated score than the initial custom skills/instructions. The paper also finds substantial mismatch between published DeepSWE estimates and a Codex target harness. These are bounded paper-reported results; the implementation was not run in this review.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report 22 of 113 DeepSWE tasks with fifth-percentile correlation >=0.50. In a 13-evaluation, eight-task Agent Layer case study, reported recorded cost declined 58.1% ($4.18 to $1.75) while calibrated score rose from 36.46% to 42.36%. The study uses single-run endpoints and transferred variance estimates.
technical.compute_or_cost: Paper reports $27.86 total model cost across 13 case-study evaluations at the stated August 16, 2026 rates. Initial and adopted eight-task endpoints are $4.18 and $1.75 respectively. Costs from published mini-swe-agent estimates did not transfer directly: paper reports Codex costs 1.5–3.5 times higher for the same eight tasks and settings.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accessible arXiv paper and linked public repository README establish that the paper and a code repository are published. Reported benchmark and case-study values are author claims; this review did not execute or reproduce the implementation.
technical.mechanism: DeltaSelect resamples one trial per task and configuration to estimate each task's conservative correlation with full benchmark scores, maps task-level fractional verifier results to a common score using linear calibration, weights by calibration residuals, and scans a fixed reliability ranking under a dollar budget. The task set and scoring specification are then frozen for baseline-versus-candidate comparisons.
technical.novelty: The paper combines conservative task ranking from repeated trial resampling, per-task fractional-score calibration, cost-constrained allocation, and target-harness baseline validation for frequent within-system coding-agent comparisons. The paper cites prior benchmark reduction and active-testing methods and frames its contribution as their combination for this use case rather than a universal evaluator.
technical.regime: DeepSWE v1.1 snapshot: 22,586 source trials, 22,417 usable trials, 18 models, 50 model-effort configurations and 113 tasks. Method resamples one of four trials per complete task-configuration cell 10,000 times. Target-harness study uses eight selected tasks; Agent Layer case study uses 13 evaluations at gpt-5.6-luna low reasoning. No independent replication reviewed.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links a public Agent Layer repository and interactive DeltaSelect page, describes the DeepSWE data snapshot, method and study provenance, but the code and data were not run or audited here. Cheapest next action is a pinned reproduction and equal-cost selector comparison on a held-out benchmark.
technical.strongest_baseline: For the eight-task case study the paper compares initial and adopted Agent Layer skill/instruction configurations under the same stated model, reasoning level, tasks, calibration and weights. The adopted endpoint is $1.75 and 42.36% calibrated score versus $4.18 and 36.46% initially. Each endpoint has one run per task, and uncertainty is transferred from repeated mini-swe-agent data.

title: DeltaSelect paper reports a budgeted task subset for repeat coding-agent A/B tests
why_it_matters: If independently validated, fixed low-cost task subsets could support more frequent coding-agent workflow comparisons. The paper's own data show that task reliability varies and that scores and prices from one harness did not transfer to another. The selector's advantage over alternatives and its usefulness beyond one benchmark, model family and custom harness remain unknown.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Google DeepMind says it and Singapore’s GovTech fine-tuned a lightweight Gemma model on local scam conversations for on-device scam detection. The stated purpose is to help applications identify manipulative conversation patterns while keeping message processing on the user’s device; deployment within applications is described as phased and future-facing.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Google describes a two-stage design: an on-device lightweight classifier screens inbound messages, then a fine-tuned Gemma model analyzes a larger conversation snapshot for messages flagged as suspicious. The announced sources provide no quantitative accuracy, latency or energy measurements.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Google says fine-tuning occurred in GovTech’s managed cloud environment using anonymized datasets derived from scam reports and intelligence feeds, excluding private or personally identifiable information; the model was stress-tested with synthetic dialogues and local corpora. The reviewed announcement provides no dataset size, protocol or independent audit.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency published the Minister for Digital Development and Information’s 14 October speech stating that GovTech was collaborating with Google DeepMind to develop real-time AI scam detection on users’ devices while keeping messages on-device. This independently corroborates the collaboration and development status, not effectiveness or deployment.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Singapore GovTech’s AntiScam Pango Terms of Use, dated 9 September 2026, describe a separate experimental/beta mobile service that uses local AI models to assess messages from supported third-party messaging apps. The terms identify Authority-fine-tuned generative model weights quantized for on-device inference and a scam-classification model. They establish an earlier institutional on-device precedent, not effectiveness or a direct comparison with the newly announced Gemma collaboration.

evidence_gaps.description: No disclosed evaluation establishes detection accuracy, false-positive burden or robustness across scam categories and language variation.
The reviewed announcement links no model card, model weights, code or implementation specification that would identify model size, screening features or reproducible device requirements.
No supported app partner, public integration date or deployment evidence is stated; the announcement describes a carefully phased future rollout.
On-device feasibility and practical benefit are not measured in the reviewed material; battery, latency and effect on user losses are unknown.

The Google DeepMind/GovTech announcement does not state how its Gemma model relates to GovTech’s separately documented AntiScam Pango beta, which already uses on-device AI and an authority-tuned quantized generative model.

importance_rationale: If the described local, two-stage classifier is deployed effectively, it could offer a privacy-preserving scam-screening path for messaging platforms and inform government–provider deployment practice; its scope is currently localized and no measured performance or rollout is documented.
limitations: The central model and pipeline claims come from the developer and government partner; independent replication was not found in this bounded review.
The sources disclose no quantitative model accuracy, false-positive rate, robustness by scam type or language, model size, latency or battery use.
Application integration and rollout are described as future or phased; no live availability, adoption or reduced-loss outcome is established.
The claim that message processing remains on-device is based on the partners’ architectural description; this review did not inspect source code, app permissions or a privacy audit.

GovTech's AntiScam Pango terms dated 9 September 2026 already describe an experimental/beta service using on-device AI models, including authority-tuned generative weights quantized for local inference; the reviewed sources do not say whether the new Gemma model replaces, complements or is separate from Pango.
organizations: Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore)
summary: Google DeepMind says it and Singapore’s GovTech fine-tuned a Gemma-based scam detector intended to analyze conversations on-device, using a lightweight classifier followed by conversation-level analysis for flagged cases. Singapore’s cybersecurity minister separately confirmed the collaboration is in development. A pre-existing GovTech AntiScam Pango beta is already described in official terms as using on-device AI, including an authority-tuned generative model; the sources do not establish whether the new Gemma work integrates with Pango or improves its performance. Neither announcement supplies measured detection accuracy, device cost or reduced scam losses.

technical.claimed_result: Google DeepMind reports a fine-tuned Gemma-based local scam detector developed with Singapore GovTech, using anonymized scam-report/intelligence data and synthetic dialogue/local-corpus stress tests. No quantitative detection or efficiency result is reported in the reviewed post.
technical.compute_or_cost: No model size, inference cost, latency, memory or battery measurements are disclosed. The two-stage architecture is presented as a way to reserve the heavier conversation analysis for messages flagged by the lightweight screen.
technical.demonstrated_result: The two dated first-party publications establish that Google DeepMind and Singapore GovTech publicly described the collaboration and its development intent on 14 October 2026. They do not independently demonstrate efficacy or app deployment.
technical.mechanism: A two-stage on-device flow: a lightweight classifier screens inbound messages; a fine-tuned Gemma model analyzes a larger conversation snapshot for flagged cases. The stated aim is to detect manipulative scam patterns locally rather than inspect messages in a cloud service.
technical.novelty: The specific new development is Google DeepMind’s partnership with GovTech and the described Gemma-based, two-stage conversational scam pipeline. On-device generative scam analysis is not new to Singapore GovTech: its earlier Pango beta terms document that broader design pattern. The new system’s relationship to Pango and comparative performance remain unknown.
technical.regime: A Gemma-based scam detector being developed by Google DeepMind and Singapore GovTech for possible integration into applications on typical Singapore smartphones; intended input is local messaging conversation data with user consent. No phone class, deployment population, tested language set or production status is specified.
technical.reproducibility: No public weights, code, dataset, benchmark protocol or independent replication was linked in the inspected announcement. The exact model, training recipe and stress-test results cannot be reproduced from the current evidence.
technical.strongest_baseline: The Google announcement contrasts local analysis with conventional server-side scanning but reports no benchmark against existing anti-scam systems. A separate GovTech AntiScam Pango beta provides an institutional precedent: official terms dated 9 September describe on-device generative and classification models for supported messaging apps. The sources give no matched comparison between Pango and the new Gemma collaboration.

title: Google DeepMind and Singapore’s GovTech describe an on-device scam-detection model
why_it_matters: The specific Google DeepMind/GovTech collaboration describes a two-stage local classifier for messaging, while official GovTech terms already document a separate beta service using on-device generative scam analysis. This makes the comparative question—whether the new Gemma collaboration improves coverage, accuracy or resource use, and how it relates to Pango—more useful than treating on-device scam detection itself as new. No comparison, rollout or efficacy result is established in the reviewed sources.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On LIBERO-Pro, the authors report 83.8% overall task success for ChunkAct versus 78.8% for Harness VLA, a 5.0 percentage-point difference. In the same high-reasoning setup they report 8.3 versus 24.2 planner calls per episode, 0.5M versus 2.2M input tokens, and 3.7k versus 8.5k output tokens. The paper says the systems share the planner, VLA primitive, perception and memory and differ in test-time memory use.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: ChunkAct compiles procedural memory offline into reusable executable chunks. At test time a planner call launches a chained chunk; execution continues without further planner calls unless a stage fails, in which case a typed exit returns the failure stage and context for recovery.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On LIBERO-Plus, the authors report an 83.9% overall success rate for zero-shot ChunkAct, 11.0 points above the strongest tabled prior VLA baseline. The paper notes that ChunkAct is evaluated zero-shot while VLA comparator values are reported from prior work after fine-tuning on the benchmark, so this is not a matched comparison.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The reported evaluation uses the LIBERO simulation benchmark family; the reviewed paper reports no physical-robot experiment. The LIBERO-Plus VLA comparison reuses results from prior work with benchmark-fine-tuned baselines, unlike ChunkAct’s zero-shot evaluation.

evidence_gaps.description: The LIBERO-Pro performance and efficiency findings have not been independently reproduced.
No physical-robot test establishes transfer to real perception, control, hardware latency, safety or recovery from chunk failures.
LIBERO-Plus comparison is not matched: ChunkAct is zero-shot, but VLA results are prior reported scores after benchmark fine-tuning.
This review found no directly linked runnable implementation or evaluation configuration on the arXiv record; the results could not be reproduced here.

importance_rationale: If reproduced beyond the reported simulation regime, compiling procedural memory into executable chunks could reduce both LLM cost and task failures in tool-using robotic agents; current evidence is one author-reported benchmark program without a real-robot test.
limitations: The 5.0-point LIBERO-Pro gain and reduced call/token counts are reported by the paper authors and have not been independently reproduced.
Evaluation is simulation-only in the reviewed paper; transfer to physical robots, safety under long autonomous execution and real-world recovery remain unmeasured.
LIBERO-Plus baseline comparisons are not matched: ChunkAct is zero-shot, while cited VLA comparator scores come from prior fine-tuned evaluations.
The reported token/call efficiency does not include a full monetary or wall-clock cost analysis covering simulator setup, offline chunk compilation, model/tool costs and retries.

The method assumes recurring, compilable action routines and returns control to the planner only at decision points or typed failures; its limits under rapidly changing scenes or unanticipated hazards need evaluation.
summary: A new paper introduces ChunkAct, which compiles an LLM agent’s procedural memory into executable action chunks and calls the planner mainly for decisions or failures. On LIBERO-Pro simulation, the authors report 83.8% task success versus 78.8% for a matched Harness VLA baseline, with 2.9 times fewer LLM calls, 4.4 times fewer input tokens and 2.3 times fewer output tokens. On LIBERO-Plus, they report zero-shot results above previously reported VLA baselines, though those baselines were fine-tuned on that benchmark. These are paper-reported results; no physical-robot evaluation or independent reproduction was performed in this review.

technical.claimed_result: On LIBERO-Pro, authors report 83.8% task success versus 78.8% for Harness VLA, with 2.9x fewer planner calls, 4.4x fewer input tokens and 2.3x fewer output tokens in a matched high-reasoning setup. On LIBERO-Plus they report 83.9% zero-shot success, 11.0 points above the strongest tabled VLA baseline, but comparator values are from prior fine-tuned runs.
technical.compute_or_cost: For LIBERO-Pro high-reasoning runs, paper reports 24.2 to 8.3 LLM calls, 2.2M to 0.5M input tokens and 8.5k to 3.7k output tokens per episode, with task success 78.8% to 83.8%. No complete monetary or wall-clock cost, offline compilation cost or uncertainty interval is provided.
technical.demonstrated_result: The public preprint provides the proposed procedure, simulator setup and reported tables. This review establishes what the authors report; no independent reproduction or physical-robot trial was performed.
technical.mechanism: ChunkAct consolidates procedural memory offline into executable routines for typed sub-goals. A planner call launches a chain of perception and control primitives; the chunk runs autonomously, verifies stages and returns a typed exit when it fails. The planner handles scene understanding, target grounding and recovery rather than reselecting every primitive.
technical.novelty: The authors combine offline compilation of procedural memory into executable robot routines with online action chunking across perception and control primitives, returning control to the LLM mainly for goal decisions and typed failures. This applies action chunking at the agentic workflow level rather than only chunking motor outputs of a learned policy.
technical.regime: LIBERO-Pro: four suites crossed with instruction-redirection and object-position-swap perturbations, eight combinations with 10 tasks each and 10 seeds per task; planner GPT-5.6-sol at high reasoning, with up to 100 LLM calls per episode, a shared VLA primitive and segmentation model. LIBERO-Plus uses one seed per task for seven perturbation axes. No physical robot is tested.
technical.reproducibility: The arXiv HTML gives benchmark definitions, implementation settings, seeds and tables, but this review did not locate a directly linked runnable code/config package or run a reproduction. The LIBERO-Pro matched experiment appears comparatively well specified; LIBERO-Plus baseline provenance differs because published prior scores are compared with a zero-shot ChunkAct run.
technical.strongest_baseline: Harness VLA is the paper’s strongest LIBERO-Pro baseline: 78.8% success, 24.2 planner calls, 2.2M input tokens and 8.5k output tokens per episode versus ChunkAct’s 83.8%, 8.3, 0.5M and 3.7k. The paper states both use the same planner, primitive, perception and memory and differ in whether memory is retrieved at test time or compiled offline.

title: ChunkAct compiles agent memory into action chunks to cut planner calls in simulated robotics
why_it_matters: If the reported matched LIBERO-Pro result reproduces, compiling repeated procedural memory into executable chunks could improve success while lowering planner calls and token use in agentic robot workflows. This would change the cost/reliability trade-off for simulator-based agentic robotics. The evidence remains bounded to author-run benchmarks; real-robot safety, transfer and operating costs are not established.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The peer-reviewed paper reports that Paper2Agent converts papers and associated code into MCP resources, prompts and tested executable tools. Across 100 computational-biology papers, it successfully agentified 74, proposing 599 tools, of which 593 passed automated validation. The 26 failed conversions were attributed mainly to missing code, data or model artifacts, environment/dependency failures, or non-generalizable scripts.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On 300 tutorial-derived questions, Paper2Agent using Claude Sonnet 4 reports 91.2 ± 1.6% accuracy, versus 80.3 ± 2.3% for Claude Code with direct repository access using Sonnet 4 and 86.3 ± 1.1% using Sonnet 4.6. The paper reports per-query cost and latency of US $0.20 and 1.6 minutes, versus US $0.38 and 4.3 minutes for the Sonnet 4 direct paper/repository baseline.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across 42 execution-based tasks from 10 non-biology computational papers, the authors report 98.1 ± 0.8% accuracy across 5 independent runs. They also describe a multi-paper psoriasis case that prioritized GPR137 using computational predictions and independent perturbation datasets; statistical support was condition-dependent, and a human researcher selected the validation analysis.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The paper states that open-ended hypothesis generation and mechanistic interpretation remain human-in-the-loop, and that agreement with a single reference on open-ended questions primarily measures faithful execution rather than analytical validity. It also identifies security, intellectual-property, attribution and maintenance challenges for executable research agents.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the paper's conversion-rate, benchmark, cost/latency or cross-domain execution results was conducted in this activation.
The 100-paper biology corpus and other task sets do not establish performance on arbitrary scientific repositories, incomplete artifacts or less curated workflows; 26/100 biology conversions failed.
The reported evaluations use Claude Sonnet 4 and do not establish transfer to other base models, orchestrators or agent hosts.
Reference-output tests do not verify scientific validity, robustness to distribution shift, containment of malicious repositories or durable operation under upstream dependency changes.

importance_rationale: If sustained beyond the authors' tested corpora, compiling scientific methods and code into tested, composable agent tools could materially change research-software reuse and reduce integration cost. The reported 74/100 conversion rate, curated benchmarks, single base model and human oversight limit the demonstrated regime, so this is major research infrastructure evidence rather than autonomous-science proof.
limitations: The experiments are author-run and this activation did not install, execute or independently reproduce the public implementation.
Only 74 of 100 computational-biology papers were successfully agentified; missing code, data/model artifacts and environment or dependency failures bound applicability.
The benchmark corpora and tasks do not establish performance on arbitrary, less curated scientific repositories or all disciplines.
The evaluated system uses Claude Sonnet 4; cross-model transfer is not established by these results.
Reference-output fidelity does not establish scientific validity. The authors state that open-ended hypothesis generation and mechanistic interpretation remain human-in-the-loop.
Executable research agents raise security, intellectual-property, attribution and ongoing maintenance issues; no general hostile-repository safety guarantee is established.
summary: A peer-reviewed Nature paper introduces Paper2Agent, which turns research papers and associated code into structured MCP resources, workflow prompts and tested executable tools. Across 100 computational-biology papers, the authors report 74 successful conversions and 593/599 proposed tools passing automated validation; 26 papers could not be agentified, often because of missing artifacts or environment failures. On 300 tutorial-derived questions, the system reports 91.2% accuracy and lower query cost and latency than a direct-repository baseline using the same model. Across 42 execution tasks from 10 non-biology papers, it reports 98.1% accuracy. Results are author-run and use Claude Sonnet 4; paper agents support execution and reuse, while open-ended scientific reasoning remains human-in-the-loop.

technical.claimed_result: Paper2Agent turns research papers and codebases into MCP tools, resources and prompts, then validates generated tools against reference outputs. The authors report 74/100 successful computational-biology conversions, tutorial-query accuracy and cost gains against direct repository access, and 98.1% accuracy on a set of non-biology execution tasks.
technical.demonstrated_result: The peer-reviewed paper and public repository describe the system and its evaluation. Nature reports benchmark and case-study results, but this activation did not independently install or reproduce the software or validate scientific conclusions produced by paper agents.
technical.mechanism: A multi-agent pipeline locates a paper's code, provisions an isolated environment, discovers and executes tutorials, extracts reusable MCP tools, tests them against reference outputs, removes repeatedly failing tools, and assembles an MCP server with resources and prompts. Multiple paper MCPs can be connected to one downstream agent.
technical.regime: Nature-reported experiments: 100 computational-biology papers, 26 data/discovery papers, 10 non-biology computational papers; 300 tutorial-derived questions and 42 execution tasks across 5 runs. Case studies use Claude Sonnet 4. Conversion depends on available code, data, models and workable environments. Open-ended research interpretation remains human-in-the-loop.
technical.strongest_baseline: For 300 tutorial-derived questions, Sonnet 4 Paper2Agent reports 91.2 ± 1.6% versus direct-repository Claude Code at 80.3 ± 2.3% with Sonnet 4 and 86.3 ± 1.1% with Sonnet 4.6; reported per-query cost/latency were US $0.20/1.6 minutes versus US $0.38/4.3 minutes for the Sonnet 4 baseline. All values are author-reported in the stated setup.

title: Nature reports Paper2Agent, a framework for turning research papers into tested, callable research tools
why_it_matters: Research papers often contain methods that are hard to reuse without locating code, rebuilding environments and reconstructing workflows. Paper2Agent reports a way to package those materials as tested, callable interfaces and gives evidence of lower query cost and latency in its evaluated tasks. If the conversion and validation process transfers to less curated work, it could change how computational methods are disseminated and composed. Its failed conversions and human-oversight requirements bound that claim.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors introduce SWE-Flux, a benchmark with 480 execution-grounded instances from 12 Python repositories, covering single-test and multi-test questions across seven dynamic-behavior categories. The gold answers are harvested from instrumented executions rather than written by annotators or judged by an LLM. The paper links a public repository, which was not inspected in this review.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across five evaluated models, the paper reports GPT-5.4 as the highest-scoring model at 37.71% overall accuracy. Its reported accuracy on dataflow questions is 6.78% for single-test questions and 0% for multi-test questions; the authors report substantial semantic rather than formatting errors in a manual analysis of 299 GPT-5.4 incorrect answers.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a selected input-perturbation study, the authors report that 52 of 58 instances yielded valid variants. GPT-5.4 accuracy fell from 100% on those selected originals to 43.1% on the perturbed instances; two models not used to guide perturbation also fell from 48.3% to 24.1% and from 46.6% to 24.1%. These results are confined to the paper's selected Python instances and evaluation setup.

evidence_gaps.description: The linked benchmark repository, instances and reported model runs were not independently inspected or reproduced.
All benchmark instances are drawn from 12 Python repositories; transfer to other languages, repository types and deployment workloads is unknown.
Models were evaluated without code execution; retrieval and tool-use constraints may contribute to observed errors and the results do not directly measure full coding-agent outcomes.
The 58 perturbed instances were selected from examples GPT-5.4 answered correctly, so their difficulty increase is conditional on that selection and does not establish a broad distributional shift.

importance_rationale: If independently reproduced, an execution-grounded repository benchmark that measures call paths, runtime state and cross-test aggregation could improve evaluation of coding-agent reliability. The current study is limited to 480 instances in 12 Python repositories and five models, so it is notable research evidence rather than a field-wide capability ceiling.
limitations: The evaluation covers 480 instances from 12 Python repositories and five models; other languages and broader repository populations are not established.
The linked repository and model evaluations were not independently inspected or reproduced in this review.
Evaluated models could inspect repositories and use navigation tools but could not execute code; the benchmark therefore measures the stated no-execution prediction setup.
The 58-instance perturbation study is selected from items GPT-5.4 initially answered correctly and does not estimate performance on a representative deployment workload.
Paper-reported benchmark accuracy is not a direct measure of end-to-end coding-agent success or safety.
organizations: The University of Texas at Dallas
summary: A September 2026 preprint introduces SWE-Flux, a benchmark for predicting dynamic code behavior in real Python repositories. It contains 480 questions across 12 repositories, with answers harvested from instrumented test executions. In the authors’ five-model evaluation, GPT-5.4 scored 37.71% overall; dataflow questions were especially difficult. An input-perturbation pipeline generated valid variants for 52 of 58 selected instances, which were harder for the tested models. These are paper-reported results; the linked benchmark repository and evaluations were not independently inspected or reproduced, and coverage is limited to Python and the selected repositories.

technical.claimed_result: SWE-Flux measures dynamic program behavior at repository level using instrumented execution oracles. In the reported five-model evaluation, the top model reached 37.71% overall accuracy, with dataflow among the weakest categories.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint describes benchmark construction and evaluation protocols, reports tables and links a repository. No independent repository inspection, execution or replication was performed in this review.
technical.mechanism: The authors run pinned repository tests in fresh containers, record selected runtime events, and use instance-specific parsers to derive structured oracle answers. Models receive repository files, test context and answer templates but not the traces or harvested answers. A separate validation agent checks whether retained questions can be answered from released materials.
technical.regime: 480 instances from 12 Python repositories, 13 question types in single-test and multi-test settings, five LLMs, repository browsing tools, a 32K-token context for open models, at most 25 tool calls and temperature 0. The benchmark does not measure other languages or general coding-agent task completion.
technical.strongest_baseline: GPT-5.4 reports the highest overall score at 37.71%, followed by GPT-5.3-Codex at 33.75%. On dataflow, GPT-5.4 reports 6.78% for single-test and 0% for multi-test questions. Results are author-reported and benchmark-specific.

title: SWE-Flux reports a repository-level benchmark for dynamic code execution reasoning
why_it_matters: Coding agents must often predict what repository code will do across calls, state changes and test suites, including when they cannot safely or practically execute it. SWE-Flux offers an execution-grounded way to measure that task and reports weak results on several dynamic reasoning categories in its tested setup. Independent artifact inspection, broader language coverage and reproduction are needed before treating its scores as general capability estimates.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In two manipulation tasks on a FANUC LR Mate 200iD and an xArm 6, the authors report that a physically triggered backdoor preserved clean-task success counts of 8–10/10 and produced attack success counts of 8–10/10. The implementation modified five demonstrations (a 0.1 poisoning ratio); results are from the paper’s small experimental setup, not evidence of a deployed incident or general VLA-model vulnerability.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For a five-rollout color-sorting defense comparison, the paper reports online sanitization reduced successful attack executions from 4/5 to 1/5 and restored defended-task success to 5/5; fine-tuning variants achieved 0/5 defended-task successes. In separate ten-minute throughput tests, counts were 31 unshielded versus 32 shielded cycles on an RTX 4090 and 32 versus 29 on a Jetson AGX Orin.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The preprint describes an online defense that uses task-aware spatial filtering and policy spatial attention to detect likely triggers in off-task image regions, then sanitizes those pixels before inference without retraining the victim policy. This establishes the method described in the paper, not independent effectiveness beyond its reported tests.

evidence_gaps.description: The author-reported attack, defense and throughput results have not been independently reproduced; no code or reproducible artifact was inspected on the arXiv record.
The attack results use two tasks and two arms with small rollout counts, and do not establish transfer to other learned policies, VLA models, production environments or threat actors.
The defense assumes triggers lie in off-task image regions and does not evaluate triggers on task-relevant objects or language/cross-modal triggers.

importance_rationale: If reproducible, physical triggers that induce semantically wrong manipulation while preserving ordinary task performance would change security reviews for learning-based robot systems. Evidence is limited to a preliminary paper study on two arms, two tasks and small rollout counts, so the consequence is meaningful but bounded.
limitations: The study is preliminary and uses two tasks and two robot arms with small rollout counts.
The paper evaluates a visuomotor policy; its results do not demonstrate that current VLA foundation models are vulnerable.
No industrial incident, prevalence estimate, or independent replication is established.
The sanitizer targets visible triggers in off-task regions; the authors discuss task-relevant and multimodal triggers as unresolved cases.
summary: A September 2026 preprint reports physical-trigger backdoor experiments on two commercial robotic arms, FANUC LR Mate 200iD and xArm 6. Across color sorting and machinery boxing, the authors report attack success counts of 8–10/10 while clean-task counts remained 8–10/10 after modifying five demonstrations at a 0.1 poisoning ratio. A task-aware online image-sanitization defense reduced attack executions in a five-rollout test and maintained similar throughput in separate ten-minute runs. These are small, author-reported experiments; they do not establish deployed industrial attacks, broad VLA-model exposure, or independent reproduction.

technical.claimed_result: Physical triggers paired with poisoned demonstrations can induce task-level manipulation errors while nominal performance remains high in the paper's two-arm, two-task setup; online visual sanitization reduces the reported attack count in a small defense test.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint supplies a method description, experimental protocol and author-reported tables. No independent reproduction or production deployment is established.
technical.mechanism: The authors modify a small share of task demonstrations to pair a physical object in an off-task workspace region with a semantically incorrect action segment. At inference, a task-aware mask and spatial attention identify likely off-task triggers and sanitize image regions before policy inference.
technical.regime: A visuomotor policy, two manipulation tasks, two commercial robotic arms, 10 attack/clean rollouts per platform-task condition, five-rollout defense comparison, and two separate 10-minute throughput windows. The defense assumes triggers remain in off-task image regions.
technical.strongest_baseline: For defense, online sanitization reports 1/5 attack executions and 5/5 defended task successes, compared with 4/5 attack executions and 0/5 defended successes for each tested fine-tuning rate. These small author-reported color-sorting results are not independently reproduced.

title: A preprint reports physical-trigger backdoors and an online defense on two industrial robot arms
why_it_matters: A robot can execute an unsafe or incorrect task while remaining within ordinary physical limits if the learned policy has been poisoned to respond to a visual trigger. The paper reports this behavior on two real arm platforms and evaluates a runtime sanitizer, giving robotics security teams a concrete threat and defense to examine. The small, paper-reported scope leaves prevalence, generalization and deployment performance unknown.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On a held-out 3,000-decision benchmark across Search, Terminal and software engineering, the paper reports AEWM at 70.5% macro-F1 versus 59.9% for DeepSeek-V4-Pro, a 10.6 percentage-point difference.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across six benchmarks, the paper reports that EditAct improves average score over the strongest baseline by 6.7, 5.2 and 3.2 points for Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, respectively; each benchmark is evaluated in three independent runs.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For Qwen3.5-35B-A3B fine-tuned on its own trajectories, the paper reports AEWM-RFT exceeds Self-RFT by 2.2-2.6 points across three reported domains without AEWM guidance at inference.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of AEWM, EditAct or AEWM-RFT results was performed; all reported scores in this record are author-run paper results.

The paper reports 52B mid-training tokens, 120K SFT examples and internal deep-search training data, but this review did not establish full data availability, total training compute or inference-time overhead relative to baselines.
EditAct benchmark results use three Qwen3.5 inference backbones; transfer to other model families and independently assembled agent scaffolds remains unknown.

importance_rationale: If sustained, directly editing an agent’s proposed reasoning-action state before execution could change long-horizon agent design, and the paper reports gains across search, terminal and software-engineering benchmarks; evidence remains author-run and Qwen3.5-centered.
limitations: Results are author-reported and have not been independently replicated in this activation.
EditAct results use Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B in three specified scaffolds; generality to other model families and agent stacks is unestablished.
DeepSearchQA and SWE-Bench Pro are described as out-of-distribution; the other four benchmarks are in-distribution relative to training.

Training uses internal deep-search data, approximately 52B mid-training tokens and 120K SFT examples; the paper does not provide a complete independently auditable compute-cost comparison in the inspected sections.
Performance scores do not by themselves establish lower total cost, higher reliability in deployment or improved outcomes on untested tasks.
summary: A 2026 arXiv paper proposes an Agent-Editing World Model (AEWM) that judges whether an agent’s proposed reasoning-action pair is critical, exploratory or noisy, then revises noisy proposals before executing them against real tools. In the authors’ three-run evaluations, EditAct improves average scores over the strongest baseline by 6.7, 5.2 and 3.2 points for Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B across six search, terminal and software-engineering benchmarks. A held-out 3,000-decision Action Judge benchmark reports 70.5% macro-F1 versus 59.9% for DeepSeek-V4-Pro. These are paper-reported results; independent replication and cost accounting remain open.

technical.claimed_result: The paper reports 70.5% macro-F1 on a 3,000-decision Action Judge benchmark versus 59.9% for DeepSeek-V4-Pro; EditAct improves six-benchmark average scores over the strongest baseline by 6.7, 5.2 and 3.2 points for Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports 52B mid-training tokens and 120K SFT examples. Total training compute, inference token overhead and cost per task versus matched baselines were not established in this review.
technical.demonstrated_result: The 81-page arXiv paper documents methods, three-run author evaluations and reported scores; no independent reproduction was performed.
technical.implementation_status: Research method described in an arXiv paper; this review did not verify deployment or execute the authors’ artifacts.
technical.mechanism: Action Judge classifies an agent’s proposed reasoning-action pair as critical, exploratory or noisy. State Revision replaces both reasoning and action for noisy proposals, then executes the selected action against the real environment so later history contains the edited state and observed feedback.
technical.regime: A 3,000-decision held-out Action Judge benchmark across Search, Terminal and SWE; EditAct on six benchmarks using Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B in ReAct, CalibForge-Eval and SearchSWE scaffolds. Three independent evaluation runs are reported per benchmark.
technical.reproducibility: The paper gives extensive methods, benchmark budgets, prompts and three-run results. Independent execution, artifact completeness, full training-data access and compute-cost reproduction remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: DeepSeek-V4-Pro for overall Action Judge macro-F1; the strongest among ReAct, step-level Best@3 and trajectory-level Best@3 for each EditAct benchmark.

title: AEWM reports agent-state editing gains across six benchmarks and three model sizes
