summary: The October 2026 X-AgentRed preprint uses a graph of tool effects and execution preconditions to generate cross-service red-team scenarios, then uses execution feedback to diversify successful paths and repair blocked ones. In one evaluation run per configuration across four target agents in a simulated ecosystem of 30 services and 914 tools, the authors report a 19.2% harmful-path rate, versus 10.5% for STAC and 2.7% for TRACE; average tool coverage is 41.5%, versus 13.9% and 23.7%. These are paper-reported simulator results, not estimates of real-world agent risk.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report mean harmful-path rates of 19.2% for X-AgentRed, 10.5% for STAC and 2.7% for TRACE, and mean tool coverage of 41.5%, 13.9% and 23.7%, respectively.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv v1 full text, experiment protocol, reported results and limitations were inspected. No independent reproduction was performed.
technical.implementation_status: The preprint describes the method and simulated experiments. No code was executed and no independent replication or deployed-service evaluation was performed.
technical.mechanism: The system represents each tool by execution preconditions, effects and possible harms. A language model assesses effect–precondition links to form the HarmFlow dependency graph; graph walks generate candidate recipes. Executed scenarios are diversified through adjacent tool substitutions after success, while blocked paths are refined by adjusting preconditions and preceding steps.
technical.novelty: Combines an explicit cross-tool dependency graph with execution-guided diversification and repair to search compositions across a simulated service ecosystem.
technical.regime: Author evaluation using ToolSimulator with 30 services and 914 tools; four target agent models; 250 scenarios per target; one run per configuration. Two model judges must agree for the main harmful-path labels.
technical.reproducibility: The paper's reported evaluation was inspected in the HTML. One run per configuration limits uncertainty estimation; no independent run or external simulator audit was performed. The arXiv-linked project page was not inspected for executable artifacts.
technical.strongest_baseline: STAC is the strongest reported baseline on mean harmful-path rate (10.5%) and TRACE covers more tools on average than STAC (23.7% versus 13.9%); X-AgentRed reports 19.2% HPR and 41.5% coverage. Comparisons come from one run per configuration in the authors' fixed simulator.

title: Graph-guided red-teaming finds more harmful cross-service paths in a simulated personal-agent ecosystem
why_it_matters: A dependency graph can expose combinations of individually benign tool actions that prompt-based red-teaming may miss. The reported benchmark advantage makes this a notable testing method for service-using agents, while a single simulated run and judge-sensitive labels leave its field relevance uncertain.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For an unforced Leray–Hopf solution on the periodic three-dimensional torus at fixed viscosity, the paper states that positive energy defect over a time window is equivalent to an eventually uniform positive lower bound on time-integrated flux through dyadic Fourier shells.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report Lean 4/Mathlib formal proofs of the reduction and related necessary conditions. They explicitly state that the library contains no Navier–Stokes object and does not connect the reduction to a formalized Leray–Hopf theory.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports 12 pseudo-spectral runs at resolutions 128³ and 256³. The runs approach the temporal flux-floor condition but lose the common floor toward the Kolmogorov scale; the authors state that these finite floating-point diagnostics establish nothing about a true solution.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The paper states that the unforced positive-defect problem remains open and that the forced Navier–Stokes and forced/inviscid Euler constructions it discusses are outside the target class.

evidence_gaps.description: The linked current Lean package and its exact theorem/import scope have not been built or independently audited; the paper identifies Lean 4.33.0 and Mathlib 4.33.0 but says the library contains no Navier–Stokes object.
No formal derivation connects the abstract sequence/function hypotheses used by the reduction to an actual unforced Leray–Hopf solution of Navier–Stokes.
The authors' finite-resolution flux diagnostics have not been independently reproduced; they do not establish the uniform fine-scale floor in any case.

importance_rationale: If the paper's formal reduction and search criteria are sound and useful, they provide a concrete way to target computational work on a major open regularity problem. This is notable methodological progress, while the actual unforced positive-defect solution remains open and the formal bridge to Navier–Stokes objects is absent.
limitations: The paper does not construct an unforced Navier–Stokes singularity or solve the positive-defect problem, which it states remains open.
The Lean library contains no Navier–Stokes object; the bridge from the abstract sequence/function theorem to formalized Leray–Hopf objects is explicitly undone.
The 12 pseudo-spectral runs are finite floating-point diagnostics and cannot establish the uniform condition at arbitrarily fine scales or witness a positive defect.
the research desk did not build the linked current Lean package, independently audit the proof, or reproduce the simulations.
The necessary conditions in the paper are not sufficient conditions for a positive defect.
summary: A September 2026 preprint defines a positive energy defect for a periodic-cube, unforced Leray–Hopf solution at fixed viscosity and reports a Lean 4 formal reduction: the defect is equivalent to a uniform positive lower bound on time-averaged energy flux through all sufficiently fine dyadic Fourier shells. The paper gives necessary admissibility conditions and argues that finite Galerkin computation cannot witness the required uniform ceiling; its 12 pseudo-spectral runs at 128³ and 256³ meet a temporal flux condition but fail to sustain the floor toward the Kolmogorov scale. This is a bounded mathematical search specification, not an unforced singularity result. The authors state that their Lean library contains no Navier–Stokes object and does not connect the reduction to a separately formalized Leray–Hopf theory; the target remains open.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report the shell-balance reduction, a set of necessary conditions for a candidate positive defect, and 12 pseudo-spectral diagnostic runs at 128³/256³. They report the time condition is nearly met but the fine-scale condition fails approaching the Kolmogorov scale.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint, its date and its stated scope and limitations are directly inspectable. This review re-read the full HTML and linked repository README but did not build the current Lean package, execute the simulations, or independently verify the mathematical argument.
technical.implementation_status: A preprint and linked Lean source repository are public. No current-package build or independent verification was performed in this review.
technical.mechanism: The paper takes the energy defect of an unforced fixed-viscosity Leray–Hopf solution over a time window, derives a shell-truncated energy balance, and identifies the limit of integrated dyadic-shell flux with the defect. A positive defect is then equivalent to a common positive lower bound on the averaged flux for all sufficiently fine shells. The Lean development formalizes the stated implications over abstract real sequences/functions under hypotheses; the paper does not encode a Navier–Stokes solution object.
technical.novelty: A formalized reduction of the positive-defect target to a uniform averaged dyadic-shell flux criterion, together with search admissibility conditions and an explicit account of why finite Galerkin computations cannot establish the required scale-uniform claim.
technical.regime: Unforced incompressible Navier–Stokes on the periodic three-dimensional torus at fixed viscosity, for a Leray–Hopf solution from smooth data. The finite numerical diagnostics use the authors' pseudo-spectral setup at 128³ and 256³; the formalized reduction is over abstract sequences/functions with the Navier–Stokes conditions supplied as hypotheses.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links a Lean 4.33.0/Mathlib 4.33.0 repository and reports 12 spectral runs. The linked current package was not built in this review; the paper says the package is not connected to an existing formalization of Leray–Hopf theory. No independent numerical reproduction was performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper contrasts the required scale-uniform flux floor with its own finite-resolution simulations, which approach the time condition but lose flux across finer shells near the Kolmogorov scale. It supplies no independent reproduction or matched computational baseline.

title: A Lean-formalized search target for the open unforced Navier–Stokes problem
why_it_matters: A precise scale-uniform flux target and explicit admissibility criteria can help researchers distinguish useful numerical diagnostics from evidence for an unforced singularity. The contribution concerns how a major open problem might be searched; it does not solve that problem, and the formal bridge to actual Navier–Stokes objects remains absent.

summary: The authors introduce SEMV, a multi-agent multimedia verification system that represents evidence as provenance-bearing support and attack arguments, routes human corrections to affected stages, and gates memory reuse through verification and conflict retention. On the 1,700-record COSMOS test set, the Qwen3.6 variant reports 91.88% accuracy versus 89.10% for the strongest directly comparable full-test baseline (unpaired two-proportion z-test p=0.006); other backbones show smaller or nonsignificant differences. In a Qwen memory ablation, unrestricted updates show 5.7% negative transfer, versus 0.2% when verification and conflict retention are added. The authors also report 96.7% correction of initial errors and 52.8% compute savings in a constructed contestation benchmark. These are author-reported results: COSMOS is controlled binary image-caption consistency, MV2026 evaluates only 10 validation and 10 private-test cases, and the 50 CTR episodes come from 10 independent source cases. No independent reproduction was conducted.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report 91.88% COSMOS accuracy for the Qwen3.6 variant versus a 89.10% directly comparable baseline and, in the Qwen memory ablation, 0.2% negative transfer with verified consolidation plus conflict retention versus 5.7% with unrestricted updates.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv paper documents the SEMV design and its author-run evaluations. It does not independently establish the reported gains, open-world fact-checking effectiveness or deployment benefit.
technical.mechanism: SEMV encodes evidence and claims as provenance-bearing support and attack arguments, routes human contestations to affected pipeline stages, and consolidates candidate memories only after provenance, support, duplication and conflict checks.
technical.regime: Author-run evaluation on COSMOS binary image-caption consistency (full test n=1,700), a very small MV2026 evaluation and a constructed contestation-trace revision set with 50 episodes from 10 source cases.
technical.reproducibility: No independent replication or code/data audit was conducted in this activation.
technical.strongest_baseline: For the full COSMOS test, the authors compare against the directly comparable Tran et al. baseline at 89.10%; the paper uses an unpaired two-proportion z-test because baseline record-level predictions are unavailable.

title: SEMV reports improved multimedia verification and safer reuse of corrected cases
why_it_matters: Evidence provenance, localized correction and safe reuse of prior cases are central to dependable multimedia verification. SEMV offers a concrete integrated design and reports controlled gains, while its small open-world and contestation evaluations leave effectiveness in professional fact-checking uncertain.

summary: Wang et al. introduce ProbeGuard, which uses the formation history of a multi-round medical question-answering consensus to decide when to abstain. Its process features track agreement, minority persistence and retrieval; for immediately unanimous answers it also checks rationale agreement and probes with counter-evidence. On MedQA, the authors report a process-score AUROC of 0.696 versus 0.512 for terminal agreement. Their stratified Learn-then-Test rule answered 55.3% of the unanimous layer at 9.0% observed risk against a 15% target across 50 splits, under an assumption that calibration and deployment questions are i.i.d. within each stratum. In specialty analysis, emergency medicine had 19.1% realized risk at the same layer-level threshold, and was not separately certified. These are author-reported multiple-choice benchmark results, not clinical deployment evidence.

technical.claimed_result: On MedQA, authors report 0.696 AUROC for the process score versus 0.512 for terminal agreement. The calibrated rule answers 0.553 of the unanimous layer at 9.0% observed risk for target α=0.15 over 50 splits. Emergency medicine has 19.1% realized risk under the layer-level threshold, without separate specialty certification.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint specifies a benchmark protocol and reports author-run results on MedQA, MMLU-Pro medicine, MedMCQA and a hard-frontier reference, using Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and HuatuoGPT-o1-8B. No independent reproduction or clinical workflow study was performed.
technical.mechanism: ProbeGuard derives abstention signals from an agentic RAG system’s execution log: agreement trajectory, persistent minority answers and retrieval saturation. For a first-round unanimous answer, it adds mutual-entailment scoring over rationale conclusions and an active retrieval probe for counter-evidence. A stratified Learn-then-Test procedure selects answer thresholds from calibration data.
technical.regime: Multiple-choice medical QA with a published multi-round RAG substrate, three 8B backbones and benchmark datasets. The risk guarantee assumes calibration and deployment examples are i.i.d. within each fixed stratum. Specialty analysis is descriptive under the aggregate layer threshold.
technical.reproducibility: No code execution or independent reproduction was performed. The paper-linked GitHub URL was reported inaccessible in a prior read-only check; no conclusion about deletion follows.
technical.strongest_baseline: For MedQA process discrimination, terminal agreement achieves 0.512 AUROC, near chance; first-round agreement reaches 0.677. The paper compares several abstention signals on the same substrate but does not provide an external clinical baseline.

title: ProbeGuard reports risk-controlled abstention from medical answer-consensus trajectories
why_it_matters: A unanimous panel can share the same misconception, so final agreement alone may hide error. The paper tests whether interaction traces and targeted counter-evidence can support abstention decisions with a stated statistical bound. Its aggregate guarantee depends on within-stratum distribution stability, while the emergency-medicine subgroup and probe cost show why deployment would need case-mix monitoring, specialty-level calibration and workflow evaluation.

summary: Zheng et al. introduce ServeLearnBench, a benchmark for learning policies that change during service interactions. Its three domains contain 53 environment windows, 4,508 feedback-bearing serving tasks and 3,210 held-out tasks. Across six models and five learning harnesses, the authors report a large gap between following a disclosed policy and inferring it from outcomes: on Retail L3 the best of 28 tested model–harness pairs scored 59.6% and the median 22.0%. They also report higher costs for hidden-policy inference and cases where adaptation reduced performance on fully specified tasks. These are author-reported results from a designed benchmark, not an independent measurement of deployed services; harnesses retained different native resource budgets.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report a substantial gap between disclosed-policy capability and learning from interaction: Retail L3 reaches 59.6% for the best of 28 tested model–harness pairs and 22.0% at the median. They report 4–101× higher cost for hidden-policy inference versus disclosed-policy following and adaptation-related regressions on Fully Specified cases.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary preprint documents a benchmark protocol and author-run evaluations across 53 windows, 4,508 serving tasks and 3,210 held-out tasks in retail, banking and sales-pitch domains. Reported scores and costs have not been independently reproduced.
technical.mechanism: An evolving-environment stream keeps the task interface stable while evaluator-side policies or preferences change between windows. Agents infer those latent rules from serving outcomes, then face disjoint held-out tasks; Hidden-Dependent and Fully Specified slices distinguish policy inference from preserving already-supported behavior.
technical.regime: Designed retail support, banking review and sales-pitch tasks with hidden environment rules or preferences that change across windows; six API models and five learning harnesses, with 28 pairs evaluated. Transfer to operational systems is unmeasured.
technical.reproducibility: No independent reproduction, code execution or complete experiment-adapter audit was performed in this activation.
technical.strongest_baseline: Oracle receives the active hidden policy and averages 95.5% on Hidden cases; it is an upper reference that removes policy inference, not a like-for-like deployable agent. Blind receives no serving history and gives a no-adaptation reference. Harness comparisons preserve native resource budgets.

title: ServeLearnBench reports that agents struggle to learn changing hidden policies from service feedback
why_it_matters: Reliable agents need to adapt when operational rules change without being explicitly supplied. This benchmark measures that problem across several service settings and makes adaptation costs and collateral regressions visible. Its reported results suggest that tool or memory updates alone do not ensure reliable policy learning, while the native-budget comparison and synthetic task regimes limit causal and deployment conclusions.

summary: A September 2026 preprint introduces R3Con, a harness that repeatedly extracts task-relevant context from large document collections, builds a flexible structure such as a table or graph, then uses a coding agent to reason over it. On CorpusQA and Loong, the authors report overall accuracy gains of 19.88 and 8.42 percentage points over the strongest evaluated baselines. They also report that 4B and 9B R3Con configurations exceeded all evaluated 35B baselines, and that a Qwen3.5-35B-A3B R3Con run exceeded a Claude Code/Sonnet 5 comparison at about 3.7 times lower reported cost. These are single-paper results on two benchmarks; both use LLM judging, and the cross-system cost comparison does not isolate model and harness effects.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report overall accuracy of 70.64% on CorpusQA and 37.43% on Loong, versus strongest listed baselines of 50.76% and 29.01%. Smaller R3Con runs using Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-4B respectively exceed all evaluated Qwen3.5-35B-A3B baselines. A separate Qwen3.5-35B-A3B R3Con run is reported to outperform Claude Code using Claude-Sonnet-5 at approximately 3.7x lower cost.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports cost estimates using the lowest listed model prices it found on OpenRouter at writing time and reports an approximately 3.7x lower cost for the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B R3Con versus Claude Code/Sonnet 5 comparison. This is not an independently audited total-compute or matched-runtime cost analysis.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint documents the R3Con design, benchmark setup and author-reported tables. No independent reproduction was performed in this review.
technical.mechanism: R3Con iteratively summarizes each source document for task relevance using the current corpus-level understanding, asks a model to propose a task-appropriate schema, populates the structure from source documents, then explores and reasons over the representation using a coding agent.
technical.novelty: The proposed pipeline couples iterative task-conditioned relevance extraction with dynamically selected structured representations before downstream coding-agent reasoning, rather than fixing the representation type in advance.
technical.regime: Two long-document reasoning benchmarks, CorpusQA and Loong, spanning education, finance, real estate, academic papers and legal cases. Baseline models are primarily Qwen3.5-35B-A3B; smaller R3Con configurations use Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B. The separate Claude Code comparison uses Claude-Sonnet-5. The authors use gpt-5.4-mini as an LLM judge.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links a public code repository. The repository implementation and benchmark runs were not independently audited or reproduced in this activation.
technical.strongest_baseline: The best reported baseline is StructRAG on CorpusQA (50.76% overall) and CodeAgent on Loong (29.01% overall); R3Con reports 70.64% and 37.43%, respectively. The paper also compares against Claude Code using Claude-Sonnet-5, but this is a cross-system comparison rather than a model-matched harness ablation.

title: R3Con reports large gains from task-focused context representation on two long-context benchmarks
why_it_matters: If replicated on broader corpora, a task-specific representation-building stage could improve multi-hop evidence integration while lowering the model scale needed for some long-context tasks. Its results remain bounded to two evaluations, author-selected baselines, and LLM-as-judge scores; the cost comparison is not a matched harness ablation.

The reported evidence is not independent and does not establish transfer to laboratory science.
limitations: All performance values are author-reported and were not independently reproduced in this activation.

Training, teacher-search, and test-time discovery costs are distinct; the 32-experiment budget is not total system cost.
No implementation link or released task manifest was found on the inspected arXiv record; this bounded search does not show that private or unindexed artifacts do not exist.
organizations: University of Science and Technology of China
University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
summary: The Oct. 6 preprint proposes a scientific-discovery policy that can revise the hypothesis class itself while choosing experiments designed to distinguish structural edits. In 400 held-out controlled dynamical environments, the authors report 89.5% exact recovery after 32 real experiments, 10 percentage points above their strongest matched baseline. On 200 mechanisms excluded from the edit grammar, they report detecting library insufficiency in 88% of cases with 5.5% false support, and report additional results on ODEBench, ODEBase and DiscoverPhysics. These are author-reported evaluations; no independent reproduction or real laboratory deployment was established in this review.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report 89.5% exact recovery on 400 held-out controlled dynamical environments with a 32-real-experiment budget, versus 79.5% for the strongest matched baseline. On 200 out-of-grammar mechanisms, they report 88% library-insufficiency detection and 5.5% false support. Additional author-reported evaluation covers ODEBench, ODEBase and DiscoverPhysics.
technical.compute_or_cost: The test-time discovery budget counts real experiments. Appendix E separately accounts for candidate fits and fitting GPU time, and the paper says teacher-search and policy-training compute are additional; the 32-experiment result is not an all-in training-plus-inference cost.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected arXiv v1 paper documents the proposed method, experimental protocol and reported metrics. the research desk did not run the code or reproduce the evaluations; empirical outcomes remain author-reported.
technical.mechanism: The policy proposes typed edits to the model class together with experiments chosen to distinguish those edits. A shared parameterization must explain the selected experiments, while anytime-valid sequential evidence determines when the current class is rejected. If no admissible edit gains support, the policy can report that its edit library is insufficient.
technical.novelty: The work treats experiment selection and expansion of the hypothesis class as a coupled sequential decision problem, including an explicit outcome for detecting insufficiency in the available edit library.
technical.regime: Controlled dynamical-system discovery with 400 held-out generated environments, 200 out-of-grammar mechanisms, a fixed typed edit grammar and a canonical budget of 32 real experiments; additional model-library and interactive-world benchmarks. The paper reports three training seeds for stochastic methods and paired test environments.
technical.reproducibility: The arXiv HTML paper and protocol appendices were accessible. No paper-specific implementation or task manifest was linked from the inspected arXiv record; no independent reproduction was performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: Falsification plus independent edit/experiment selection under the matched controlled protocol, reported at 79.5% exact recovery versus 89.5% for the joint policy at budget 32.

title: Preprint couples structural theory revision with diagnostic experiment selection
why_it_matters: Scientific discovery systems can fail when every candidate theory shares the same missing mechanism. The paper directly studies that gap by coupling structural revision to diagnostic experiment choice. If its controlled and benchmark results hold under independent testing and transfer to real experiments, this could change how automated discovery systems allocate experiments; current evidence does not establish laboratory impact.

Its exact technical path, accessed data and extent across other sites remain unresolved, so it is evidence for incident-response and disclosure questions rather than proof of a broader compromise.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors describe extracting papers into source-linked claims, inference factors, ordered reasoning chains, study settings and weak points, then organizing them into question, workflow and evidence views with incremental identity-preserving updates.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On SciFact-Open at a 50-paper budget, the paper reports 818 known-positive claim-paper pairs retrieved versus 443 for the released retriever, with recall rising from 39.38% to 72.71%. The pooled reference set includes judge- and MultiVerS-admitted candidate positives; original human annotations take precedence.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On two ScholarQABench subsets, adding reasoning graphs to the same retrieved papers, reranker and writing budget raises citation F1 by 5.3 and 5.1 percentage points, respectively, in the paper’s matched comparison.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: With GPT-5.4 fixed as the answer model, the paper reports LKM retrieval accuracy gains of 9.3, 4.2 and 14.7 points over no retrieval on ChemBench, PubMedQA and SciBench. The paper reports no paired confidence intervals for these point estimates.

evidence_gaps.description: The paper’s 100-paper extraction audit estimates hallucination but does not measure omitted claims/evidence; no independent audit or reproduction was performed.

The paper says the question/workflow/evidence landscape views and Evidence Engine categorization are not directly evaluated; the 1.4-billion-claim scale and service latency are author-reported production statistics.

importance_rationale: If the matched retrieval and citation results generalize, persistent source-linked reasoning graphs could materially change scientific retrieval and evidence synthesis. A 6 reflects the tested system contribution while separating it from unverified production-scale figures and unmeasured omission/categorization errors.
limitations: The author preprint is under review and its experimental results are not independently reproduced here.
The extraction audit samples 100 papers and measures hallucination but not omission; the authors note figure, table and equation evidence may be incompletely captured.
Question/workflow/evidence landscape categorization is not directly evaluated in the paper.
The reported 1.4-billion-claim production scale and 740-ms median latency are author-reported and vary with a continuously updated service snapshot.
The evidence-discovery pooled reference set adds judge- and MultiVerS-admitted pairs; QA point estimates do not include paired confidence intervals.
organizations: Institute of Theoretical Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
summary: A September 2026 preprint describes a scientific retrieval system that stores paper-level claims, premises, reasoning chains, conditions and source links, then connects them into question, workflow and evidence views. The authors report nearly twice as many known supporting and contradicting evidence pairs retrieved on SciFact-Open, a 5-point citation-F1 improvement from adding reasoning graphs over the same retrieved papers, and gains on three fixed-model scientific QA benchmarks. The reported evaluations are author-run; omission errors, independent reproduction and direct evaluation of the landscape’s evidence categorization remain open.

technical.claimed_result: The preprint reports nearly doubled known-positive evidence pairs on SciFact-Open, +5.3/+5.1 citation-F1 points from graph reasoning on two ScholarQABench subsets, and +9.3/+4.2/+14.7 QA points on ChemBench/PubMedQA/SciBench over no retrieval.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper reports benchmark results under described fixed budgets and a matched graph ablation. These results remain author claims and have not been independently replicated in this activation.
technical.mechanism: Papers are parsed into source-linked reasoning objects (questions, claims, premises, inference factors, ordered chains, settings and weak points). Typed links support hybrid retrieval and navigation from a conclusion to its evidence and source; cross-paper views organize questions, workflows and evidence.
technical.regime: Author-run deployed service; SciFact-Open 279 claims, 50 papers per claim; ScholarQABench 100 and 108 questions; ChemBench n=2,785, PubMedQA n=500 and SciBench n=580.
technical.reproducibility: Paper documents procedures and provides a public API description; no independent API trial, frozen corpus access or reproduction was performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: Released SciFact-Open retriever at 50 papers; same retrieved candidates/reranker/writer budget without reasoning graphs on ScholarQABench; no-retrieval condition with GPT-5.4 fixed on three QA benchmarks.

title: Large Knowledge Model reports source-linked reasoning graphs and scientific retrieval gains
why_it_matters: The work tests a shift from retrieving passages to retrieving structured claims together with how they were supported and under what conditions. If its reported gains hold under independent evaluation, this could improve evidence tracing and reuse in scientific research systems; current results do not establish that the full production-scale knowledge base is complete or self-correcting.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors define three linked asset layers: source-grounded paper facts with conditions and evidence references; domain organization; and scoped cross-paper syntheses with coverage and supporting or limiting evidence.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On 797 MDAQA questions using the same answering model, the paper reports an 18.41 score versus 8.46 for full-text across five scored dimensions, and 5.5k versus 20.8k generation tokens per question. The score is a sum of judge-scored dimensions; usage excludes asset construction and judging.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across four task families and ten task settings, the authors report that quality gains concentrate on tasks needing cross-paper evidence and query-time token costs fall where measured. These are the authors’ benchmark results, not independent evidence of general superiority or total end-to-end savings.

evidence_gaps.description: The reported query-token reduction excludes the one-time construction of research assets and judging costs; the end-to-end break-even point and update/revision costs are not established.

The paper’s multi-task results are author-reported; no public implementation, frozen asset collection or independent reproduction was inspected. Some benchmark conditions use constructed gold and LLM-based judging.

importance_rationale: If the reported cross-task gains generalize, preserving evidence-linked research assets could materially change scientific-agent workflows and reduce repeated context processing. A 6 reflects results across several task settings, bounded by author-run studies, constructed assets/benchmarks and excluded construction costs.
limitations: The accessible evidence is an author preprint and has not been independently reproduced.
Quality results vary by task; gains are reported as concentrated on cross-paper evidence tasks rather than universal.
The 797-question QA score is a five-dimension sum produced under the paper’s evaluation protocol; results are judge- and dataset-dependent.
Query-time token comparisons exclude construction and judging costs, so they do not establish total cost savings.
Some appendices describe self-constructed benchmarks and single-judge or author-generated gold limitations.
summary: A September 2026 preprint describes a research-asset framework that keeps source-grounded paper statements, domain organization and scoped cross-paper syntheses as distinct but linked objects. Across four task families, the authors report that gains concentrate on multi-paper evidence tasks and that query-time token use falls where measured. On a 797-question multi-paper QA set, the paper reports a higher five-dimension score than its full-text baseline while using fewer generation tokens. Construction and judging costs are excluded from that comparison; results are author-reported and rely on benchmark- and judge-specific methods.

technical.claimed_result: On 797 MDAQA questions the authors report 18.41 versus 8.46 on a five-dimension score and 5.5k versus 20.8k generation tokens per question; they also report cross-task quality gains and lower query costs where measured.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper specifies matched model and source conditions for selected evaluations and reports results across four task families. Results remain author-reported and have not been independently reproduced in this activation.
technical.mechanism: A shared interface compiles source-grounded statements, domain-level organization and evidence-scoped cross-paper syntheses as versioned, provenance-linked assets; tasks request views at different evidence granularities.
technical.regime: Four task families, ten task settings; multi-paper QA on 797 MDAQA questions; token/time accounting excludes knowledge construction and judging.
technical.reproducibility: No independent implementation or reproduction was performed; public code or frozen assets were not inspected.
technical.strongest_baseline: Task-specific baselines including full-text under matched base models and, for selected conditions, matched source-paper collections and context budgets.

title: ScholarStack reports cross-task reuse of layered scientific research assets
why_it_matters: Research agents repeat source processing across retrieval, question answering, literature synthesis and claim checks. The paper evaluates whether retaining scoped, provenance-linked intermediate research assets can improve cross-paper tasks and reduce query-time work. Its evidence supports a bounded author-reported framework result, not a general claim that reusable assets always improve scientific work or total cost.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors describe a four-layer bus fabric with cross-domain port-ID routing and shadow-device auto-enumeration to provide unified xPU addressing across host domains.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On a custom 64-xPU 3D-mesh system compared with the paper’s 64-port RoCE configuration, the authors report communication latency at 10–50% of the comparator for tested packet sizes, 2–15x bandwidth, and DeepSeek R1 inference throughput gains of approximately 30–80%.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports an approximately 80% reduction in interconnect cost and 5% reduction in interconnect power for its Co-Fabric link configuration versus its RoCE comparison. These figures describe the compared interconnect components, not whole data-center cost or power.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or public implementation/hardware artifact was inspected. The reported results use a custom 64-xPU 3D-mesh Co-Fabric system and a specific RoCE comparator configuration.

The paper reports component-level interconnect cost and power reductions; full system cost, energy, deployment yield, failure behavior and the sensitivity of results to comparator link rates are not established.

importance_rationale: If the reported 64-xPU results generalize, cross-host load/store semantics with substantially lower communication latency could affect scale-up architecture and large-model serving economics. A 6 reflects a consequential systems design claim, bounded by a single vendor-authored testbed and missing independent reproduction.
limitations: All quantitative system results are reported by the paper authors and have not been independently reproduced.
The principal evaluation uses one custom 64-xPU 3D-mesh configuration and a paper-specified RoCE setup; results may depend on topology, link rates, xPU model, workload and software.
The reported cost and power reductions apply to interconnect components, not whole-system or facility costs.
Expansion to larger clusters is described as potential/future work; the 64-xPU evaluation does not demonstrate thousand-xPU operation.
summary: A September 2026 preprint describes Co-Fabric, a bus-based xPU interconnect that uses hardware port-ID routing and shadow-device enumeration to present a unified address space across host domains. On a reported 64-xPU 3D-mesh testbed, the authors report lower communication latency and higher bandwidth than their RoCE comparison system, plus faster DeepSeek R1 inference. These are single-paper results on a custom system; independent reproduction and transfer to other hardware are not established.

technical.claimed_result: For the stated 64-xPU setup, the authors report 10–50% of RoCE latency, 2–15x bandwidth on tested packet sizes, 30–80% higher DeepSeek R1 inference throughput, approximately 80% lower interconnect cost and 5% lower interconnect power.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accessible preprint specifies a 64-xPU, dual-cabinet test configuration and presents reported AllReduce, scaling and DeepSeek R1 inference measurements. The measured outcomes remain author claims rather than independently demonstrated the research desk results.
technical.mechanism: A four-layer bus-based fabric routes xPU traffic across host domains using switch port identifiers and exposes remote devices through shadow-device enumeration into a unified address space.
technical.regime: Custom 64-xPU 3D-mesh hybrid southbound/northbound configuration across two cabinets; DeepSeek R1 671B inference uses SGLang, INT8, DP4/TP16 and 1K input/1K output tokens in the captioned workload.
technical.reproducibility: No independent reproduction was performed; no public implementation artifact was located in the reviewed source.
technical.strongest_baseline: A paper-configured 64-port Ethernet/RoCE system; the paper describes comparable 64-xPU resources but this review did not reconstruct the component-level matching or test an independent system.

title: Co-Fabric reports cross-host xPU fabric gains on a 64-device system
why_it_matters: Large-model training and inference can be limited by accelerator-to-accelerator data movement. If the reported cross-host protocol and system results transfer beyond this custom testbed, they could change scale-up fabric design and the cost/performance trade-off between dedicated interconnect and Ethernet/RoCE.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across six selected released policies, the authors report a 1.58-point range in clean LIBERO averages versus 14.62 points in non-language robustness and 31.08 points in LIBERO-Para paraphrase success. Restricting the comparison to the three protocol-faithful systems preserves the separation.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper distinguishes protocol-faithful, near-reproduction and pending-verification results; only protocol-faithful rows are used for strict comparisons. It does not infer causal effects of VLA versus WAM architecture from the checkpoint set.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports observed latency, peak VRAM, runtime mode and setup burden for the evaluated checkpoints, while cautioning that those observations are not controlled intrinsic efficiency rankings.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction was performed. Three of six reported systems are not protocol-faithful, and the paper’s strict cross-model comparison covers only the other three.
The evaluation uses LIBERO-family simulation and six purposively selected checkpoints; no real-robot task, broader benchmark census or architecture-causal comparison is established.

importance_rationale: If the reported diagnostic separation persists, robot-policy selection would need to consider visual robustness, language sensitivity and execution cost alongside clean success. A 5 reflects a useful evaluation contribution across six released checkpoints, bounded by simulation-only scope and three protocol-faithful systems.
limitations: The paper reports simulation-only results on a purposive set of six released checkpoints; it does not claim coverage of all open robot policies.
Three entries are protocol-faithful; one is near-reproduction and two are pending verification. Strict claims should use only the faithful subset.
Latency and memory are observed runtime profiles, not controlled cross-model efficiency measurements.
Results do not establish causal advantages of VLA or WAM architectures, real-world robustness or safety.
No independent reproduction was performed in this review.
organizations: Southern University of Science and Technology
summary: An October 2026 preprint evaluates six released vision-language-action and world-action robot policies across clean LIBERO tasks, visual/embodiment perturbations, instruction paraphrases and observed runtime costs. Across the six systems, the paper reports only a 1.58-point spread on clean LIBERO but larger spreads on visual robustness and paraphrase success. Three systems are marked protocol-faithful; near-reproduction and pending-verification rows remain diagnostic and are excluded from strict comparisons. Results are limited to selected checkpoints in LIBERO-family simulation, not real-robot performance or causal architectural comparisons.

technical.claimed_result: Across six systems, clean LIBERO averages span 1.58 points, robustness summaries span 14.62 points and paraphrase results span 31.08 points; the diagnostic spread persists among three protocol-faithful systems.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper defines an explicit checkpoint and comparability protocol and reports three-run benchmark summaries. Numerical outcomes remain author-reported and unreplicated here.
technical.mechanism: A shared evaluation schema reports clean LIBERO success, visual/embodiment perturbation robustness, semantics-preserving instruction paraphrase sensitivity, and runtime/reproducibility status as separate axes.
technical.regime: Six selected open robot-policy checkpoints in LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Para simulation; three protocol-faithful, one near-reproduction, two pending verification.
technical.reproducibility: Paper describes an author-linked GitHub harness and evaluation records. Repository inspected at index level; no code/model execution or independent reproduction was performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: Three protocol-faithful released checkpoints compared under fixed checkpoint/inference configuration and three run-level seeds on LIBERO-family protocols.

title: IndustrialVLA-Bench separates clean simulation scores from robustness and instruction sensitivity
why_it_matters: A clean benchmark score may hide important differences in robustness, instruction handling and deployability for executable robot policies. This evaluation makes those dimensions and evidence tiers visible together, while explicitly limiting strict comparisons to runs that meet its protocol-fidelity criteria.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The preprint defines and evaluates a repeated naming-game model with homogeneous, fully connected populations instantiated from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Phi-4, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that fewer than 10% of single-intermediate paths reduce additive committed effort below the direct-transition requirement; this fraction declines for longer paths.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across evaluated model populations, an integrated single-stage approach with a third convention available yields cost-effective transitions in 15–40% of cases, versus 12–23% for isolated two-stage routes over the same triplets.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The results concern a controlled naming-game model with homogeneous populations; the paper does not demonstrate attacks on deployed heterogeneous agent networks or validate real-world intervention success.

evidence_gaps.description: The reported model outcomes were not independently reproduced in this activation.
No evidence in the paper establishes that these convention dynamics occur in heterogeneous, deployed agent populations.

importance_rationale: If analogous tipping pathways occur in deployed interacting-agent populations, attackers or accidental perturbations could redirect collective conventions through intermediate states, changing how stability is assessed. Score 6 reflects the potential consequence of this bounded mechanism; the evidence is a controlled naming-game study, not a field demonstration.
limitations: This is a preprint and the findings are author-reported; no independent reproduction was run here.
The model uses homogeneous, fully connected populations and a naming-game coordination task, which narrows transfer to real agent networks.
The authors state that fewer than 10% of single-intermediate routes are sub-additive; advantageous routes are the exception in the modeled landscape.
No deployed attack, field measurement or validated defense is shown.
summary: A September 21 preprint studies how committed minorities can redirect conventions in homogeneous, fully connected naming-game populations of four open-weight LLMs. The authors report that fewer than 10% of single-intermediate paths reduce total committed effort versus a direct transition. In evaluated triplets, allowing a third convention during a single stage produces cost-effective transitions in 15–40% of cases across model populations, compared with 12–23% for isolated two-stage routes. These are results from a controlled model, not observed attacks or evidence about deployed heterogeneous agent networks.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report fewer than 10% of single-intermediate paths are sub-additive. For evaluated triplets, integrated single-stage competition with an additional available convention gives cost-effective transitions in 15–40% of cases versus 12–23% for isolated two-stage routes across the four modeled populations.
technical.compute_or_cost: Not a hardware or inference-cost result; transition cost is measured as committed population fraction and related path objectives.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint presents a model and reports simulated results over four homogeneous LLM populations; this activation inspected the paper text but did not rerun the simulations.
technical.implementation_status: Research model in a preprint; no deployed system or operational attack demonstrated.
technical.mechanism: Pairwise convention transitions are assigned critical-mass thresholds and connected into a directed transition landscape; path optimization then compares direct and intermediate routes, with both additive and maximum commitment costs.
technical.regime: Homogeneous, fully connected naming-game populations using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Phi-4, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B; controlled convention sets and committed minority interventions.
technical.reproducibility: Methods and supplementary figures are described in the preprint; no independent reproduction or model execution was performed in this activation.
technical.strongest_baseline: Direct pairwise convention transition; the comparison also includes isolated multi-stage paths over the same evaluated triplets.

title: A controlled agent-population study finds indirect convention shifts can lower tipping thresholds
why_it_matters: The paper suggests that pairwise tests of an agent population’s resistance may miss paths through intermediate conventions, while also finding those cost-reducing paths are uncommon in its model. If such structure transfers to deployed systems, safety evaluations may need to consider the available convention set and sequences of interventions. No real-world attack or mitigation effectiveness is established.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The preprint presents a recovery design combining initialized-engine snapshots, GPU Memory Service (GMS) for persistent read-only model allocations, and a preinitialized Shadow Engine.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across four eight-GPU model configurations on vLLM and SGLang, the authors report Shadow Engine recovery in 4.6–6.2 seconds, or 12.8–29.0× faster than their warm-restart baselines.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Replaying an 18-week production failure trace, the authors estimate the design could reclaim 79% of GPU-hours lost to recovery.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The reported fast path covers device-preserving engine-process failures; device-invalidating failures require rebuilding model state, and the production savings result is a replay estimate rather than prospective live deployment measurement.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of latency, memory overhead or production-trace savings was established in this activation.

importance_rationale: If fast recovery works across production workloads, it could materially improve inference availability and reduce capacity held to mask warm-restart windows. Score 6 reflects this systems-level consequence under device-preserving failures, not independent confirmation or universal transfer.
limitations: Results are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced in this activation.
The 12.8–29× figures are for eight-GPU replicas and injected engine-process failures where GPUs and model allocations survive; a device failure follows a slower rebuild path.
The comparison uses cached weights/compilation for warm restart; the paper says this is optimistic relative to most trace recoveries, but benchmarks remain specific to the tested systems.
The 79% GPU-hour benefit is estimated by replaying one production trace, not by a prospective deployment experiment.
Shadow engines consume 4.3–8.1 GiB per GPU in tested configurations; this is not literally zero-cost standby capacity.
summary: A Sept. 21 preprint from NVIDIA authors presents GPU Memory Service (GMS), initialized-runtime snapshots and Shadow Engines for recovering LLM inference replicas without reloading model weights when a worker process fails but its GPU remains intact. Across four eight-GPU model configurations on vLLM and SGLang, the paper reports Shadow Engine recovery in 4.6–6.2 seconds, 12.8–29.0× faster than a warm restart. A separate replay of the authors’ production failure trace estimates 79% of recovery-related GPU-hours could be reclaimed. These are author-reported results for device-preserving process failures; device loss and broader deployment behavior remain open.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report 12.8–29.0× lower recovery latency than warm restart across four eight-GPU model configurations and estimate 79% of recovery-related GPU-hours could be recovered on an 18-week production trace.
technical.compute_or_cost: Shadow Engine standby adds 4.3 GiB/GPU for Qwen3.8-27B and 7.4–8.1 GiB/GPU for larger tested models, trading KV-cache headroom for recovery speed.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper specifies and implements the above components. In the reported test setup, GMS + Shadow Engine recovery measured 4.6–6.2 seconds across four vLLM and four SGLang model/configuration rows; independent execution was not performed here.
technical.implementation_status: Paper reports implementations in Dynamo, vLLM and SGLang; code links are linked from the paper, but no build or independent reproduction was run in this activation.
technical.mechanism: Snapshots capture initialized engine runtime state while excluding request KV pages; GMS owns physical model-weight allocations outside engine processes so they survive device-preserving process failure and can be reattached read-only; a Shadow Engine shares model state and is promoted after failure, leaving recovery mainly to allocate fresh KV backing and register with the serving plane.
technical.regime: Eight GPUs per replica; Qwen3.8-27B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro across vLLM 0.27.1 and SGLang 0.5.18. Evaluated failure injection kills engine process trees while devices and resident allocations remain; separate device-invalidating recovery is slower.
technical.reproducibility: Paper contains configuration and workload details; code availability is indicated by authors. Independent reproduction and assessment of deployment prerequisites remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: Warm restart with model weights already in host page cache and compilation artifacts cached; authors describe this as optimistic relative to most recoveries in their production trace.

title: Dynamo paper reports GPU-resident state reuse cuts LLM-serving recovery to seconds
why_it_matters: If the reported results transfer to live serving, preserving resident model allocations while rebuilding runtime state could reduce capacity loss and spare-GPU overprovisioning for fault-tolerant inference. The immediate consequence is strongest for clusters where process failures leave devices and allocations healthy; this does not establish recovery from GPU/device failure.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors describe an instrument-mounted logger using inertial, time-of-flight and Hall sensors to estimate tool state without an external camera or tracker, with per-channel latency matching against robot ground truth.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The policy trained from hand-held instrument demonstrations completed appendectomy in three of four additional live rabbits under shared autonomy with the surgeon selecting the surgical phase.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report training on 849 in-vivo demonstrations from four live rabbits and use of a policy configuration selected through 31 simulator configurations.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The study is limited to four deployment animals on one day; the surgeon selected surgical phase because the vision-based predictor agreed with the surgeon on only 24.6% of policy control steps under the deployment endoscope.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent animal replication or human clinical evaluation was inspected; current report uses four deployment animals.

importance_rationale: If hand-held instrument sensing can repeatedly supply usable training demonstrations for robotic surgery, it could open a broader data source and alter surgical-policy development. The score reflects the potential pipeline consequence, not the small four-animal outcome or readiness for clinical use.
limitations: Author-reported, not independently reproduced in this activation.
The deployment set contains four live rabbits; the policy completed the task in three.
This was shared autonomy: a surgeon selected the phase because the vision-based phase predictor performed poorly under the deployment endoscope.
No human-patient or clinical safety evidence is reported.
The robot provides calibration ground truth and executes the policy, even though it did not collect training demonstrations.
summary: A Sept. 22 preprint reports an end-to-end pipeline that records instrument pose and jaw state from sensors mounted on a surgeon’s ordinary laparoscopic tools, aligns the sensor channels against robot ground truth, and trains a bimanual policy without robot-collected demonstrations. After closed-loop simulator selection among 31 configurations, the authors retrained on 849 demonstrations from four live rabbits and tested on four additional rabbits; the policy completed appendectomy in three of four under shared autonomy with electrosurgery armed. A surgeon chose the surgical phase because the vision-based phase predictor failed under the deployment endoscope. This is a small animal study, not full autonomy or clinical evidence.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report successful appendectomy completion in three of four additional live rabbits, with electrosurgery armed, after training on 849 hand-held in-vivo demonstrations; the surgeon manually supplied procedure phase.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint describes an end-to-end sensing and training pipeline. It reports 3/4 appendectomy completions on additional live rabbits under shared autonomy; no independent result was established here.
technical.implementation_status: Research prototype and two demonstration corpora are described as released by the paper authors; code/data were not independently run here.
technical.mechanism: A compact instrument-mounted logger combines IMU orientation, time-of-flight insertion depth and Hall-sensor jaw state. Per-channel latencies are aligned to robot ground truth before forming observation/action pairs. A diffusion policy with DINOv3 is selected using simulator closed-loop rollouts, then retrained on in-vivo demonstrations.
technical.regime: Bimanual laparoscopic appendectomy using two FR3 arms and standard instruments. Four live rabbits supplied demonstrations and four additional rabbits were deployment subjects; each deployment animal had one run. The study was submitted to ICRA 2027.
technical.reproducibility: Paper reports simulator and in-vivo protocol details and links data corpora. Independent replication, additional-animal testing and clinical translation are open.
technical.strongest_baseline: In simulator ablations, selected DINOv3 policy with one unfrozen block reached 81% full-approach completion versus 12% for ResNet-18 and 44% with frozen DINOv3; these are simulator configuration comparisons, not an independent baseline for live-animal completion.

title: Instrument-mounted demonstrations train an appendectomy policy tested in live rabbits
why_it_matters: If the pipeline generalizes, it could turn otherwise discarded motion from hand-held minimally invasive surgery into policy-training data and reduce dependence on robot-specific demonstrations. The current result is an early in-vivo animal demonstration with explicit human phase control, not evidence of patient safety or autonomous surgery.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The study evaluates two open-weight instruction-tuned models across medical misinformation and hate-speech tasks, using N=500 evaluation examples per domain and condition; override success is measured only on cases where the model’s instruction-free baseline conflicts with the target policy.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Zero-shot system prompting leaves 20.0%–49.1% of conflicting cases unresolved under the more permissive target policy across the reported model/domain conditions. Results differ by model and policy direction; LoRA improves some conditions and worsens others.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The paper describes behavioral results, not a mechanism proving why prior behavior persists; the results cover two open-weight models and two domains, and some medical LoRA training pools exhausted before the planned 1,500 examples.

evidence_gaps.description: Override-success and LoRA findings have not been independently reproduced with repeated seeds and additional models.
The divergence zones and policy mappings are constructed from observed baselines and selected label mappings; LoRA training pools were exhausted in some medical conditions.

importance_rationale: If replicated, policy override resistance that differs by model, policy direction and domain could change how operators assess controllability before deploying models under a policy different from their training prior. The study covers only two open-weight models and two domains and does not establish a universal failure rate.
limitations: Author-reported results; no independent reproduction was conducted.
Only two open-weight models and two policy domains were evaluated; results do not establish behavior for closed models or deployment settings.
Override success is conditional on empirically constructed policy-divergence cases and the chosen policy prompts and label mappings.
Some medical LoRA conditions exhausted the training pool well below the planned 1,500 examples, which may bias results.
The paper’s behavioral audit does not establish a mechanism or universal resistance to system prompts or fine-tuning.
summary: The Alignment Inertia preprint measures whether system prompts and LoRA fine-tuning override each model’s observed policy behavior on cases where that behavior conflicts with a target policy. It evaluates Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 on medical-misinformation and hate-speech datasets. Zero-shot prompting leaves some conflicting cases unresolved, with results varying by model, domain and policy direction; LoRA sometimes improves and sometimes worsens override success. These are author-reported behavioral results conditional on the study’s constructed divergence zones and adaptation data, not a universal measure of prompt or fine-tuning reliability.

technical.claimed_result: Across Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 on medical-misinformation and hate-speech datasets, zero-shot system prompts do not override every observed policy conflict. Under the permissive target policy, the reported residual inertia is 20.0%–49.1%; LoRA effects vary by model, domain and policy direction, including regressions.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint documents the protocol, datasets, models and author-reported measurements. No independent reproduction was performed.
technical.mechanism: The study defines each model’s empirical policy from an instruction-free baseline and measures override success only on examples where the target policy conflicts with that baseline. It compares zero-shot system prompting with LoRA adaptation and uses TRAK to analyze adaptation-example influence.
technical.novelty: An intervention-relative audit of whether downstream policy instructions override an empirically observed model behavior, separating prompt-time control from LoRA changes and measuring both permissive and restrictive policy shifts.
technical.regime: Two open-weight models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2); medical misinformation and hate speech; 500 evaluation examples per domain/condition; selected policy mappings and divergence zones. LoRA used target-policy examples but exhausted some medical pools below the 1,500-example target.
technical.reproducibility: The paper describes prompts, datasets, sample sizes and adaptation settings. the research desk did not reproduce the study; repeated-seed and independent-model validation remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: Instruction-free empirical baseline and the same model under zero-shot system prompting, compared with LoRA adaptation on target-policy examples. Measures are conditional on observed policy conflicts rather than a model-wide safety score.

title: Alignment Inertia measures when system prompts and LoRA fail to override prior behavior
why_it_matters: An operator may need to make a model more permissive or restrictive than its observed training prior. If the reported, direction-dependent resistance replicates, testing controllability on actual policy conflicts could expose cases that a generic instruction-following score misses. The study’s small model/domain set does not establish behavior across providers or deployments.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors introduce EmbodiedMemory-Bench with 2,554 interactive episodes spanning four embodied-task families and compare memory methods under matched backbones.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In Table 2, the authors report that adding maximal historical RGB context lowers Gemini-3-Flash average success rate by 10.4 percentage points in the reported comparison; the paper also reports task-specific gains for its external action-outcome memory under matched-backbone comparisons.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The paper describes evaluation as primarily simulated and reports that Robotics-ER coverage was reduced to a 10% subset because of API instability; physical-robot performance is not established.

evidence_gaps.description: The author-reported matched-backbone benchmark results have not been independently reproduced.
Most reported evaluation is simulated, and the Robotics-ER subset covers only 10% due to API instability; physical-robot performance and transfer are unknown.

importance_rationale: If the reported benchmark comparisons hold, task-specific action-outcome memory can outperform simply accumulating raw multimodal history in some simulated embodied-agent tasks, affecting memory design and evaluation for long-horizon agents. The paper does not establish physical-robot performance or broad transfer.
limitations: Results are reported by the paper authors and have not been independently reproduced.
Evaluation is primarily simulated; the paper does not establish physical-robot performance or deployment benefit.
Robotics-ER uses a 10% subset because of API instability, limiting coverage of that task family.
Task-specific matched-backbone results do not establish that action-outcome memory is superior across all tasks, models or memory budgets.
summary: The EmbodiedMemory-Bench preprint evaluates memory methods over 2,554 interactive episodes in four embodied-task families. The authors report matched-backbone comparisons for external action-outcome memory and show that adding maximal historical RGB context can reduce Gemini-3-Flash average success by 10.4 percentage points in the reported comparison. The results are primarily from simulation; the Robotics-ER subset is limited to 10% because of API instability. The paper does not establish physical-robot performance, independent reproduction or deployment benefit.

technical.claimed_result: The paper evaluates 2,554 interactive episodes in four task families. Its Table 2 reports task-specific matched-backbone comparisons for external action-outcome memory and reports a 10.4-point average-success decrease for Gemini-3-Flash when maximal historical RGB context is added.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accessible preprint documents its benchmark, methods and author-reported results. the research desk did not independently reproduce them.
technical.mechanism: External memory records action-outcome information for retrieval during embodied tasks; the benchmark compares this approach with alternative memory/context conditions, including accumulated visual history.
technical.novelty: A multi-task embodied-agent memory benchmark with matched-backbone comparisons that distinguishes structured action-outcome memory from raw multimodal context accumulation.
technical.regime: 2,554 interactive episodes across four task families, primarily simulated. Robotics-ER is represented by a 10% subset due to API instability. Reported results are bounded to the paper's tasks, models and memory configurations.
technical.reproducibility: The preprint provides benchmark and comparison descriptions. No independent reproduction was performed; physical-robot performance is not established.
technical.strongest_baseline: Matched-backbone memory/context conditions in Table 2. The paper's results are task-specific and do not show universal superiority across all tasks or memory budgets.

title: EmbodiedMemory-Bench reports simulation results for action-outcome memory
why_it_matters: The benchmark makes a concrete comparison between structured action-outcome memory and raw multimodal history in embodied-agent tasks. If the task-scoped results reproduce, they could guide memory-system design and evaluation. The result is simulation-bounded and does not support a physical deployment claim.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: CART uses a closed-loop Challenger–Target–Judge design in which findings from earlier rounds guide later probe selection and adaptation, while retaining probe lineage and scoring records.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across Frontier, JAH and Agentic case families, the authors report higher discovered failure rates and average risk scores with adaptive testing than direct replay of stored seed prompts for targets with available baselines; the largest separation is reported in Agentic evaluation.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The main comparisons fix Claude as Challenger and Gemini as Judge, and static replay uses the same Gemini Judge and scoring rubric; per-run budgets are 1,000 rounds for Frontier/JAH and 3,200 for Agentic.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The paper states that observed test-volume share is not real-world failure prevalence, capabilities and test sets differ across conditions, and Judge/Challenger pairing and risk-score calibration affect which evidence is found.

evidence_gaps.description: The adaptive-versus-static comparisons have not been independently reproduced with repeated seeds and independent probe generators or judges.
Adaptive and static probes can differ in capability coverage and difficulty, and the paper's composite risk score is not independently calibrated to real-world harm.

importance_rationale: If the paper's benchmark-scoped result generalizes, adaptive probe generation can reveal failures missed by static seed replay and change how red-team budgets are allocated for frontier models and tool-using agents. The result does not measure real-world failure rates.
limitations: Results are paper-reported and depend on the selected Challenger, Judge, prompts, budgets, seed sets and scoring rubric; no independent replication was performed.
Observed test-volume share and failure rates are not real-world prevalence estimates. Adaptive and static conditions can exercise different capabilities and test difficulty.
Risk scores are LLM-Judge dependent. The paper reports stronger peer agreement on binary verdicts than on rationales and score calibration.
Each Challenger–Judge interaction cell in the role matrix is one aggregate run, so interaction effects are not separated from run-level randomness.
Larger seed banks, taxonomies and budgets increase retrieval, inference and validation costs.
summary: The CART preprint presents closed-loop red teaming in which a Challenger adapts probes using earlier results while a separate Judge scores the evidence. Across Frontier, JAH and Agentic case families, the authors report higher discovered failure rates and average risk scores than direct replay of seed prompts for targets with available baselines. The main comparisons fix Claude as Challenger and Gemini as Judge; static replay uses the same Judge and rubric. Budgets are 1,000 rounds for Frontier and JAH and 3,200 for Agentic. The paper reports the largest gap on tool-mediated Agentic cases and says observed test-volume share is not a measure of real-world failure prevalence. The result supports adaptive testing as a way to expose benchmark-conditioned weaknesses, not a claim that deployed models fail at the observed rates.

technical.claimed_result: On Frontier and JAH suites (1,000-round per-run budgets) and an Agentic suite (3,200 rounds), adaptive testing reports higher failure rates and average risk scores than replaying stored seed prompts for available targets. The largest separation occurs in Agentic cases. In a separate 282-judgment peer audit, six independent peers agree on binary verdicts 98.9% of the time, while rationales and risk-score calibration are less stable.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accessible preprint defines the framework, evaluation data families, comparison protocol, scoring roles and author-reported results. No independent reproduction was conducted; the results remain claims from the paper.
technical.mechanism: CART separates a Challenger that creates or adapts probes, a Target that responds or acts, and a Judge that assesses evidence. It stores results and lineage and uses earlier findings to direct later testing under a fixed budget, with diversity controls to reduce repetitive probes.
technical.novelty: Adapts red-team probes during a fixed-budget run based on observed weaknesses while preserving lineage and separating generation, target response and judgment; contrasts this closed-loop search with direct benchmark seed replay.
technical.regime: Paper evaluations on three families: Frontier curated risk cases, JAH harmful/refusal/multistep benchmark cases, and Agentic cases involving tools, retrieved content, state and multistep actions. 1,000 rounds each for Frontier/JAH and 3,200 for Agentic. Targets include seven named model families. Results are observed under the authors' prompts, budgets, Judge, Challenger and risk rubric.
technical.reproducibility: The paper describes probe lineage, run budgets, random seeds, complete call logs and peer audits; the public preprint is inspectable. the research desk did not reproduce the experiments. Some role-comparison cells are one aggregate run, and the paper does not establish real-world prevalence.
technical.strongest_baseline: Direct replay of stored seed prompts, evaluated with the same Gemini Judge and rubric as CART. The main comparison fixes Claude as Challenger and Gemini as Judge; a separate Frontier-family experiment varies these roles. This controls evaluator identity for the static/adaptive comparison but does not establish that LLM-judged risk scores are ground truth.

title: CART reports adaptive red teaming finds failures missed by static prompt replay
why_it_matters: If the reported comparison holds, fixed benchmark prompts can understate weaknesses that appear when the test context adapts to earlier model behavior. Adaptive, provenance-tracked probes could change how model and agent evaluations allocate a fixed test budget. The paper's results are Judge- and setup-dependent and do not estimate real-world failure prevalence.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: COMPASS couples local language-model reasoning states to a learned multi-agent spatial transformer (MAST), which exchanges multi-hop neighbor information and emits low-level actions plus a feedback token.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: With a frozen Qwen3-1.7B reasoning engine trained on N=32 and N=64 expert rollouts, the authors evaluate 30-second flocking rollouts through N=1,024 agents and report heading error decreasing from 2.79° at N=8 to 0.34° at N=1,024.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report comparisons with a centralized Claude Opus 4.8 controller and a language-only communication ablation; they report fragmentation and slower movement for the language-only method at N=64 and reduced coordination for the centralized controller as team size grows.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The paper reports modeled flocking rollouts and held-out prompt trials, but does not report physical robot execution, deployment reliability, or transfer beyond the tested flocking and direction-command setup.

evidence_gaps.description: The scale, heading-error and coordination results have not been independently reproduced, and no author artifact was located or executed in this review.
Physical robot execution, communication delay/loss, energy cost, safety and failure recovery are not established by the reported modeled flocking rollouts.

importance_rationale: If the bounded rollout result is reproducible, decentralized learned coordination around language-model intent could change design choices for large simulated robot collectives. The evidence is one flocking task in modeled rollouts and does not establish physical deployment or broader transfer.
limitations: The paper reports modeled rollouts and does not describe a physical robot trial or hardware deployment.
Evidence is limited to flocking and direction-following; it does not establish transfer to manipulation, obstacle-rich navigation or heterogeneous fleets.
The 1,024-agent scale result is an author-reported rollout; no independent reproduction or artifact execution was performed.
The learned controller is trained on expert rollouts at N=32 and 64; transfer from those modeled training sizes to physical fleet behavior remains untested.
summary: A robotics preprint presents COMPASS, which couples per-agent language-model reasoning states to a learned multi-agent spatial transformer (MAST) that exchanges local neighbor messages and generates both low-level actions and a feedback token. The frozen Qwen3-1.7B configuration is trained on 32- and 64-agent expert rollouts, then evaluated in 30-second flocking rollouts up to 1,024 agents. The authors report mean heading error decreasing from 2.79° at N=8 to 0.34° at N=1,024, with comparisons against a centralized Claude Opus 4.8 controller and a language-only communication ablation. This is an author-reported result on a narrow modeled flocking task; the paper does not report physical robot trials, and independent replication or artifact execution was not performed.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report evaluating 30-second rollouts at N=8,16,32,64,128,256,512 and 1,024 after training on N=32 and 64. In the cardinal-direction scale experiment, heading error decreases from 2.79° at N=8 to 0.34° at N=1,024. The language-only communication ablation fragments the N=64 flock into 15 groups and averages 2.5 m/s versus a 5 m/s target.
