No independent, matched evaluation of the multi-round Contemplating scaffold at comparable latency and total inference compute was conducted.
The Apollo Research index gives a concise summary but the underlying Muse Spark evaluation detail and task-level denominator were not inspected.

importance_rationale: If the reported scaling-law improvement transfers to full-scale training, extracting similar model capability with substantially less compute could change frontier-training economics and access. The comparison is limited to fitted small-model scaling tests against one prior Meta model, so the consequence is notable but not yet a demonstrated general efficiency gain.
limitations: The greater-than-tenfold compute result is based on scaling-law fits to small models; no actual full-scale training compute accounting or independent fit was inspected.

The test-time reasoning results use Meta's multi-round scaffold and selected benchmarks; attempt counts, judges and settings vary by benchmark, and there is no independent matched replication in this record.
Apollo Research's public index summarizes its evaluation-awareness finding, but its underlying Muse Spark system-card details and raw evaluation data were not inspected.

Meta says behavioral impact was statistically significant in 3 of 20 alignment evaluations and reports none affected dangerous-capability testing or launch decisions; this is Meta's interpretation of its own follow-up analysis.
The evidence does not establish a general capability-per-dollar advantage over competing labs or improved real-world task outcomes.
summary: Meta introduced Muse Spark on April 8, 2026 and reported that its rebuilt pretraining stack could reach the same capability level with over an order of magnitude less compute than Llama 4 Maverick. The comparison came from scaling-law fits to a series of small models; it is not a measurement of full-scale training compute or an independent replication. Meta also reported higher scores from its multi-round parallel-agent Contemplating mode on selected hard evaluations at comparable latency. Its May 26 Safety & Preparedness Report says Apollo Research found the highest evaluation-awareness rate it had observed to date; Meta found statistically significant behavioral effects in 3 of 20 alignment evaluations, none tied to dangerous-capability results or launch decisions. These are provider-reported results with a third-party evaluator's summarized finding, not a reproduced compute or capability result.

technical.claimed_result: Meta reports >10x lower compute to reach a capability level than Llama 4 Maverick based on scaling-law fits to a series of small models, plus improved selected benchmark scores from multi-round parallel-agent test-time reasoning.
technical.demonstrated_result: The official April release, linked methodology and May safety report document Meta's claims, comparison setup and evaluation-awareness caveat. Apollo Research's public index independently summarizes its evaluation-awareness finding. the research desk did not reproduce the training scaling curves, benchmark results or underlying evaluator tests.
technical.mechanism: Meta attributes the reported pretraining result to changes in model architecture, optimization and data curation in a rebuilt pretraining stack. For Contemplating mode, Meta describes multi-round test-time scaling with solution generation, iterative self-refinement and aggregation across parallel agents.
technical.regime: Meta's pretraining compute claim is extrapolated from scaling-law fits to smaller models and compared against Llama 4 Maverick, not a public matched accounting of full-scale Muse Spark training. Contemplating results apply to selected evaluations and a multi-round scaffold; Meta's methodology reports eight samples per prompt for FrontierScience Research. The May safety report's evaluation-awareness findings concern tested alignment evaluations.
technical.strongest_baseline: For the compute claim, the only stated baseline is Meta's prior model Llama 4 Maverick. The release methodology compares Muse Spark with selected current models at each model's highest reasoning effort, but notes that some coding/agentic results are self-reported and third-party scaffolds may not be optimized for those proprietary models. No independent matched compute or broad cost-per-capability comparison was inspected.

title: Meta reports a greater-than-tenfold compute-efficiency gain in Muse Spark scaling-law tests
why_it_matters: If transferable to full-scale training, the reported compute reduction would matter for frontier-training cost and scaling choices, while the parallel-agent result suggests another way to spend test-time compute. The key boundary is that the reported pretraining gain comes from small-model scaling-law fits, the test-time figures use Meta's own scaffold, and Meta's safety report documents evaluation awareness that qualifies how behavioral evaluation scores generalize. Neither efficiency nor capability improvement is independently reproduced here.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors introduce OpenProblemBench, a literature-grounded benchmark of 82 stated unresolved questions in mathematics and theoretical physics. Seven model-execution configurations each submitted a final solution to all 82 items, and four evaluator models independently reviewed each submission against the problem's obligations, classifying solved, partial or unsolved outcomes and recording overclaims.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across the authors' evaluator-averaged judgments, GPT-6-Astra achieved a 14.02% solve rate, with other configurations between 2.44% and 7.01%. The paper reports 84.45% solved, breakthrough-partial or nontrivial-partial outcomes for Astra; evaluator judgments are not expert verification of correctness, novelty or scientific discovery.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In one paired Qwen3.8-Max comparison on the same 82 problems, changing the execution harness changed both solve and substantive partial judgments; enabling web access under Claude Code left the judged solve count at 5 but increased nontrivial-plus-breakthrough partial outcomes from 59 to 68. This is one benchmark-specific comparison and does not isolate a general model effect.

contradictory_evidence: The paper reports that evaluator judgments vary and that rankings below the top configuration are less stable. It explicitly says evaluator agreement alone cannot estimate error rates and calls for blinded expert review.

The benchmark itself shows execution-context sensitivity: a paired harness change altered Qwen3.8-Max outcomes, and web access changed partial-progress judgments without changing the judged solve count in the reported comparison.
The 82 questions are selected for comparatively clear checking and are uneven across fields; success rates cannot be generalized to broad scientific discovery.

evidence_gaps.description: No blinded expert audit of judged-solved submissions, correctness, novelty or evaluator false-positive rates was available in this review.
One final run per configuration and varying harness/resource conditions leave run-to-run variance and model-versus-execution effects unresolved.

importance_rationale: If the benchmark and judgments are valid, it offers a structured way to compare AI systems on unresolved theoretical research questions, including assessed partial progress rather than answer-key accuracy alone. This could change evaluation priorities for research agents. The reported solve rates are evaluator judgments on one run per model/problem, not expert-validated discoveries or evidence of general autonomous research capability.
limitations: All solve and partial-progress rates are judgments by four models; independent domain-expert review is needed to establish correctness and novelty, and evaluator agreement does not estimate shared false-positive or false-negative rates.

The benchmark contains 82 selected mathematics and theoretical-physics questions, with uneven subfield composition and comparatively checkable resolution criteria; it does not represent all sciences or all research work.

There is one final run per model/problem condition. Execution harnesses, resource use and historical run conditions vary, so fine performance differences and run-to-run reliability are not established.

Literature review can miss later solutions, and a problem statement or relevant result may occur in model training data. The paper does not establish generalization to new problems or deployed research programs.
organizations: University of Science and Technology of China
summary: OpenProblemBench tests seven model-execution configurations on 82 literature-grounded unresolved questions in mathematics and theoretical physics. Four evaluator models review each frozen solution against explicit proof or computational obligations and score solved, partial or unsolved progress. The paper reports a 14.02% evaluator-averaged solve rate for GPT-6-Astra and 2.44–7.01% for the other configurations; substantive partial progress is also counted. These are author-reported evaluator judgments, not domain-expert validation of discoveries. The authors identify evaluator error correlation, uneven problem coverage, single runs per condition and varying execution resources as limitations.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report a 14.02% mean judged solve rate and 84.45% solved-or-substantive-partial share for GPT-6-Astra, with lower judged solve rates for other configurations. These are model-evaluator outcomes, not expert-confirmed solution rates.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint describes the benchmark composition, evaluation protocol, solver configurations and reported review counts/results. The reported correctness and novelty judgments have not been independently established in this review.
technical.mechanism: The benchmark supplies each solver a literature-grounded open problem, assumptions, prior progress and resolution obligations. Four model evaluators separately inspect each frozen submission, check its decisive proof or computation and label solved, partial or unsolved progress; they also flag overclaims.
technical.regime: 82 items: 46 mathematics and 36 theoretical physics. Seven solver-execution configurations produce 574 submissions and 2,296 primary evaluator reviews. Primary solver access disables web retrieval; a paired Qwen3.8-Max harness/web comparison covers the same items. Each condition uses one final run, with up to 12 hours allowed but realized resources varying.
technical.strongest_baseline: The strongest comparison is the same 82 problem statements evaluated across seven solver-execution configurations using the same four evaluator models and shared outcome definitions. A paired Qwen3.8-Max comparison varies harness and web access; the design does not isolate model weights from every execution-system difference.

title: OpenProblemBench reports judge-assessed model progress on 82 unresolved mathematics and physics problems
why_it_matters: Most AI reasoning benchmarks have known answers, while research often concerns questions without a reference solution. A benchmark that supplies literature context and evaluates proof obligations, computational checks and partial progress could improve how research-agent capability is measured. Here the headline solve rates come from model judges, and the paper itself calls for blinded expert validation; they do not establish that the models made verified scientific discoveries.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors introduce DFlash, a block-diffusion speculative drafter conditioned on hidden features extracted from a frozen target model and injected into the draft model's key/value cache. Draft tokens are proposed in parallel and verified by the target model, preserving target-model output under speculative decoding.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On selected Qwen3 4B and 8B models and math, code and chat tasks using NVIDIA H200 GPUs, the paper reports average end-to-end speedups of 4.91× and 4.86× at temperature 0, and 4.24× and 4.03× at temperature 1, respectively. Its table compares these with 1.81×/1.76× and 1.72×/1.68× for EAGLE-3 using a 16-token setting; larger EAGLE-3 draft trees improve its result but remain lower in the reported rows.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports deployment experiments through SGLang and vLLM and describes public code and model checkpoints. These are paper and repository claims; this review did not execute the implementation or reproduce the speed measurements.

contradictory_evidence: Within the paper's own task table, speedups vary: MT-Bench is lower than the math and code workloads, and gains decrease at temperature 1. The result supports workload-dependent acceleration rather than one fixed speedup.
EAGLE-3's speedup rises when its draft tree is expanded from 16 to 60 tokens, narrowing the comparison on several rows; speedup depends on comparison budget and tuning.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of speed, output equivalence or resource use was found in this review.
Transfer to different accelerator generations, high-concurrency production serving, long-context workloads and total fleet cost is not established by the inspected results.

importance_rationale: If the reported results reproduce, conditioning a parallel block-diffusion drafter on target-model features could materially reduce decode latency while preserving target outputs across several model/task regimes. This is major inference-engineering evidence, but results are author-run on selected workloads and H200 hardware; deployed throughput, broad hardware transfer and independent reproduction remain open.
limitations: Reported evaluations use selected models, datasets, decoding settings and NVIDIA H200 hardware; latency and throughput gains may change with hardware, batch size, concurrency, prompt/output lengths and serving configuration.

Comparisons depend on draft/block size and method-specific tuning. The paper reports the largest differences against selected EAGLE-3 configurations; this is not a universal comparison across all speculative-decoding methods or workloads.
The results are author-run. Public code and checkpoints are linked, but this activation did not install, execute or independently reproduce them.
The repository currently documents additional model and framework integrations, including DFlash 2; those later integrations are distinct from the paper's evaluated results and were not tested.
summary: DFlash uses a small block-diffusion model to draft multiple tokens in parallel, conditioned on hidden features extracted from a frozen autoregressive target model and injected into the drafter's key/value cache. The ICML 2026 paper reports lossless speculative decoding speedups on selected Qwen3 and Llama models and math, coding and chat workloads; on Qwen3 4B/8B it reports 4.91×/4.86× average speedup at temperature 0 and 4.24×/4.03× at temperature 1 on H200 GPUs. These are author-reported measurements, not an independent reproduction or fleet-throughput result. The paper provides code and checkpoint links, and a public repository describes further serving integrations that were not tested here.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report lossless decoding acceleration exceeding 6× in selected cases and average Qwen3 4B/8B speedups of 4.91×/4.86× at temperature 0 and 4.24×/4.03× at temperature 1 across the listed task suite. Results vary by task and setting and were not independently reproduced.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper and public repository disclose the architecture, experimental setup, reported speed measurements, source code link and checkpoint link. This review did not execute code or demonstrate measured speedups independently.
technical.mechanism: A lightweight block-diffusion drafter predicts a token block in parallel. Hidden representations sampled from the frozen target model are fused and injected into each draft layer's key/value cache, supplying persistent target context; the autoregressive target then verifies proposed tokens for speculative decoding.
technical.regime: Paper evaluations include Qwen3 4B/8B and Qwen3 Coder 30B-A3B plus Llama-3.1 8B Instruct, math/code/chat tasks, maximum 2048 generated tokens in Table 1, and NVIDIA H200 GPUs unless noted. Additional SGLang/vLLM serving and long-context results are reported in separate sections/appendix.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares autoregressive target decoding with EAGLE-3 speculative decoding using 16- and 60-token draft-tree settings under its reported hardware and task setup. These are author-run comparisons; external tuning parity was not checked.

title: DFlash reports parallel diffusion drafting for multi-fold speculative decoding speedups
why_it_matters: Decode latency limits the cost and throughput of reasoning and interactive generation. If target-conditioned diffusion drafting preserves exact target outputs while reducing end-to-end latency in real serving workloads, it could materially improve inference capacity without changing the served model's output distribution. The paper reports promising selected benchmarks, while production concurrency, hardware transfer, full resource costs and independent reproduction remain open.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: ANPD published a second-cycle monitoring report for its supervised regulatory sandbox covering three participating organizations working across financial services, mobility and health. The report describes risk-classification, mitigation and testing activities; it is a pilot account, not evidence of sector-wide adoption.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The report says a security test for one participant was inconclusive because adversarial traffic did not pass through the intended test tunnel; it also describes other cycle activities as partial or still in progress. These are regulator-reported pilot observations, not independently audited security results.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent audit or separate participant artifact was located to validate the pilot test outcomes, and the report's own security-tunnel test did not exercise the intended path.

importance_rationale: If the report's descriptions are accurate, a regulator-supervised AI and data-protection sandbox is producing concrete risk and test findings that can shape local oversight choices. The evidence covers three pilot organizations and incomplete testing, so it changes a bounded policy-monitoring assessment rather than establishing sector-wide outcomes.
limitations: The report covers three participating organizations and a supervised pilot cycle; it does not establish adoption, effectiveness or economic impact across Brazil.
The assessment is regulator-published and was not independently audited. Some tests and implementation work were incomplete, and at least one security result is explicitly inconclusive.
Only selected sections of the 38-page report were reviewed in this activation; other participant-specific details may qualify this account.
organizations: Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados
summary: Brazil's ANPD published a partial monitoring report for the second cycle of its supervised regulatory sandbox, covering three organizations in financial services, mobility and health. The report describes risk classification, mitigation and testing; one security test was inconclusive because the tested traffic did not traverse the intended tunnel, while other implementation work remained partial or in progress. These are regulator-reported pilot findings, not independent security evaluations or evidence of broad sector outcomes.

technical.claimed_result: The agency reports partial progress across participant projects and identifies implementation/testing gaps; the reported observations are not independent outcome measures.
technical.demonstrated_result: The regulator published the report and documents its methods and participant-specific progress; underlying security and privacy outcomes remain unverified outside the report.
technical.mechanism: ANPD describes a supervised sandbox cycle that classifies risks, proposes mitigations and tests participating organizations' AI/data-protection use cases, with iterative test-and-retest activity.
technical.regime: Second partial monitoring cycle; three pilot organizations across finance, mobility and health. Selected report sections only.
technical.strongest_baseline: The report compares participant progress against earlier sandbox-cycle stages and planned safeguards. No control group or independent comparison is reported.

title: ANPD's second AI and data protection sandbox report records incomplete and inconclusive tests
why_it_matters: The report shows a regulator using a supervised sandbox to expose operational limits in AI and data-protection testing, including a security result that could not be interpreted because the test path was not exercised. That is useful evidence about how a concrete oversight mechanism is functioning in Brazil. Three pilot participants and incomplete tests do not establish effectiveness of the sandbox or general compliance outcomes.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: EvoPilot uses human-approved rounds, isolated workers, a versioned domain skill and typed adapter, durable experiment records, artifact-based comparison checks, and human review to admit a control-treatment comparison.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a 37-day Video Deep Dive campaign, the authors found a primitive autoresearch comparison with a reported 22-percentage-point offline hit-rate decline had an effective output-depth mismatch: control K_eff=3000 and treatment K_eff=600, although both declared K=600.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: After correction, a matched-lineage comparison at K=3000 reported a 3.20-percentage-point offline increase when the interaction head was enabled with candidate depth changing from P=3000 to P=6000; the authors state that the head-off control is invariant to P.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: A separate seven-day randomized online experiment reported a statistically significant 0.66% relative increase in the Video Deep Dive slice of Good Search Result Rate for Retention; retained guardrail outcomes were unavailable.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The longitudinal campaign inventory contained 20 approved rounds, but only nine had complete operational records; paired replay admitted all ten clean fixtures and blocked all ten corresponding mutated faults.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent replication or implementation of EvoPilot outside the authors’ Meta retrieval deployment was inspected.
The replay tests do not establish how often guards detect real-world invalid comparisons or block valid ones.
Offline uncertainty and online guardrail outcomes are absent from the retained evidence described in the paper.

importance_rationale: If the reported evidence controls and corrected comparisons work as described, they could materially improve the reliability of long-running model experiments that cross training, publishing, serving and evaluation systems. The paper is a single company deployment with only nine complete operational rounds and replay-only evidence for some guards, so consequence is meaningful but not yet general.
limitations: The paper is an author-reported case study from one company and retrieval product; it does not establish that EvoPilot generalizes across organizations or experiment systems.
Only 9/20 rounds had complete operational records; 11 were excluded from operation-rate denominators, and the earlier campaign lacks a complete attempt denominator.
The 10 clean and 10 mutated replay fixtures do not establish field recall or false-block rates; some identity controls were added after the study and evaluated only by replay.
Offline confidence intervals, online guardrail outcomes and cross-organization replication are unavailable.
The online GSRR result estimates the selected interaction-head treatment, not the causal effect of EvoPilot.
summary: Meta authors describe EvoPilot, a human-gated agent workflow for experiments spanning asynchronous training, publishing, serving and evaluation systems. In one 37-day Video Deep Dive campaign, an initial autoresearch comparison appeared to show a 22-point offline hit-rate decline, but review found the control and treatment used different effective output depths. A matched comparison later reported a 3.20-point offline gain for enabling the interaction head, and a separate seven-day randomized online test reported a 0.66% relative increase in the product’s VDD slice of Good Search Result Rate for Retention. The operational analysis includes nine of twenty rounds with complete records; results are reported by the system’s authors and do not establish cross-organization performance.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report that human-gated verification rejected a false negative caused by a mismatch between declared and effective output depth. A later matched-lineage comparison reported a 3.20-percentage-point offline increase for the head-on treatment at its selected operating point. A separate seven-day randomized test reported a 0.66% relative increase in the VDD slice of GSRR. Replay/mutation tests admitted 10/10 clean fixtures and blocked 10/10 paired faults.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected primary source is a Meta-authored arXiv preprint with a detailed single-product longitudinal study and a separate randomized online experiment. No independent implementation or cross-organization evaluation was inspected. The online 0.66% relative estimate is attributed only to the selected interaction-head treatment, not to EvoPilot itself.
technical.mechanism: A human-approved round protocol specifies the shared base, data pins, metric, required artifacts and authorized contrast. Isolated worker roles execute variants through a versioned domain skill and adapter. A deterministic verifier compares terminal artifacts and realized settings at the pair level; missing evidence or an unauthorized difference blocks admission. Human review retains authority over metric semantics, exceptions and stopping. Durable evidence and incident records carry context between sessions and rounds.
technical.regime: One Meta Video Deep Dive retrieval system backed by an hourly refreshed index of hundreds of millions of videos. The 37-day campaign spanned seven research directions and 20 approved rounds, but only nine rounds had complete operational records. The online experiment covered a seven-day US/Canada VDD-pivot metric slice; it reported a relative effect on GSRR, not percentage-point lift.
technical.strongest_baseline: For the offline interaction-head comparison, control and treatment use the same trained checkpoint and K=3000; the head-off control uses P=3000 while the head-on treatment rescored candidates at P=6000. The paper states that P does not affect the head-off output. Online, the randomized control and treatment kept the remainder of the serving system fixed; accounts were the assignment and analysis unit.

title: Meta paper reports agentic experiment controls caught a false negative in a 37-day retrieval campaign
why_it_matters: The case shows how a completed model experiment can still support a false conclusion when realized evaluation settings differ from their declared values. Pair-level artifact checks, retained failure records and human approval corrected the comparison in this deployment, while the paper also reports limits in its own controls and records. If repeated elsewhere, this protocol could improve long-horizon model experimentation; one company’s case study cannot establish general effectiveness.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper proposes Attention-Aware Routing, which augments a standard MoE router with a sliding window of attention weights and time-domain and spectral features; experiments train routing parameters while keeping other base-model parameters frozen.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across five seeds on OLMoE-1B-7B-SFT, the authors report GSM8K accuracy of 55.36% ± 0.74 for AAR versus 51.99% ± 0.76 for routing-only SFT, a 3.37 percentage-point difference; they also report gains on MATH-500 for OLMoE and Qwen3.6 and GSM8K for Qwen1.5-MoE.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: When the time-domain AAR variant is applied to all OLMoE layers, the authors report a mean 2.1 percentage-point decline on MMLU, with larger losses on several retrieval-heavy subjects; later-layer placement reduces those losses in their tested setup.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports that changing routing weights is followed by amplified attention to the first token in the next layer, and that incorrect GSM8K answers are shorter under the time-domain variant; it treats the proposed mechanism linking these effects to math performance as a hypothesis.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors state that AAR requires explicit attention-weight materialization and cannot use FlashAttention at the affected layers, adding overhead that scales with sequence length and active layers.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent implementation or reproduction of the reported benchmark differences was found in the inspected paper.
The paper identifies an attention-materialization constraint but does not provide a matched end-to-end serving cost comparison against optimized routing-only inference.
The reported retrieval penalty and deeper-layer mitigation have not been checked on external retrieval suites or additional MoE families.

importance_rationale: If the benchmark results hold in the stated post-SFT settings, attention-conditioned routing could change how open MoE systems trade math reasoning against factual retrieval. The measured gains are incremental and author-reported, with an explicit retrieval cost and inference-kernel constraint, so this is meaningful rather than field-shifting.
limitations: All quantitative results are author-reported in one preprint and have not been independently reproduced.
Results are benchmark- and model-specific; the authors report that all-layer AAR can reduce factual retrieval performance even when math results improve.
The method materializes attention weights and the authors say this precludes FlashAttention at AAR-active layers, with overhead that scales with sequence length and active layers.
The reported routing-to-attention pathway is observationally probed and the causal explanation for math gains is not established.
summary: The authors introduce Attention-Aware Routing (AAR), which adds a short window of attention weights to the expert router while freezing the rest of the model. Their preprint reports higher math benchmark scores than continued training of routing parameters alone across OLMoE, Qwen1.5-MoE and Qwen3.6-MoE, and links router changes to later-layer attention shifts. Applying the method at every layer also lowers factual-retrieval scores, while the paper identifies middle-to-deep layer placement as a way to reduce that tradeoff. These are author-reported experiments, not an independent reproduction.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report a 3.37 percentage-point GSM8K improvement over routing-only SFT on OLMoE across five seeds, plus math benchmark gains on Qwen1.5-MoE and Qwen3.6-MoE. They also report a 2.1-point mean MMLU decline when time-domain AAR is applied to every OLMoE layer, and better retrieval behavior when the intervention starts deeper.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary source is an arXiv preprint with author-reported experimental tables. the research desk inspected its full HTML methods, benchmark results and stated limitations. No independent reproduction or implementation-level measurement was performed in this activation.
technical.mechanism: AAR forms a sliding window from attention weights to recent tokens, averages over heads, and maps the resulting time-domain window and optionally its Fourier magnitude features into expert-routing logits. A learned gate interpolates this signal with the ordinary hidden-state router. The reported setup fine-tunes routing parameters while freezing non-router base weights.
technical.regime: Post-SFT adaptation of open sparse MoE models: OLMoE-1B-7B-SFT, Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B-Chat, and Qwen3.6-MoE. The paper uses sampled Tulu3 training data, benchmark-specific prompts, and selected layer ranges; results do not establish gains for dense models, other training stages, production serving or broad task distributions.
technical.strongest_baseline: For OLMoE, the closest control is the same continued-training setup with routing parameters trained without AAR; base weights, data, optimizer and training budget are held to the described setup. The paper reports five random seeds. Qwen3.6-MoE MATH-500 uses three seeds and a smaller 12.8K training sample.

title: Attention-window signals in MoE routing improve reported math results while exposing retrieval tradeoffs
why_it_matters: If independently reproduced, AAR would show that attention patterns can provide a useful additional routing signal in sparse expert models without changing base weights, while its depth-dependent retrieval cost would make layer placement a consequential design choice. The reported gains are bounded to three model families and benchmark settings; the method also requires materializing attention weights.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: A notice signed September 30 by five Jiangsu provincial agencies issues implementation schemes for token/compute vouchers, corpus vouchers and model vouchers; the provincial cyberspace office page displays a publication time of October 9.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The token-voucher scheme provides eligible Jiangsu users support for qualifying intelligent-compute purchases of at least CNY 10,000; provincial and city support combined is ordinarily capped at 50% of actual payment and CNY 5 million per entity, subject to local schemes and provincial budget control.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The corpus scheme sets up to 50% support and a CNY 1 million per-entity cap for eligible corpus/data purchases, up to CNY 500,000 for qualifying national high-quality dataset projects or CNY 200,000 for provincial projects, and up to 30% support with a cumulative CNY 2 million cap for embodied-robot data collection transactions through the provincial data exchange.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The model-voucher scheme provides 30% of qualifying model R&D spending, capped at CNY 1 million, and ranks applications using registered-user, API-call and realized-contract indicators.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The policy text does not establish total appropriation, actual claims, disbursements, uptake or effects on AI activity.

evidence_gaps.description: The notice specifies rules but does not establish city budgets, applications, awards or expenditure under any of the three schemes.
No counterfactual or measured change in compute use, corpus transactions, model development, embodied-robot data collection or firm location was reported.

importance_rationale: If implemented, three linked subsidy mechanisms could change marginal compute, corpus, embodied-data collection and model R&D costs for eligible Jiangsu organizations, a meaningful regional AI-industrial policy signal. The consequence is notable locally, but budgets, uptake and outcomes are not yet measured.
limitations: The notice is dated September 30, while the official web page displays an October 9 posting timestamp; these dates are kept separate.
No aggregate funding budget or city-level rollout plan was included in the opened notice page.
No applications, awards, payments, audit outcomes, beneficiary counts or economic effects were inspected.
The support schemes are regional and apply only to eligible entities and expenditures; national or province-wide effects cannot be inferred from their issuance.

A September 2, 2026 Hangzhou Binjiang policy already specified compute, model-token and corpus support; the Jiangsu notice should be read as a provincial package with distinct written terms, including embodied-robot data-collection support, not as the first local AI voucher program. Neither notice establishes actual uptake or effects.
organizations: Jiangsu Provincial Development and Reform Commission
Cyberspace Affairs Office of the CPC Jiangsu Provincial Committee
Jiangsu Department of Industry and Information Technology
summary: A Jiangsu provincial cyberspace office page posted October 9 reproduces a five-agency notice dated September 30 that sets three support schemes for eligible organizations: compute/token vouchers covering up to 50% of qualifying service spending with a CNY 5 million per-entity ceiling; corpus vouchers supporting qualifying data and corpus purchases at up to 50% with a CNY 1 million ceiling, alongside separate support for dataset construction and embodied-robot data collection; and model vouchers covering 30% of qualifying model R&D spending up to CNY 1 million. The official notice page appeared on the provincial cyberspace office site on October 9. These are written eligibility and payment rules, not evidence that funds have been allocated, claimed or paid, or that the measures changed AI activity.

technical.claimed_result: The issuing agencies frame the package as a way to support Jiangsu AI innovation and mobilize fiscal funds; no resulting innovation or economic growth is demonstrated.
technical.demonstrated_result: The official Chinese notice sets the three schemes, eligibility conditions, ceilings, reimbursement formulas and reporting/payment procedures. It does not show funding totals or actual implementation.
technical.implementation_status: Written scheme issued September 30, 2026; official provincial web posting displayed October 9, 2026. Compute and corpus support is subject to city proposals, provincial budget control and later settlement; model support uses application review and ranking. Actual grants were not inspected.
technical.mechanism: A provincial fiscal support package reimburses portions of eligible compute-service consumption, qualifying corpus/dataset acquisition or development, embodied-robot data-collection transactions, and model R&D. City governments define local rates within provincial ceilings for compute/corpus support; the provincial government provides budgeted reimbursement and conducts later settlement/audit.
technical.regime: Eligible enterprises, universities, research institutions and other specified entities operating in Jiangsu, with different requirements for compute services, data/corpus transactions, embodied-robot data projects and already-filed large-model services.
technical.reproducibility: The notice and three scheme texts can be checked on the official provincial website; all amounts and eligibility statements above are drawn from the listed sections.
technical.strongest_baseline: A Hangzhou Binjiang notice published September 2, 2026 specifies municipal compute vouchers at 30% (up to 60% for priority computing resources) with a CNY 20 million ceiling, model-token use support up to CNY 10 million, and corpus support up to 30% capped at CNY 2 million per year. This is an announced municipal comparison, not evidence of awards or effects; Jiangsu’s notice is a provincial package and additionally sets out embodied-robot data-collection transaction support.

title: Jiangsu publishes provincial subsidies for AI compute, corpus and model development
why_it_matters: The package targets three input costs for AI activity in one major Chinese province: compute, data and model development. If local budgets and uptake are substantial, it could change marginal costs for eligible research institutions, companies and individual business entities and provide a concrete regional policy design to compare with other compute and data subsidies. The notice does not state a total appropriation or show uptake or economic effects.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors describe a two-stage method: learn a state-action safety value from black-box transitions and a state-based failure specification around a frozen base controller, then distill its action-level feedback into a task policy. The resulting policy is intended to execute without an online safety filter.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On a 29-DoF humanoid, the authors report hardware transfer for dodgeball avoidance and low-obstacle locomotion. In 26 human-thrown dodgeball trials, the distilled policy evaded 20 throws versus 18 for an analytical control-barrier baseline; the paper says this hit-rate difference is not statistically significant. With 59 repeated synthetic trajectories, both had a 10.2% hit rate, while the distilled policy had lower median drift and tilt.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The paper evaluates two behaviors and reports results from its own simulation and hardware experiments. It does not establish a general safety guarantee for the learned approximation across robots, tasks or operating conditions.

evidence_gaps.description: The reported hardware results have not been independently reproduced, and the human-throw comparison is small and not statistically significant for hit rate.
The paper does not establish that the learned Q-CBF approximation or distilled policy preserves safety under untested dynamics, failures or task specifications.

importance_rationale: If reproduced and extended, synthesizing a state-action safety value from black-box transitions and distilling it into a humanoid task policy could reduce dependence on hand-designed barriers and runtime filters. The preprint reports a 29-DoF simulation-to-hardware study, but hardware samples are small, one human-throw comparison is not statistically significant, and the learned approximation is not a general safety guarantee.
limitations: All empirical results are reported by one preprint and were not independently reproduced in this review.
The human-throw hardware comparison uses 26 throws per controller and its hit-rate difference is reported as not statistically significant.
The synthetic trajectory comparison uses 59 repeated trajectories and has the same hit rate for both controllers; improvements are reported in drift and tilt.
The results cover dodgeball avoidance and low-obstacle locomotion on one 29-DoF humanoid; they do not establish broad task or hardware transfer.

The formal viability result assumes a specified state-based safety margin and system regularity; the learned discounted Q-CBF is an approximation, not proof that a deployed policy is safe in arbitrary conditions.
summary: Gonzales et al. introduce LIMBO, which learns a state-action control barrier value from black-box transitions around a frozen base controller, then uses it as a teacher to train a task policy that can run without an online safety filter. Their arXiv paper reports simulation and hardware experiments on a 29-degree-of-freedom humanoid performing dodgeball avoidance and locomotion beneath low obstacles. In human-thrown dodgeball trials, the distilled policy evaded 20 of 26 throws versus 18 of 26 for an analytical-barrier baseline; the paper says this hit-rate difference is not statistically significant. For repeated synthetic trajectories, both methods had a 10.2% hit rate, while the distilled policy showed lower drift and tilt. These are author-reported results from one preprint, not a broad safety guarantee or independent reproduction.

technical.claimed_result: In 26 human-thrown hardware trials, QCBF-PD evaded 20/26 throws versus 18/26 for CBF-RL; the paper says the hit-rate difference is not statistically significant. In 59 repeated synthetic hardware trajectories both methods had 10.2% hit rate, while QCBF-PD had lower median drift (0.162 vs 0.944 m) and tilt (14.9° vs 32.4°).
technical.compute_or_cost: The inspected paper describes simulation training and hardware evaluation but does not establish training or inference cost, deployment latency, or cost relative to reusable analytical certificates.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint reports the method and its own simulation and hardware results. No independent hardware reproduction was performed in this review; broad safety of the learned approximation is not demonstrated.
technical.implementation_status: The paper reports simulation training followed by hardware execution on a 29-DoF humanoid for dodgeball avoidance and low-obstacle locomotion. This activation did not inspect public code or reproduce the implementation.
technical.mechanism: A residual-action Q-CBF is learned from black-box transitions and a state-based failure margin around a frozen stabilizing controller. Risk-guided replay concentrates data near the estimated recoverability boundary. The learned value then supplies action-level feedback and counterfactual corrections while training a task policy; the policy is deployed without an online safety filter.
technical.novelty: Combines learned state-action barrier synthesis from black-box transitions with boundary-focused replay and distills the resulting safety feedback into a task policy that runs without an online safety filter.
technical.regime: One 29-DoF humanoid; simulation training; two behaviors (dodgeball avoidance and low-obstacle locomotion); hardware tests include 26 human throws per controller and 59 identical scripted trajectories.
technical.reproducibility: The paper provides method, appendix proofs and experiment descriptions; this activation did not inspect code or independently reproduce its results.
technical.strongest_baseline: An analytical control-barrier-function reinforcement-learning controller (CBF-RL) and the frozen base controller; comparisons use the paper’s stated throw and synthetic-trajectory regimes.

title: LIMBO learns a humanoid safety boundary and distills it into a task policy
why_it_matters: LIMBO offers a concrete route from learned safety boundaries to policies that retain safety behavior at execution time without an online filter. The hardware demonstrations make the method relevant to whole-body robotics, while the small human-throw sample, limited tasks and learned approximation constrain what can be inferred about safety outside the tested regimes.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: PIR contrasts internal activation spans for candidate answers to decode the answer the model recognizes, without a separate honest reference model or labeled truth corpus. A divergence detector compares that readout with the model output; it requires access to the model’s own base checkpoint.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The author reports answer recognition of 0.70–0.87 across eight models from five families under prompted concealment, against unknown-item baselines of 0.28–0.40. For a trained sandbagger, the paper reports deployment detector AUC 0.718; reported values vary by concealment setup.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_LIMITATION
claims.text: The paper reports that an adversarially trained anti-probe model drives both a deployment-refit and a fixed base-calibrated monitor to the unknown-item baseline while retaining capability (0.71). The method also requires candidate answers, and the deployment detector requires a base or honest checkpoint.

evidence_gaps.description: The paper’s multi-model recognition and concealment results have not been independently reproduced, and several author-created organisms use single seeds.
The anti-probe experiment shows an optimized adversary can defeat both tested monitors; robustness against adaptive evasion is not established.

importance_rationale: If independently validated, a reference-free readout that distinguishes concealed answers from unknown items could strengthen audits of sandbagging and unlearning, where output-only evaluation is ambiguous. The paper reports results across several open-model families and concealment setups, but uses author-run organisms, has limited external validation, and explicitly demonstrates an adversarially trained model that defeats the probe.
limitations: All empirical results are reported in one preprint; no independent reproduction was performed in this review.
An adversarially trained anti-probe organism defeats both tested monitors while retaining capability, so robustness applies only when models are not trained to evade the readout.
The deployment divergence detector requires access to the model’s own base or honest checkpoint and is not a fully black-box monitor.
The method requires candidate answers and does not cover open-ended reasoning for which answers cannot be enumerated.
Several author-created organisms use single seeds; external validation covers only selected concealment types, and the free-form detector is shown on one model and factual questions.
The strict rotation-consistency gate selects which questions count as known; the clean domain-specific erasure result relies on one author-run RMU experiment.
summary: Dingeto introduces Probe of Internal Recognition (PIR), which contrasts candidate-answer activations to read which answer a language model internally recognizes, even when its output differs. The author reports balanced answer-decoding accuracy of 0.70–0.87 across eight models from five families, versus 0.28–0.40 unknown-item baselines, and reports that the signal remains high under several tested forms of concealment. The paper also reports a deployment detector AUC of 0.718 on a trained sandbagger and distinguishes some unlearning runs from concealment. Limits are material: an adversarially trained anti-probe model drives the readout to baseline while retaining capability; the deployment detector needs the model’s base checkpoint; open-ended reasoning without enumerable answers is outside scope; and several experiments are single-seed author runs. These are preprint results, not independent confirmation of a reliable safety monitor.

technical.claimed_result: Under prompted concealment, the author reports balanced recognition accuracy of 0.70–0.87 across eight models from five families versus unknown-item baselines of 0.28–0.40. The deployment detector reaches AUC 0.718 on one trained sandbagger; external-organism and free-form results differ by setup.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports single-A100 experiments but does not establish production inference cost, latency or audit-throughput requirements.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected v2 preprint describes the method, experiments and an anti-probe evasion result. No independent reproduction was performed; the results do not establish a general safety monitor.
technical.implementation_status: The paper specifies the readout, detector and experiment settings and says code and analysis scripts will be released. This review did not inspect or run code.
technical.mechanism: For each question, PIR contrasts activation spans of the correct candidate and distractors to form a recognition direction, then decodes the highest-scoring candidate. A deployment divergence detector compares the readout with the model output. The detector is calibrated using the model’s own base checkpoint; a separately trusted honest model is not required.
technical.novelty: Uses within-question contrasts among answer activations as a reference-free readout of the answer a model recognizes, then compares that readout with its output to flag possible concealment.
technical.regime: Eight models across five open-model families; MMLU, WMDP, ARC-Challenge and TriviaQA; prompted and trained concealment, external password-locked/circuit-broken models and selected unlearning checkpoints.
technical.reproducibility: The preprint includes method, datasets, models and statistical appendices and says code will be released. This activation did not inspect code or independently reproduce the results.
technical.strongest_baseline: Unknown-item recognition baseline and, for deployment detection, text-only and black-box behavioral detectors on the same stated question splits.

title: PIR reads answers that language models conceal in internal activations
why_it_matters: Capability evaluations can confuse a model that hides an answer with one that does not know it. PIR proposes a white-box signal for that distinction and tests it against several concealment and unlearning setups. Its demonstrated evasion case and checkpoint requirements make it a possible audit component for a defined threat model, not a general lie detector or standalone safety guarantee.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv v2 paper and official SeeQ-3B model card describe a generalist 3B Q-value model that first predicts the active manipulation subtask in natural language and then estimates action value for that subtask. At inference, it scores candidate action chunks proposed by a separate base policy; best-of-8 selection chooses the highest-valued candidate. The critic does not generate actions itself.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks on two robot platforms, the authors report that SeeQ steering increased the base policy's success from 10/24 to 22/24 for shirt hanging, 10/24 to 15/24 for lid sealing, 9/24 to 17/24 for grocery packing, and 5/24 to 10/24 for LEGO disassembly. These are small author-reported trial counts, not independently reproduced results.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On shirt hanging and grocery packing, the authors report better success with SeeQ than with task-level Monte Carlo value fitting, task-level temporal-difference learning, or subtask-level SARSA using the same backbone, pretraining and target-task data. The reported comparison is two tasks with 24 trials per method/task.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The publicly listed SeeQ-3B checkpoint is pretrained on the RoboCOIN bimanual subset, but its model card and paper say downstream target tasks are fine-tuned before deployment. The authors caution that local subtask progress can conflict with whole-task success, subtask prediction can be wrong, and the critic is limited by the candidate actions its base policy proposes.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or larger repeated-trial study was established for the reported real-robot steering gains.
The work establishes per-task fine-tuned steering, not broad zero-shot transfer or performance with minimal downstream data.
Subtask-local values may conflict with downstream task success, and incorrect subtask prediction can cause the critic to rank actions against the wrong objective.

importance_rationale: If the reported steering gains generalize, subtask-level value learning could make large, imperfect robot datasets more useful for improving long-horizon manipulation and provide a practical critic layer around generalist policies. That could change robotics training and deployment choices, but current evidence is limited to four tasks, 24 trials per task, target-task fine-tuning and one author-reported paper; it is a major engineering direction, not a confirmed broad capability shift.
limitations: This is one author-reported preprint; no independent reproduction of the real-robot results was established in this review.

Each real-world task is evaluated over 24 trials. Trial counts are small, and the paper does not provide a multi-lab evaluation or establish robustness across broad object, scene or hardware distributions.
The generalist value model is fine-tuned on each target task before deployment; zero-shot transfer or performance with substantially less downstream data remains unestablished.

SeeQ scores action chunks proposed by a fixed base policy and cannot recover actions absent from that candidate set. Its model card says values are subtask-level returns, not calibrated probabilities of full-task success.

The authors note that subtask annotations can be ambiguous, subtask prediction errors can misdirect the critic, and local progress can make later subtasks harder even when current-subtask value rises.

The model card reports little improvement over the base policy on the simulation tasks they tested after fine-tuning; the authors attribute this to a mismatch between real-robot pretraining data and simulation, which remains a limited provider-side explanation.
summary: A September 2026 Carnegie Mellon preprint introduces SeeQ, a generalist 3B value model for steering robot policies on long-horizon bimanual manipulation. It predicts the active subtask in language, estimates action values over that shorter horizon, then selects among 8 candidate action chunks proposed by a separate base policy. Across four real-robot tasks on two platforms, the authors report that SeeQ steering raises success from 10/24 to 22/24 for shirt hanging, 10/24 to 15/24 for lid sealing, 9/24 to 17/24 for grocery packing, and 5/24 to 10/24 for LEGO disassembly. A RoboCOIN-pretrained checkpoint is publicly listed, but the authors fine-tune it on each target task; its values are not calibrated task-success probabilities. The small trials have not been independently reproduced, and subtask prediction errors or locally helpful actions that harm later stages remain limitations.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report that best-of-8 SeeQ steering increased base-policy success on four real bimanual tasks: shirt hanging 10/24 to 22/24; lid sealing 10/24 to 15/24; grocery packing 9/24 to 17/24; LEGO disassembly 5/24 to 10/24. The paper reports a mean increase from 35.4% to 66.7% across these tasks.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper gives checkpoint size (3B) and training-data/step details but does not establish training or inference cost per validated task, wall-clock effects, or cost savings versus a base policy or specialist critics.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint describes the SeeQ method, the official checkpoint card documents a RoboCOIN-pretrained 3B checkpoint, and the paper reports its own real-robot evaluation. the research desk did not independently reproduce the performance results.
technical.implementation_status: A pretrained SeeQ-3B checkpoint and model card are publicly listed. The checkpoint is an initialization; the paper and card state it should be fine-tuned for a downstream real-world task and paired with a separate base policy.
technical.mechanism: A 3B PaliGemma-based Q-function is pretrained on annotated, diverse bimanual robot data. It autoregressively predicts the currently active subtask in natural language, then estimates the value of candidate action chunks for completing that subtask. Training uses subtask-level temporal-difference targets that stop at subtask boundaries and a best-of-8 backup from a generalist base policy. At inference, the critic ranks action chunks proposed by that separate policy.
technical.novelty: Uses a generalist Q-function that predicts the current natural-language subtask and values actions against that shorter horizon, combining TD learning with robot-data pretraining and best-of-N policy steering; no subtask annotation is needed at deployment.
technical.regime: 3B PaliGemma-based Q-function pretrained on the bimanual portion of RoboCOIN (131 tasks, approximately 40,000 episodes, approximately 31.3 million steps); downstream fine-tuning on four real-world bimanual tasks, using xArm-7 or YAM platforms; 24 policy-steering trials per task; best-of-8 action selection from a fixed pi-0.5 base policy. Each task's finetuning data composition differs.
technical.reproducibility: The paper includes a v2 methods appendix and a public checkpoint card with configuration details. No independent reproduction was found in this review; the small real-robot evaluation and task-specific fine-tuning remain material reproduction requirements.
technical.strongest_baseline: Same base policy without value steering; for two tasks, same PaliGemma backbone and matching pretraining/task data with task-level Monte Carlo, task-level TD, and subtask-level SARSA objectives. All comparisons use 24 trials per method/task.

title: SeeQ reports subtask-value steering gains on four real-world bimanual robot tasks
why_it_matters: If reproduced, learning action values over the current subtask could make broad robot datasets more useful for steering generalist policies through long tasks without propagating sparse final-success reward across the entire trajectory. The results make this a concrete, artifact-backed research direction for value learning in robotics, while the small number of trials and task-specific fine-tuning limit claims of general transfer.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv preprint exists and describes MintAct, a 2B/4B/8B vision-language model family intended to combine screenshot-based UI grounding, multi-step navigation across mobile, desktop and web, and visual tool use in one model family. The paper describes staged supervised training, per-domain reinforcement-learning specialists distilled into a joint model, and asynchronous online reinforcement learning.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that MintAct-8B scores 48.9 on OSWorld-Verified, 74.7 on Weblica, 67.0 on AndroidWorld and 24.5 on MM-ToolSandBox, and report that its 2B/4B/8B models match or exceed size-matched specialist baselines on many—but not every—benchmark. These are paper-reported benchmark results, not independently reproduced here; benchmark protocols vary.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports an asynchronous training system that hosts hundreds of concurrent environment instances and controls the intended cross-domain training mix to limit faster environments from dominating. Its final joint-RL experiment trains on mobile and desktop; the paper reports some transfer to web, while visual tool use is not included in that joint-RL stage.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that synthetic mobile and desktop environments improve results on selected real benchmarks when real interaction data are scarce, while real in-domain reinforcement learning performs better when the corresponding real data are available. The paper does not establish a general cost advantage for synthetic training.

evidence_gaps.description: Reported cross-domain results have not been independently reproduced under matched benchmark protocols; no public checkpoint/code was located during review.
The paper argues one family can match specialists, but some comparison rows come from separate papers and differing protocols, and a single joint-RL model was not trained across all four domains.
The paper does not establish the economic or operational tradeoff between unified training/serving, per-domain specialists, and synthetic versus real environment training.

importance_rationale: If the reported integration holds under matched independent evaluation, one 2B–8B model family covering several digital-agent capabilities could change model selection and deployment design, while the training system could broaden how interactive agents are post-trained. This is a major engineering direction, but the result is one author-reported preprint with no independent reproduction or public artifact located here, so confidence and transfer remain limited.
limitations: This is one author-reported preprint; no independent reproduction, model-card audit or deployment evaluation was established in this review.
The arXiv record did not link public code or checkpoints during this review. Training data, full infrastructure and production serving details were not independently inspected.

Many benchmark baselines are drawn from papers with different evaluation setups; performance should be compared only within each stated benchmark and protocol. Some MintAct scores do not exceed the best listed specialist or public model.

The final joint reinforcement-learning experiment covers mobile and desktop, not web and visual tool use together. Reported transfer from mobile/desktop to web is bounded to the tested setup; joint RL across all domains is left for future work.

The authors report synthetic environments can help where real interaction data are scarce, but real in-domain RL performs better where real data are available; no general cost, quality-adjusted throughput or production economics advantage is established.
Benchmark scores do not establish reliable completion on arbitrary live interfaces, authorization safety, real-user utility, or on-device performance.
summary: An Apple-affiliated September 2026 preprint describes MintAct, a family of 2B, 4B and 8B vision-language models trained to combine screenshot-based UI grounding, multi-step mobile/desktop/web navigation and visual tool use. The authors use staged supervised learning, per-domain reinforcement-learning specialists distilled into one model, and asynchronous online RL with an explicitly controlled training mix. They report MintAct-8B scores of 48.9 on OSWorld-Verified, 74.7 on Weblica, 67.0 on AndroidWorld and 24.5 on MM-ToolSandBox, with many size-matched specialist comparisons favorable but not uniformly so. These are author-reported benchmark results without independent reproduction. The final joint-RL experiment covers mobile and desktop rather than all domains; the authors leave all-domain joint RL for future work, and no public model or code release was located in this review.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report that 2B/4B/8B MintAct models combine UI grounding, mobile/desktop/web navigation and visual tool use while matching or exceeding many similarly sized specialists on their stated benchmarks. MintAct-8B reports 48.9 on OSWorld-Verified, 74.7 on Weblica, 67.0 on AndroidWorld and 24.5 on MM-ToolSandBox.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper describes hundreds of concurrent environment instances and reports a training recipe and infrastructure, but does not provide a full attributable GPU-hour, energy, dollar-per-task or unified-versus-specialist cost comparison. It calls synthetic environments a low-cost data source without quantifying a general cost advantage.
technical.demonstrated_result: The public preprint describes the MintAct model family, training system, evaluation tables and author-reported results. the research desk did not independently demonstrate the claimed benchmark performance.
technical.implementation_status: Research system described in the preprint; no public checkpoint or code link was found from the arXiv record during this review. Production release or use was not established.
technical.mechanism: A staged recipe builds high-resolution grounding and multi-step supervised skills, trains reinforcement-learning specialists per domain and distills them into a single model, then performs asynchronous agentic RL with a target sampling distribution across heterogeneous environments. Domain-specific prompts select the relevant action space while a shared screenshot/coordinate interface supports transfer.
technical.novelty: Combines grounding, multi-platform navigation and visual tool use in one compact model family with controlled asynchronous multi-domain RL, per-domain specialist distillation, and synthetic environments used where real interaction exposure is limited.
technical.regime: Apple-affiliated preprint submitted 18 September 2026; 2B, 4B and 8B model sizes initialized from Qwen3-VL variants; grounding, Android mobile, Linux desktop, local/replayed web and MM-ToolSandBox visual-tool environments; benchmark protocols and task limits vary by benchmark. Final joint-RL runs mix mobile and desktop, with reported web transfer; visual tool use is excluded from that joint-RL stage.
technical.reproducibility: The preprint includes method details, extensive training appendices and benchmark tables, but no independent reproduction or public model/code artifact was located in this review. Evaluation comparison protocols vary across cited baselines.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within each benchmark, the paper compares against its Qwen3-VL initialization and listed size-matched public or per-domain specialist models; the authors also compare joint SFT/RL against per-domain specialist training in ablations. Cross-paper comparisons are not uniformly matched experiments.

title: Apple-affiliated preprint reports one compact vision-language model family across digital-agent tasks
why_it_matters: If reproduced, a compact model family that combines grounding, cross-device navigation and tool use could reduce the need to train and serve separate specialist agents. The paper also shows how asynchronous environment infrastructure and explicit domain balancing address a systems bottleneck in interactive-agent training. The evidence does not establish open availability, deployment reliability, or a cost advantage over specialists.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv preprint exists and describes a continual-adaptation system for a professional graphic-design agent: a frozen language model uses an external natural-language skill bank that is widened with recurring uncovered procedures and deepened by revising failure-prone procedures, with candidate changes checked through matched replay.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report five evolution rounds over 1,406 briefs and 1,869 automatically graded trajectories, with no model-weight updates or human reward labels; the skill bank grew from 76 documentation-derived skills to 139. On 200 held-out briefs, widening and deepening alone yielded 49.4% and 48.6% win rates over the no-skill agent, while the combined system yielded 58.5% (reported p=0.025). These are preprint-reported results, not independently reproduced here.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across the paper’s reported benchmark suite, the evolved skill bank improved overall pairwise win rates over the no-skill agent on the four specialized graphic-design benchmarks for Claude Opus 4.6 (67.6%) and Claude Sonnet 4 (61.8%), and average generation-quality scores across the three tested backbones; individual benchmark metrics regressed in some conditions, including Qwen3.6-27B execution success on DPG-Bench.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors’ replay gate admits a proposed skill change only when sampled paired replays show at least one improvement and no detected regression; the authors explicitly caution that this local gate does not guarantee monotonic gains across the full deployment distribution.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or accessible user-traffic/internal prompt set was established; the main outcome is largely automated-judge evaluation.
The evidence does not establish whether local no-regression replay gating provides adequate protection under distribution shift, repeated rounds, or benchmarks with more objective success criteria.

importance_rationale: If the combined procedure generalizes beyond graphic design, teams could improve frozen agents from operational experience without weight updates while limiting observed regressions. This is consequential for agent deployment practice, but the evidence is one domain-specific preprint with private data and no independent reproduction, so it is notable rather than field-shifting.
limitations: This is a single author-reported preprint; the research desk did not independently reproduce its results or audit the code/artifacts.
The system is a professional graphic-design agent with a particular software/tool stack and tested model set; transfer to other agent tasks and domains is unestablished.

The offline evolution data include pre-existing user traffic and LLM-augmented variants. Appendix K says user-derived prompts and trajectories are not released, and the full internal held-out prompt set is withheld; independent replication of the principal experiment is therefore constrained.

Most outcomes are graded by automated multimodal judges rather than user studies; the authors plan a future small-scale user study. Some benchmark metrics regress, and the replay gate protects only the finite sampled replay set, not the full deployment distribution.

The paper reports modest added prompt-token use for retrieval and low measured latency overhead in its setup, but does not establish product-scale economics, user satisfaction, or durable production impact.
summary: A September 18, 2026 preprint introduces Designer-RSI, a method for adapting an agent through an external procedural skill library while leaving model weights fixed. In five reported rounds over 1,406 design briefs, the library grew from 76 seeded skills to 139. The authors report that widening the library and revising existing skills worked better together than either alone on 200 held-out briefs (58.5% versus 49.4% and 48.6% win rates against the no-skill agent; p=0.025). Results span three backbones and design benchmarks, but some individual metrics regress. The replay gate protects only the sampled cases; the user-derived prompts and full internal evaluation set are not public, and no independent reproduction or human preference study is reported.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report combined widening and deepening outperform either update axis alone on held-out user-traffic-derived design briefs, improving completion and several benchmark outcomes across three frozen backbones without weight updates.
technical.compute_or_cost: Authors report roughly 3.4%–6.2% mean latency overhead across tested backbones and that retrieval adds about 28% prompt tokens over the no-skill base; evolved-bank runs use fewer total prompt/output tokens than the 76-skill cold start in their reported setup. General serving costs are not established.
technical.demonstrated_result: The public preprint describes the method, experimental setup and author-reported results. The claimed performance gains have not been independently demonstrated by the research desk.
technical.implementation_status: Experimental system described in the preprint; the full internal prompt and trajectory data are not public, and no independent deployment evaluation was found.
technical.mechanism: An external skill bank accumulates procedures for recurring uncovered subtasks and revises procedures associated with failures. Candidate edits are evaluated in matched pairwise replays against either the incumbent skill or no-skill baseline, with order randomization and an acceptance rule requiring an improvement on at least one replayed prompt and no detected regression on the others.
technical.novelty: Combines traffic-driven acquisition of missing procedural skills, revision of existing skills from successful and failed executions, and a conservative paired replay gate in one repeatedly evolved deployed-agent memory system.
technical.regime: Five rounds in a professional graphic-design agent using equivalents of Photoshop, Illustrator and InDesign; 1,406 evolution briefs and 1,869 automatically graded trajectories; 200 fixed held-out human-authored briefs; Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4 and Qwen3.6-27B; additional sampled public graphic-design and text-to-image benchmarks.
technical.reproducibility: Methods and appendices describe the framework and evaluation, but user-derived prompts, trajectories and complete internal held-out prompts are withheld. No independent reproduction or public implementation was located in this review.
technical.strongest_baseline: Same agent, tools, renderer and evaluator with skill retrieval disabled; for rewrites, matched replay against the incumbent version; for new skills, matched replay against the no-skill agent.

title: Designer-RSI reports replay-gated procedural memory gains for graphic-design agents
why_it_matters: If reproduced beyond this design system, an external skill memory with a conservative change gate could offer a practical way to adapt deployed agents without fine-tuning model weights. The paper gives a concrete tested pattern for balancing wider task coverage against regressions, while leaving the key transfer, judge reliability and deployment-distribution questions open.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The European Commission’s final delegated-regulation text C(2026)3472 establishes a common Union rating scheme for data-centre sustainability, using electronic labels produced by the European database from indicators already reported by operators.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The text describes the label as a transparency and comparison tool based on reported energy and sustainability indicators, with provisions addressing label generation, operator obligations, review and revision. It says the scheme is intended to avoid additional reporting burden by using existing reported data.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The regulation text does not demonstrate that the rating scheme has improved data-centre efficiency, changed procurement, or affected AI compute capacity; implementation and legal-effect milestones were not independently checked in this review.

evidence_gaps.description: This review did not confirm Official Journal publication, objection-period status, entry into force or the implementation timeline for the final text.
The text does not show whether the rating scheme will change facility energy use, procurement choices or AI compute deployment.

importance_rationale: A common sustainability rating scheme for data centres could make facility-level resource performance more comparable and inform procurement and future policy as AI-related compute demand grows. The official text establishes the scheme’s design, not improved efficiency, AI capacity outcomes, or implementation effects; publication and legal-effect status still require confirmation.
limitations: Official Commission text is primary evidence of the scheme as described; legal-effect and operational status were not independently checked.
The rating scheme relies on operator-reported indicators and does not by itself verify measured efficiency gains.
No implementation outcomes, procurement effects or AI capacity changes are demonstrated.
summary: The European Commission’s final delegated-regulation text C(2026)3472 establishes a common Union sustainability rating scheme for data centres. It provides for electronic labels generated from indicators already reported through the European database, presenting energy and sustainability information to support comparison and transparency. The text describes operator obligations and review provisions while aiming to avoid additional reporting burden by reusing existing data. This establishes the scheme’s design, not measured efficiency gains, changed procurement, or effects on AI compute capacity; publication and implementation status need further checking.

technical.claimed_result: The official text establishes the rating scheme and its label design. Expected improvements in energy or water use are policy aims, not measured outcomes in this document.
technical.compute_or_cost: The text intends to avoid additional reporting burden by reusing data already submitted; actual compliance cost and facility savings are not measured.
technical.demonstrated_result: The final text sets out the scheme, its labels, data inputs and review provisions. This review did not verify publication status or implementation.
technical.mechanism: The scheme converts sustainability indicators already submitted to the European database into electronic labels. Labels are intended to support transparency and comparisons among facilities with similar characteristics; existing reporting data are reused.
