technical.regime: EU data centres covered by the energy-efficiency reporting framework; the text describes labels, operator reporting, database checks and periodic review.
technical.reproducibility: Official Commission/EUR-Lex text reviewed; no independent implementation data or outcome evaluation was available in this check.
technical.strongest_baseline: The text presents the rating label as a new common comparison layer building on the prior EU data-centre reporting database and indicator framework.

title: EU final text establishes a common sustainability rating scheme for data centres
why_it_matters: Comparable public information on data-centre energy and sustainability could influence procurement and future policy as demand for AI compute expands. The official text establishes a rating framework but does not show that facilities have improved efficiency or that the scheme has changed investment or compute capacity.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv v2 paper defines two functions standard softmax attention lacks: abstention when no key is worth reading and filtering interference within read values. It specifies separate mechanisms for each and explains how a value gate can combine both effects.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In matched models trained from scratch at 10M–350M parameters with paired seeds, the author reports that gating gains are almost entirely due to abstention at 10M, while filtering contributes about as much as abstention at 350M; the two benefits are largely additive.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Value-read interference injection tests reportedly show distinct protection from abstention and filtering, and the paper says similar patterns appear in pretrained models up to 20B parameters.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not establish that the decomposition improves downstream capabilities or production-model performance; independent reproduction was not reviewed.

evidence_gaps.description: Training and injection results have not been independently reproduced in this review.
The reported mechanistic gains do not establish downstream capability improvements, quality under other training regimes or production-model impact.

importance_rationale: If value gating benefits arise from two distinct mechanisms—letting a head abstain and filtering interfering value content—the decomposition could sharpen attention design and help explain why gate gains change with model scale. Evidence is one author-team study with matched small models and limited pretrained checks; broader capability and deployment impact remain unestablished.
limitations: Single author-team arXiv v2 paper; no independent replication reviewed.
From-scratch matched training comparisons cover 10M–350M parameters and three paired seeds per variant; pretrained checks do not constitute independent reproduction.
The paper measures training and mechanistic outcomes, not a general downstream capability improvement or production deployment effect.
summary: An arXiv v2 paper argues that softmax attention lacks two distinct functions: abstaining when no context item is useful and filtering interference within values it reads. The author specifies separate mechanisms and reports matched training comparisons from 10M to 350M parameters in which gating gains shift from mostly abstention at the smallest scale to filtering contributing about as much at the largest; the effects are largely additive. Interference-injection experiments and checks on pretrained models up to 20B are also reported. This is one author-team study; downstream capability gains, production impact and independent reproduction remain unestablished.

technical.claimed_result: The paper reports that gating benefit is mainly abstention at 10M, while filtering contributes about as much at 350M; the effects are largely additive. Similar patterns are reported in pretrained models up to 20B.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper studies training loss and mechanistic outcomes; it does not establish deployment efficiency or total system cost.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper defines mechanisms, variants and matched training/evaluation procedures. Empirical results remain author-reported and were not independently reproduced here.
technical.mechanism: A query-controlled sink logit supplies abstention by reserving probability mass for a zero-valued phantom key. A value-dependent gate suppresses individual reads based on their content. Combined variants supply both functions; their contributions can be measured separately.
technical.regime: FineWeb-Edu training of matched causal language models at 10M, 50M, 124M and 350M parameters with three paired seeds; validation loss, interference-injection tests and checks on pretrained models up to 20B.
technical.reproducibility: The v2 HTML and experimental appendices were reviewed; no code execution or independent reproduction occurred.
technical.strongest_baseline: Matched standard softmax attention without a gate or explicit abstention mechanism, trained with the same data order and seed; combined variants are also compared against the sink-logit-only model.

title: A preprint separates abstention and noise filtering as two functions of attention gates
why_it_matters: The distinction offers a mechanistic way to interpret attention gating: a head may need to choose not to read, and it may separately need to suppress interference in the content it reads. If reproduced, the scale-dependent decomposition could inform attention architecture comparisons. The paper does not establish downstream capability improvements or production impact.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv v1 paper specifies a zero-trained-parameter Memory Decision Layer between retrieval and generation. It combines relevance, reliability and task-risk signals using orthogonal projections, separates a confidence norm from directional consistency, and maps them to adopt, suppress, silent or opt-out actions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the authors’ benchmark setup with constructed conflicting memories, they report that MDL reduced hallucinations relative to standard RAG and yielded 0.0% hallucination on tested high-risk samples across several model settings. On the Gemma TruthfulQA comparison, MDL reported 0.0% high-risk hallucination versus 11.9% for RAG, while overall hallucination was 4.8% for both.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports about 0.14 ms total added latency for its controller and lexical signal aggregation, measured with embeddings precomputed; it also reports residual hallucinations under active memory use and a 55.6% decision accuracy in a high-risk, high-relevance medical subset.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The study does not establish reliable performance on naturally occurring memory conflicts or production agent workloads. Its reported zero rates apply only to the tested samples; independent replication and broader adversarial evaluation remain open.

evidence_gaps.description: The reported effect has not been independently reproduced; the experimental memory stores were constructed from benchmark correct/incorrect answers and distractors.
Generalization to naturally occurring, multi-turn memory conflicts and production distributions is unknown; tested high-risk zero rates are sample-bounded and an active-action residual error remains.
The latency report treats embeddings as precomputed and does not establish end-to-end production overhead under variable memory-store sizes and concurrent load.

importance_rationale: If a lightweight, interpretable decision stage can reduce harmful adoption of conflicting retrieved memories, it could improve agent reliability in settings where relevance alone is an unsafe trust signal. The reported evidence comes from one preprint using benchmark-constructed memory conflicts and limited model/sample regimes; real deployment effectiveness is not established.
limitations: Single author-team arXiv v1 preprint; no independent replication inspected.
Memory conflicts are constructed from benchmark reference answers and incorrect answers; hallucination scoring uses embedding similarity.
Some model/sample settings are small; reported zero hallucination rates are bounded to tested samples.
The paper reports 8.0% residual hallucination under active decisions and reduced decision accuracy in a high-risk, high-relevance medical subset.
Reported controller latency assumes precomputed embeddings and is not an end-to-end production measurement.
summary: An arXiv v1 preprint proposes the Memory Decision Layer, a zero-trained-parameter controller that evaluates retrieved memories before generation using relevance, reliability and task risk, then chooses whether to adopt or abstain. In benchmark experiments with constructed memory conflicts, the authors report lower hallucination rates than standard retrieval-augmented generation in tested settings, including zero hallucinations in the tested high-risk samples for several models. On one Gemma TruthfulQA comparison, MDL and standard RAG both had 4.8% overall hallucination, while high-risk rates were 0.0% and 11.9%, respectively. The paper reports about 0.14 ms added latency when embeddings are precomputed, but also residual active-action errors. These are single-team paper results, not independent confirmation or evidence of production performance.

technical.claimed_result: In one Gemma TruthfulQA comparison, MDL and standard RAG both report 4.8% overall hallucination; their high-risk rates are 0.0% and 11.9%. The authors report zero high-risk hallucinations on tested samples for several other model settings and about 0.14 ms added latency with precomputed embeddings.
technical.compute_or_cost: Controller plus lexical aggregation is reported at about 0.14 ms per decision with embeddings precomputed. End-to-end costs and production throughput are not established.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper specifies the controller, signal calculations, benchmark setup, baselines and measurements. Outcomes and latency remain author-reported and have not been independently verified in this review.
technical.mechanism: A retrieval-to-generation controller combines relevance, reliability and task-risk signals through orthogonal subspaces and meta-memory fusion. It separately exposes confidence magnitude and directional consistency, applies risk inversion, and selects an action including explicit abstention.
technical.regime: TruthfulQA and HaluEval with benchmark-constructed conflicting memories, reference-based hallucination scoring and tested Gemma, DeepSeek and Gemini model backends; some settings have few questions or seeds.
technical.reproducibility: The paper states that public benchmarks and code/configuration are released under MIT; this review inspected the paper but did not run code or reproduce results.
technical.strongest_baseline: Standard RAG with the same question, model, sampling and constructed memory store; additional comparisons include memory-free generation, CRAG and Self-RAG variants and supervised classifiers.

title: A preprint tests a lightweight trust gate for conflicting memories in language-model agents
why_it_matters: A decision stage between retrieval and generation could let agents abstain when retrieved memories conflict or carry high task risk, addressing a failure mode that relevance scoring alone does not handle. The paper reports benchmark improvements with low controller latency, but the memory conflicts are constructed, the sample regimes are limited, and real-world effectiveness remains unestablished.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a mechanistic study of GPT2-XL trained on random walks through Manhattan, the authors report that intersection and street representations form a faithful internal map; targeted interventions indicate that these representations causally influence navigation, alongside a goal compass.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper attributes failures under out-of-distribution stress and detour tests to localization errors caused by interference among superposed intersection features, while the representations remain available; strengthening the position signal or reducing interference improves reported behavioral measures.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The study does not establish that this mechanism or its proposed indicators generalize beyond the examined TaxiGPT models, training setup and Manhattan navigation task; no independent replication was reviewed.

evidence_gaps.description: The reported mechanistic findings have not been independently reproduced in this review, and the study concerns a single synthetic navigation setup.
Transfer of the proposed distinction and mechanistic indicators to other model architectures, training regimes and non-navigation tasks is unknown.

importance_rationale: If the causal distinction between faithful environmental representations and unreliable localization generalizes, behavioral failures may conceal usable internal world models and motivate mechanistic diagnostics beyond output-only evaluation. The evidence is a single TaxiGPT study in a synthetic Manhattan navigation regime, so transfer to broader models and tasks remains unestablished.
limitations: Single author-team arXiv v1 preprint; no independent replication reviewed.
Case study of GPT2-XL trained on random walks through Manhattan; results do not establish transfer to other models or tasks.
Stress and detour tests are out-of-distribution regimes; findings are specific to the tested setup.
summary: An arXiv v1 mechanistic study reports that GPT2-XL trained on random walks through Manhattan represents intersections and streets in an internal map and uses these representations, position tracking and a goal compass to navigate. The authors attribute failures in out-of-distribution stress and detour tests to interference among superposed position features that disrupts localization, rather than the absence of a map; interventions that strengthen the position signal improve reported behavior. This is a single synthetic navigation case study, with broader transfer and independent replication unestablished.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report decodable intersection and street structure, causal effects of position and goal-compass interventions, and localization failures under out-of-distribution stress linked to superposition interference.
technical.compute_or_cost: No deployment cost or broad capability benchmark is claimed in this case study.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper specifies its model, probes, interventions and measurements. The results remain author-reported; this review did not reproduce them.
technical.mechanism: Intersection and street features are encoded in superposition. A rolling window of past positions supports localization, while a goal compass guides route choice. Interference can recruit an incorrect intersection feature under stress; affordance grouping limits some resulting errors.
technical.regime: GPT2-XL trained on random walks through Manhattan; mechanistic probes and causal interventions on routes, stress tests and adversarial detours.
technical.reproducibility: arXiv HTML v1 and appendices reviewed; no independent replication or code execution performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper reanalyzes behavioral failures previously interpreted as evidence of an incoherent map, using internal representation probes and causal interventions rather than a comparative external model baseline.

title: A preprint finds a faithful internal map can coexist with unreliable navigation in TaxiGPT
why_it_matters: The study separates what a model represents from whether it can reliably locate and use those representations. If replicated in other environments, this distinction could improve mechanistic evaluation of apparent model failures. The evidence comes from a single GPT2-XL TaxiGPT setup trained on Manhattan random walks and does not establish generalization to other tasks or deployed models.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv v1 paper defines graph-structured skills as shared global guidance plus execution-step nodes and context-conditioned paths, and specifies a population-based optimizer using structure-aware mutation and crossover.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across five agent benchmarks and 14 model–harness–benchmark settings, the authors report GraphSkillEvo is best in 13. Averaged over the five benchmarks, the reported gain over SkillOpt is 4.01 percentage points for GPT-5.4-nano without a harness, 1.76 points for GPT-5.4 without a harness and 1.33 points for GPT-5.4 with the Codex harness; each result averages three optimization runs.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For the two no-harness model settings, the paper reports lower aggregate optimization-token use than SkillOpt: 61.94M versus 81.08M tokens for GPT-5.4 and 75.94M versus 103.54M for GPT-5.4-nano. This is optimization-token use, not total deployment inference cost.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not establish that the reported gains generalize beyond its evaluated models, benchmarks and harnesses; GraphSkillEvo trails SkillOpt on LiveMath for GPT-5.4-nano, and no independent reproduction was inspected.

evidence_gaps.description: Reported performance has not been independently reproduced; code and pretrained skills are linked but were not executed or audited here.
External validity is unknown outside five benchmarks, two GPT-5.4 variants and the tested harnesses; total deployment inference and maintenance costs are not reported.

importance_rationale: If reproduced across other models and task families, structured reusable skills with explicit workflow transitions could change how agent procedures are authored and optimized, while the reported advantage is modest on average and limited to five benchmarks, two GPT-5.4 variants and two execution settings.
limitations: Single author-team arXiv v1 preprint; no independent reproduction inspected.
Five benchmarks, two GPT-5.4 variants and two execution settings; three optimization runs per reported result.
GraphSkillEvo trails SkillOpt on LiveMath under GPT-5.4-nano.
Reported token totals concern skill optimization, not total deployment inference, tool or maintenance cost.
The author repository and pretrained artifacts were inspected by README only; code was not executed.
organizations: Southern University of Science and Technology
summary: A September 18 arXiv preprint represents reusable agent skills as a directed graph of execution steps and context-dependent paths, then optimizes them with population-based mutation and crossover. Across five benchmarks, the authors report higher average success than SkillOpt in three model/harness settings: +4.01 percentage points for GPT-5.4-nano without a harness, +1.76 points for GPT-5.4 without a harness, and +1.33 points for GPT-5.4 with the Codex harness. Results average three optimization runs; GraphSkillEvo is best in 13 of 14 evaluated settings, but trails on GPT-5.4-nano LiveMath. The authors also report lower aggregate optimization-token counts for the two no-harness settings. These are single-preprint results, not independently reproduced.

technical.claimed_result: Across five benchmark averages, the paper reports gains over SkillOpt of 4.01 percentage points for GPT-5.4-nano without a harness, 1.76 points for GPT-5.4 without a harness, and 1.33 points for GPT-5.4 with Codex harness; best in 13/14 settings.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports lower total optimization-token counts than SkillOpt for no-harness GPT-5.4 (61.94M vs 81.08M) and GPT-5.4-nano (75.94M vs 103.54M); it does not establish overall deployed-system cost.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper and its public code repository specify the graph skill representation, optimizer and evaluated benchmark/model settings. Performance remains author-reported and has not been independently reproduced in this review.
technical.mechanism: Skills combine global guidance with directed execution-step nodes and context-conditioned workflow paths. A population of candidate skills is refined through trajectory-informed structure-aware mutation and crossover.
technical.regime: SearchQA, SpreadsheetBench, DocVQA, LiveMathematicianBench and ALFWorld; GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.4-nano, with and without the Codex harness as applicable; test-set success rates averaged over three optimization runs.
technical.reproducibility: Paper-linked public GitHub repository contains code, split manifests and pretrained GPT-5.4-nano skill artifacts; full benchmark data payloads require separate materialization. README inspected; no installation or execution performed.
technical.strongest_baseline: SkillOpt, the authors’ iterative skill-optimization baseline; comparisons also include no-skill, human-written and LLM-generated skills.

title: A preprint reports that graph-structured skills improve agent benchmark results over a skill-optimization baseline
why_it_matters: Explicit execution steps and context-conditioned paths could make reusable agent procedures easier to optimize and follow. If the reported results reproduce, skill-graph optimization offers a practical method to improve task success and reduce optimization tokens in the tested settings. The measured gains are modest on average, come from one author team and a limited benchmark/model set, and do not establish lower total system cost or general transfer.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The CPC Central Committee and State Council issued an Opinion dated October 9, 2026, containing 19 tasks for developing new-quality productive forces.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The Opinion calls for AI to lead research-method change and for AI-plus industrial applications, AI terminals, compute/algorithm/data supply, application pilots, and safe, reliable and controllable AI governance.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The inspected release does not establish implementation budgets, delivered programs, deployment levels, measured productivity gains or realized safety outcomes.

evidence_gaps.description: The inspected Opinion establishes policy directions but provides no measured implementation, budget execution, AI deployment or outcome data.

importance_rationale: If the central policy direction is implemented, coordinated priorities spanning AI-enabled research, industrial deployment, compute/data supply and safety governance could influence national R&D allocation and the operating environment across major sectors. The score reflects that possible consequence, while this record establishes the adopted text and stated tasks only—not delivery, impact or compliance requirements.
limitations: The source is an official republication of an authorized Xinhua text; the inspected page is not a technical implementation report.
The Opinion states broad tasks but does not quantify dedicated AI funding, delivery dates for every action, installed capacity, adoption, or achieved productivity and safety effects.
Policy direction does not by itself establish a new binding rule or a specific compliance obligation for an individual organization.
organizations: Communist Party of China Central Committee
State Council of the People's Republic of China
summary: An October 9 Opinion issued by the Communist Party of China Central Committee and State Council sets 19 tasks for developing new-quality productive forces. It calls for AI to change research methods, AI-plus deployment in traditional industries and new terminals, stronger compute/algorithm/data supply, application pilots, and monitoring and governance for safe, reliable and controllable AI. These are adopted policy directions; the inspected release gives no implementation results or complete budget and schedule for the AI measures.

technical.claimed_result: The issuing bodies frame the Opinion as a plan to develop new-quality productive forces and increase total-factor productivity through science, industry, institutional, talent and production-system changes.
technical.demonstrated_result: The official Chinese text states policy aims and tasks. Sections 2(5), 3(9)–(10) call for AI-led research-method change, AI-plus industrial and terminal use, core technology work, compute/algorithm/data supply, pilots and safety monitoring; section 5(15) calls for AI governance. No implementation result was measured in this review.
technical.mechanism: The Opinion links organized and exploratory research, enterprise innovation, technology transfer, traditional-industry modernization, emerging and future industries, national data/compute infrastructure, AI-plus deployment, market governance and workforce development through 19 central tasks and a cross-government implementation role.
technical.regime: National policy direction spanning research, manufacturing and services, data and compute infrastructure, emerging technologies, AI applications, market governance and workforce systems. Delivery depends on subsequent programs, budgets, standards and local implementation.
technical.strongest_baseline: The directly inspected official Chinese Opinion is the primary baseline for what the issuing bodies adopted. No implementation audit or comparison with prior policy delivery was performed.

title: China sets cross-sector science and AI-plus priorities in a top-level productivity policy Opinion
why_it_matters: If carried through, the Opinion could steer China’s science funding, industrial modernization, AI infrastructure, pilot deployments and governance across multiple ministries and sectors. Its breadth makes implementation and delivery evidence more consequential than the policy wording alone; the text does not establish funded amounts, deployed capacity or measured AI outcomes.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors define a root-scoped quiescence certificate that accounts for registered old-root carriers and pre-fence acceptances, excludes later protected acceptance under the retired root, and allows exact rebind to a current independent authorization witness.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Under the paper’s stated mediation, manifest, and channel-accounting assumptions, the authors prove post-cut issuer non-expansion, support-sound projection, compositional soundness, independent-support preservation, merge-order independence, and crash/replay stability.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports 17/17 registered outcomes from a provider-free late-effect suite, agreement by a separately implemented checker on all 17 traces, and rejection of 44/44 consistently rehashed semantic regressions.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not demonstrate behavior with remote MCP, A2A, OAuth, scheduler, or other provider implementations, nor does it establish global system idleness, rollback, business completion, or effects outside the declared mediation boundary.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent execution of the proof checker or registered late-effect suite was performed.
No implementation or test evidence was inspected for actual remote provider adapters or production agent runtimes.

The paper cites RISU Bounded Agent Closure v0.3, whose Phase-1 specification verifies submitted closure evidence for a fixed profile and explicitly excludes actuators, integrations, orchestration and distributed protocols; the paper presents its active cut/fencing protocol as complementary. No comparison with a deployed orchestration system or actual provider adapter was performed.

importance_rationale: If implemented across real providers, a bounded certificate that accounts for delegated and in-flight work could materially improve how agent systems revoke authority and prevent late external effects. The result is an author-proposed protocol with a local provider-free evaluation, not evidence of deployment or broad adoption.
limitations: All formal and evaluation claims are reported by the paper authors; the proof and artifact were not independently audited or reproduced here.
The test suite is provider-free and uses a local protected sink; endpoint labels do not establish actual MCP, A2A, OAuth, scheduler or cloud-provider behavior.
The guarantee is relative to a retired authorization root and complete bounded manifest; it does not mean global idleness, rollback, business completion or physical cessation.
Correctness depends on complete mediation/accounting, sound sink fences and exact cross-provider channel conservation; opaque endpoints may leave the result indeterminate.

The paper’s cited RISU Bounded Agent Closure v0.3 specification was inspected and appears complementary in scope: it verifies submitted evidence for a fixed profile but expressly has no actuators, integrations, orchestration or distributed protocol. Neither source establishes a deployed end-to-end provider implementation.
summary: A September 18 preprint defines root-scoped authorization quiescence for agents whose work can survive in queues, callbacks, delegated credentials and provider operations. It combines a durable root-epoch cut, sink-side fences, carrier accounting and provider evidence into a bounded certificate. The paper proves conditional safety properties and reports a provider-free 17-case late-effect suite plus a separately implemented checker; the results were not independently reproduced in this review.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report 17/17 registered provider-free runner outcomes, 17/17 separate checker decisions and rejection of 44/44 semantically modified and consistently rehashed traces. The local protected sink rejects scheduled late effects under cut-plus-fence cases while cancellation-only and cut-only cases admit them.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected primary paper specifies the protocol, its assurance assumptions, proof claims and serialized local test design. No external provider was invoked and the research desk did not rerun the authors’ artifact; the paper’s empirical results remain author-reported.
technical.mechanism: The protocol durably retires a root epoch, stops old-root authority expansion, installs operation-time fences at protected sinks, accounts for carriers and transfers, and composes provider-frontier leaf certificates into a cutset. Multi-root support uses antichains of minimal sufficient root sets; ongoing work can continue only through an exact rebind to a current witness independent of the retired root.
technical.regime: Formal claims apply to registered endpoints and protected sinks whose authority lineage, carriers and cross-provider transfers are completely mediated or conservatively represented. The executed suite uses a provider-free local ledger, child worker processes, logical endpoint shapes and inert typed effects.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares cancellation acknowledgement alone and root cut without sink fencing against the same scheduled unit and local protected-effect oracle under cut-plus-fence. Its cited RISU v0.3 artifact is a complementary fixed-profile evidence verifier, not an active protocol or provider integration; no matched tests against remote provider implementations are reported.

title: A preprint formalizes how to verify revocation across long-running agent work
why_it_matters: If the method holds under real provider adapters, it gives agent systems a more precise shutdown guarantee than cancellation acknowledgement or token revocation alone, while preserving work that has an independent authorization root. The paper explicitly limits its guarantee to registered, completely mediated paths, so it does not establish global idleness or real-world deployment safety.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: ANPD’s public page states that public input on the proposed 2027–2028 regulatory agenda is open from 2026-09-01 to 2026-10-16.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a draft technical note for the 2027–2028 agenda, ANPD says the generative-AI and personal-data regulatory action is retained with adaptations and identifies proposed topics: legitimate-interest grounds for personal data used in training, development and operation; safeguards for sensitive training data; and transparency, governance and data-subject rights.

evidence_gaps.description: The final 2027–2028 agenda and the resulting legal instrument, if any, are not yet established.

importance_rationale: If adopted, this work could shape Brazilian privacy compliance for generative-AI training data, including legal basis, sensitive-data safeguards, transparency and rights of data subjects. The score reflects potential consequence of the draft agenda’s bounded direction; the proposal is not binding and final scope is pending.
limitations: The agenda and technical note are draft planning documents under consultation; they do not create a binding requirement.
The final agenda may change after public input, and the note supplies no final rule text, implementation schedule or measured compliance/economic impact.
ANPD’s reported text-analysis results are agency-reported and do not independently establish the prevalence of AI-related regulatory issues across Brazil.
organizations: Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD)
summary: Brazil’s data-protection authority ANPD is consulting on its proposed regulatory agenda for 2027–2028. A Portuguese-language draft technical note says the generative-AI and personal-data action would continue with adaptations and identifies issues for further rulemaking: whether legitimate interest can support personal-data use in training, development and operation; safeguards for sensitive data used in training; and transparency, governance and data-subject rights. Public input was listed as open through 2026-10-16. This is a draft planning direction, not an adopted rule or confirmed legal obligation.

technical.claimed_result: The draft says the AI and personal-data action will be retained with adaptations and frames the listed topics as proposed regulatory work for the 2027–2028 cycle.
technical.demonstrated_result: Official Portuguese-language sources identify the draft agenda, its proposed AI/data-protection topics and a public consultation open from 2026-09-01 through 2026-10-16. No adopted AI rule is established by these documents.
technical.implementation_status: Draft agenda under public consultation; no final agenda or binding rule is established in the inspected sources.
technical.mechanism: The ANPD agenda-setting process carries selected data-protection issues into future regulatory work. The draft describes continuing an AI-and-personal-data action and identifies potential parameters for personal-data use in generative-AI training/development/operation, sensitive-data safeguards, transparency, governance and rights.
technical.regime: Brazilian personal-data protection under the LGPD and ANPD’s proposed 2027–2028 regulatory agenda; generative-AI training, development and operation are within the draft action’s scope.
technical.reproducibility: The draft note and ANPD agenda page are publicly accessible in Portuguese. The proposal and consultation dates can be checked directly; policy adoption and implementation outcomes remain future developments.
technical.strongest_baseline: The ANPD’s existing 2025–2026 agenda already included AI and personal-data work; the draft describes continuation with adaptations rather than a newly adopted substantive rule.

title: Brazil’s ANPD proposes carrying AI training-data safeguards into its 2027–28 regulatory agenda
why_it_matters: If carried into the final agenda and later rulemaking, the proposal could influence how developers and deployers assess personal data used throughout generative-AI development and operation in Brazil. Its stated topics connect training-data legal basis and sensitive-data safeguards with transparency and individual rights. The open consultation gives affected parties a defined near-term point to shape the regulator’s priorities.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The arXiv v2 paper identifies TierKV as an accepted EuroSys 2027 paper and describes a predictive three-tier KV-cache system for mobile LLM inference.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across eight text, vision and audio models on three mobile SoCs, the authors report reducing RAM-resident KV-cache footprint by 12.5–34%; maximum supported context length increases by up to 2.6× in the tested memory regime.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports prefill throughput improvements up to 17.6× over MNN-LLM for selected text models and an average end-to-end speedup of 1.10× over llama.cpp across evaluated workloads; decoding throughput decreases in some cases due to SVD reconstruction.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not establish these gains on other device families, models, workloads or independent implementations; its maximum prefill gain is not a general end-to-end speedup.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the system, speed, memory or accuracy measurements was conducted.
Cross-device generality and behavior under realistic prompt-length distributions, thermal throttling and competing storage/memory load remain uncertain.

importance_rationale: If replicated across representative mobile workloads, reducing KV-cache memory while preserving long-context access could materially expand on-device inference capability and privacy-preserving deployment. The reported results are bounded to the tested models and SoCs, with baseline-dependent speedups and no independent implementation audit.
limitations: Author-reported system measurements; no independent implementation audit or reproduction was performed.
The maximum 17.6× prefill throughput comparison is against MNN-LLM on selected workloads; average end-to-end improvement over llama.cpp is 1.10×.
Comparisons are incomplete where baseline frameworks do not support the same model or long-context regime.
SVD reconstruction lowers decode throughput in some cases; prefill gains do not imply faster decoding in every workload.
Device results are limited to three evaluated mobile SoCs; thermal throttling and external validity remain concerns.
summary: Shu et al. describe TierKV, an accepted EuroSys 2027 system that predicts cache demand from prefill states and jointly places tokens in exact, low-rank and flash-offloaded tiers. In the authors’ eight-model, three-mobile-SoC evaluation, it reduced RAM-resident KV cache by 12.5–34% and improved prefill throughput by up to 17.6× versus MNN-LLM; the largest speedup is baseline-specific. Average end-to-end speedup was 1.10× versus llama.cpp, while decoding throughput fell in some cases from SVD reconstruction. These are paper-reported results; no independent reproduction was performed.

technical.claimed_result: The authors evaluate eight text, vision and audio models on three mobile SoCs. They report 12.5–34% lower resident KV-cache memory, up to 17.6× prefill throughput versus MNN-LLM in selected cases, and 1.10× average end-to-end speedup versus llama.cpp; SVD reconstruction reduces decoding throughput in some configurations.
technical.compute_or_cost: The framework adds approximately 10k lines of C/C++/OpenCL and Python according to the paper. One-time per-model calibration uses two A6000 GPUs and is reported as under 20 minutes.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accepted EuroSys 2027 paper (arXiv:2609.21172v2) and its method, platform, baselines, tables and accuracy/multi-turn results were inspected. Reported measurements were not independently reproduced.
technical.implementation_status: Research system described in an accepted EuroSys 2027 paper; implementation and results are author-reported. Code was not inspected or run in this activation.
technical.mechanism: Before decoding, Predictive Multi-Tier Cache Optimization uses prefill hidden states to estimate sequence demand and jointly assigns cache tokens to exact, SVD-compressed resident and flash-offloaded tiers under memory and fidelity constraints.
technical.regime: Eight models across text, image and audio workloads on Adreno 740/750 and Mali-G715 mobile SoCs; OnePlus 12 end-to-end comparisons include llama.cpp, MNN-LLM and MLC-LLM where supported.
technical.reproducibility: Evaluation spans eight models and three mobile SoCs; the multi-turn retrieval comparison reports 3 seeds × 5 questions. No independent implementation or replication was conducted.
technical.strongest_baseline: Three mobile inference frameworks are compared, but availability differs by model; MLC-LLM supports only a subset. The reported 17.6× maximum is against MNN-LLM, while the paper reports 1.10× average end-to-end speedup versus llama.cpp.

title: TierKV combines predictive KV-cache compression and flash tiers for mobile LLM inference
why_it_matters: On-device inference is constrained by shared memory and storage bandwidth. Jointly planning compression, cache residency and offload before decoding is a concrete systems approach to longer contexts under fixed device memory, but measured gains depend on the workload and comparator.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: Chen et al. posted arXiv:2609.21392v1 on 2026-09-18 and define ODU as evaluation of demand presence and contextual demand understanding in audio/audio-visual interactions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that ODU-Bench contains 2,078 scenes: 1,801 synthetic scenarios and 277 human-recorded interactions performed by 30 actors; annotations underwent media-grounded human verification.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In Table 3 and the contextual-recovery analysis, the authors report that Gemini 3.1 Pro recovers 44.7% of key points requiring visual, acoustic or dialogue context and has a 40.6% false-trigger rate on audio-visual no-demand scenes; 11 of 14 evaluated models exceed 50% false-trigger rates across no-demand scenarios.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: These benchmark results do not establish corresponding failure rates in deployed assistants or the expected user harm, nor do they independently validate the benchmark, annotations, or judge scores.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or audit of ODU-Bench annotations, model outputs, or LLM judge scores was conducted.
The benchmark is challenge-driven and 87% synthetic by scene count; its false-trigger and contextual-recovery rates may not estimate natural deployment traffic.

importance_rationale: If representative, difficulty recovering multimodal intent and avoiding false triggers affects when assistants should act and how safely they handle underspecified speech. The benchmark is a meaningful evaluation contribution, but synthetic-heavy data and unreplicated author-reported results do not establish deployment prevalence.
limitations: Single-group v1 preprint; results are not independently reproduced.
1,801 of 2,078 scenes are synthetic; 277 human-recorded interactions involve 30 actors, so natural traffic and population coverage are not established.
The evaluation uses an LLM judge for key-point matching; appendix diagnostics are author-reported and not independently audited.
The text-only baseline uses a different input interface and is left unranked; not every comparison is matched.
The paper does not establish deployed false-trigger rates, downstream harms, or performance under broad unselected interaction distributions.
summary: Chen et al. introduce ODU-Bench, a benchmark of 2,078 audio and audio-visual demand/no-demand scenes, and report results for 14 native multimodal models. In the paper’s reported evaluation, the best-scoring model recovers 44.7% of key information specifically requiring visual, acoustic or dialogue context; 11 of 14 models trigger on more than half of no-demand scenarios, and Gemini 3.1 Pro triggers on 40.6%. These are author-reported benchmark results, not independently reproduced estimates of real-world assistant behavior.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report 2,078 scenes (1,801 synthetic and 277 human-recorded) and evaluation of 14 native multimodal configurations. The best model’s context-dependent key-point recovery is reported as 44.7%; Gemini 3.1 Pro has a 40.6% false-trigger rate in audio-visual no-demand scenes; 11/14 models exceed 50% false-trigger rate on no-demand cases.
technical.compute_or_cost: No comparable serving cost or latency analysis is claimed in the reviewed result.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv v1 paper, task definition, dataset composition, evaluation protocol, results table and appendix diagnostics were inspected. No independent execution or reproduction was conducted.
technical.implementation_status: Author-reported arXiv v1 research benchmark with paper-linked dataset and demo; artifacts were not independently downloaded or executed.
technical.mechanism: The benchmark separates demand presence, contextual intent/key-point recovery, temporal localization, transcription and user profile; no-demand examples test whether request-like cues cause false triggering.
technical.regime: ODU-Bench v1, 2,078 scenes, comprising 1,801 synthetic scenarios and 277 human-recorded interactions by 30 actors; 14 native audio/audio-visual model configurations with modality-specific evaluations.
technical.reproducibility: Paper reports human verification of annotations and appendix checks of judge stability and key-point recoverability. Independent reproduction, dataset audit and robustness to less challenge-selected traffic remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares 14 model configurations under a common benchmark and includes a text-only ASR-input baseline that is not ranked because its interface differs. Judge-stability and key-point-recoverability diagnostics are reported in the appendix; independent benchmark audit remains absent.

title: ODU-Bench reports contextual intent and false-trigger gaps in multimodal assistants
why_it_matters: Correctly deciding whether a user has made a request, and recovering intent from context rather than speech alone, is a distinct prerequisite for multimodal assistants. The benchmark reports substantial bounded failures on these behaviors, while its synthetic-heavy composition and judge-based evaluation limit generalization to deployed use.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that, after one recursive training step, increasing explicit synthetic-review exposure across 0%, 33%, 66% and 100% settings reduced rating-distribution spread and semantic diversity relative to the official-review-only training baseline.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors state that this is a controlled synthetic-exposure experiment and not a measurement of naturally occurring AI assistance in peer review; they study one recursive step and leave compounding across later generations open.

evidence_gaps.description: The experiment does not measure how much AI-generated or AI-edited review text actually enters scientific training corpora or whether real review pipelines show the same effect.
The study tests one recursive training step; cumulative effects over repeated generations are unknown.

importance_rationale: If the controlled effect generalizes to review systems trained on model-generated feedback, it could affect how scientific evaluation data are curated and how judgment diversity is monitored. This is meaningful for AI-assisted research evaluation, but the paper tests one synthetic-training step on one review corpus and does not measure real-world prevalence or multi-generation accumulation.
limitations: All empirical outcomes are reported in one arXiv preprint and were not independently reproduced in this activation.
The experiment varies explicitly generated review proportions in ICLR data; it does not estimate real-world AI-assisted review prevalence.
The official review corpus is labeled official rather than human-written because reviews may contain unobserved AI assistance.
Only one recursive training step is examined; further compounding or stabilization is unknown.
The semantic-diversity measures and rating distributions are proxies for judgment variation and do not establish review quality, fairness or decision accuracy.
The TrustReviewer interventions are author-proposed mitigation methods; their efficacy and external validity were not independently verified here.
summary: Ho, Liu and Huang train a Llama 3.1 8B reviewer on ICLR 2018–2023 reviews, use it to generate reviews for ICLR 2024 papers, then train four successors on mixtures containing 0%, 33%, 66% or 100% explicitly synthetic reviews. With other training settings held fixed, their paper reports that synthetic exposure compressed rating distributions and monotonically reduced same-paper and corpus-level semantic diversity in the tested one-step setup. This is a controlled author-reported experiment, not a measurement of real-world AI assistance in peer review: the official reviews may themselves include unobserved AI assistance, and the paper does not test whether the effect compounds over further generations.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report that synthetic exposure reduced rating diversity and semantic diversity in same-paper and corpus-level comparisons. They report approximately 11% and 5% reductions, respectively, between 0% and 100% synthetic exposure.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected v1 preprint describes the experiment, metrics and reported observations. No independent reproduction or evaluation of TrustReviewer was performed here.
technical.mechanism: A reviewer initialized from Llama 3.1 8B is trained on official ICLR 2018–2023 reviews, generates reviews for ICLR 2024 papers, and produces successor models trained on mixtures of official and explicitly synthetic reviews. The mixture level is varied while initialization and training settings are held fixed.
technical.regime: One controlled recursive step; synthetic-review proportions of 0%, 33%, 66% and 100%; held-out review generation on 2,000 papers sampled across 2018–2025. Official reviews may include unobserved AI assistance.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links code and a dataset collection. This activation inspected the paper text but did not inspect or execute those artifacts.
technical.strongest_baseline: Successor reviewers trained only on official reviews (0% explicitly synthetic exposure) provide the controlled baseline; initialization, filtering, and optimization are held constant across mixture conditions.

title: A controlled study reports reduced diversity after training successive paper-review models on synthetic reviews
why_it_matters: If AI-generated reviews enter later reviewer-training corpora, they could narrow the judgments learned by successor models. This paper reports a controlled one-step test of that pathway and finds lower rating and semantic diversity as explicitly synthetic review exposure rises. The result identifies a risk worth measuring in AI-assisted evaluation, while leaving natural prevalence, the effect of multiple generations and performance of the proposed mitigation methods open.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors present a framework that combines GUI exploration, coding and execution/visual verification in reproducible Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android and Web environments.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On the authors’ 250-task RecreationBench, they report GPT-6 Astra at 58.06% overall, ahead of Claude Opus 5 at 44.16%; only 2.8% of tasks had full programmatic passes for GPT-6 Astra.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that agents reproduce static interface structure more reliably than interactions and computed outputs on their benchmark.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent team has rerun RecreationBench or checked whether its hidden tests and scores generalize to other computer-use tasks.
Transfer beyond reference-recreation tasks, the five supported platforms and the paper’s model/harness configurations is not established.

importance_rationale: If useful beyond the authors’ benchmark, a five-platform environment joining GUI operation, coding and execution-grounded verification could change how long-horizon computer-use agents are trained and evaluated. Its significance is major for this subfield, while benchmark representativeness and reported model results remain unreplicated.
limitations: Results are reported by the paper authors and were not independently reproduced in this activation.
RecreationBench comprises 250 reference-recreation tasks; its representativeness of real computer-use work and transfer to other task formulations remain uncertain.
The overall score is not equivalent to full task correctness; 2.8% full programmatic pass coverage for GPT-6 Astra is the paper’s reported value under its scoring protocol.
The benchmark compares the listed frontier models under paper-specific inference configurations; it does not establish general ranking across workloads, prompts, models or harnesses.
The reported association between broader exploration and stronger scores is descriptive and does not establish that exploration caused the performance difference.
summary: The authors introduce RecreationWorld, a framework for training and evaluating agents that alternate between exploring a running application through its interface, implementing a recreation in code, and executing it for feedback across Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android and Web. Their held-out RecreationBench has 250 tasks and reference-grounded hidden tests. In the authors’ evaluation of ten models, GPT-6 Astra scored 58.06% overall, but only 2.8% of tasks had a full programmatic pass; the paper reports that interface structure was reproduced more reliably than interactions and computed outputs. These are author-reported results from a new benchmark, not an independent capability comparison or a measure of general computer-use ability.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report GPT-6 Astra achieved 58.06% aggregate score (Claude Opus 5 44.16%) and that GPT-6 Astra obtained full programmatic passes on tasks totaling 2.8% coverage. They report static structure was reproduced more reliably than interactions and computed outputs.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected v2 paper contains the framework description, benchmark protocol and reported results. The release artifacts and model evaluations were not independently rerun here.
technical.mechanism: Agents alternate GUI exploration, code implementation and execution/visual verification while reproducing an application from a running reference. Reference behavior supports hidden programmatic and visual assertions; the framework also uses generated trajectories for training.
technical.regime: Five-platform framework across Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android and Web; 250 held-out benchmark tasks; ten frontier models evaluated using the paper’s specified direct-MCP configurations.
technical.reproducibility: The paper points to benchmark and environment releases; this activation inspected the paper but did not download/run the artifacts or independently verify their completeness.
technical.strongest_baseline: The reported model comparison includes ten frontier systems; GPT-6 Astra is compared with Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol under the paper’s benchmark configurations. This is not an independently matched evaluation across all inference stacks.

title: A paper introduces a five-platform benchmark for hybrid computer-use agents and reports a large gap between aggregate scores and full behavioral tests
why_it_matters: Computer-use agents often need to combine interface exploration with code changes and then verify the running result. RecreationWorld offers a way to train that loop and score behavior against an executable reference. Its reported results also show why an aggregate score can overstate full behavioral fidelity: the leading model’s score was 58.06%, while full programmatic passes covered 2.8% of tasks in this benchmark. Independent replication and transfer beyond the authors’ task set remain open.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that supervised fine-tuning increased average text-turn success from 33.2% to 58.4% across four Qwen3 and Gemma 3 model sizes when each turn was evaluated with gold history.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report smaller average gains on tool turns than text turns; exact tool-call accuracy and argument matching remained low and regressed for some Gemma 3 settings.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the paper’s table of 77 tool workflows, fine-tuned Qwen3-4B completed 3, Qwen3-14B completed 8, and neither Gemma 3 model completed any; the holistic judge marked 0 of 77 workflows successful for every model condition.

evidence_gaps.description: The reported differences have not been independently reproduced, and no public code or dataset artifact was located in the paper.

importance_rationale: If the result generalizes, evaluation and training choices for tool-using agents would need to distinguish local action prediction from closed-loop task completion. Its consequence is meaningful for agent evaluation, while the evidence comes from one paper, a narrow customer-support regime, and unreplicated author-run experiments.
limitations: One author-reported study; no independent reproduction was performed in this activation.
The workflows are generated from a proprietary customer-support dataset, with GPT-5 agents simulating users and workflow agents and separate model judges filtering/evaluating conversations.
The held-out evaluation contains 84 conversations; the results table reports 77 tool workflows. Conclusions apply to this study’s task and evaluation setup.

Closed-loop execution uses deterministic parsing, a deterministic user simulator and up to two retries after an invalid tool call; other tool interfaces or recovery policies may produce different results.
A 0/77 holistic-judge score is not evidence that these models cannot succeed on other workflow types.
summary: Laskar et al. compare gold-history next-action scoring with closed-loop execution on generated multi-turn customer-support workflows. Across Qwen3 4B/14B and Gemma 3 4B/12B, their paper reports that supervised fine-tuning increased average text-turn success by 25.2 percentage points, while tool-turn gains were smaller; the best fine-tuned model completed 8 of 77 tool workflows and no model passed the holistic workflow judge. The result is limited to the authors’ task generator, proprietary workflow dataset, and tested models; it does not establish that turn-level metrics are generally useless.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report average text-turn success increased 25.2 points with SFT, tool-turn gains were smaller, and the best model completed 8/77 tool workflows; all model conditions scored 0/77 on holistic workflow judgment.
technical.demonstrated_result: The public preprint contains the described setup and reported table. The experiment was not rerun or independently reproduced here.
technical.mechanism: The paper contrasts per-turn predictions conditioned on gold histories with tool use and workflow replay conditioned on each model’s own prior outputs. The evaluation includes text similarity, LLM-judged turn success, exact tool-call checking, closed-loop replay and holistic workflow judgment.
technical.regime: Four fine-tuned Qwen3 and Gemma 3 models at 4B, 12B and 14B parameter sizes in 130 generated customer-support workflows; 84 held-out conversations and 77 tool workflows reported in the completion table.
technical.reproducibility: The paper describes its generated dataset and protocols but identifies no public code or dataset release; the workflow conversations originate from proprietary business conversations.
technical.strongest_baseline: Each fine-tuned model is compared with its corresponding zero-shot/base setting using the same paper-defined training and held-out workflow setup; no independent benchmark or matched external method was compared.

title: A paper reports that stronger next-turn metrics did not transfer to customer-support workflow success
why_it_matters: A model can become more likely to produce the expected next response without becoming more reliable at executing a multi-step task using its own prior outputs. If the reported pattern holds, tool-agent evaluation should report local action quality alongside closed-loop completion. The paper tests one customer-support setting and does not establish generality across workflow domains or agent architectures.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports a 500-issue benchmark covering SWE-bench Verified and a Python fragment of SWE-bench Pro, with formal specifications, verifying implementations, ground-truth patches and recorded gate outcomes.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On SWE-bench Verified, the authors report that a correct supplied specification increases issue resolution from about 85% unaided to about 95%; verification catches defects that the held-out tests miss.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: When the agent must synthesize its own specification, end-to-end resolution shows no gain over the unaided baseline; only 56% of synthesized specifications pass the paper’s five-property audit, with faithfulness the main failure.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper states that its verify-implies-resolve guarantee depends on audited axiom soundness and fidelity of refinement from the verified implementation to the executed patch; specification audits are evidence from a language-model panel, not a mathematical proof of the full pipeline.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent recomputation of the benchmark outcomes, repeated-run variation or verification-vs-test comparison has been performed.
The authors’ axiom-soundness and refinement-fidelity evidence, including language-model audit panels, has not been independently red-teamed.
Transfer to other programming languages, repositories, issue distributions and verification backends is not established by the headline result.

importance_rationale: If the reported benchmark results hold in this formal-methods regime, supplying a faithful machine-checkable specification can materially raise issue-resolution success and expose a class of defects hidden by tests. The work changes evaluation and verification design for repository agents, but self-generated specification synthesis remains weak and the result is not a general proof of autonomous software correctness.
limitations: The guarantee is conditional on the soundness of axioms and fidelity of the refinement from verified implementation to executed patch.
The specification audit is a calibrated language-model panel; its verdicts are evidence, not proof.

Model-generated specifications and artifacts remain difficult to synthesize faithfully: only 56% of specifications in the cited synthesis setting passed the five-property audit, with faithfulness the dominant failure.
A few instances use manual modeling or relax a secondary no-leakage property, limiting their evidential strength.
All outcome, benchmark and audit results are author-reported; the research desk has not independently rerun the pipeline or inspected bundle artifacts.

The central comparison is conditional on supplied formal specifications and specific SWE-bench tasks; it does not establish autonomous formal verification across arbitrary repositories or software properties.
summary: The v2 SWE-Proof paper builds a 500-issue benchmark from SWE-bench Verified and a Python subset of SWE-bench Pro, pairing each issue with a formal specification, a verifying implementation, and a ground-truth patch. On SWE-bench Verified, the authors report that a correctly supplied specification raised resolution from an 85% unaided baseline to about 95%, while adding verification to an end-to-end agent that writes its own specification did not improve its roughly 85% baseline. In a separate specification-synthesis test, only 56% of model-written specifications passed the paper’s five-property audit; incomplete behavioral coverage (faithfulness) was the main failure. The results are author-reported. Their guarantee depends on audited axioms and faithful refinement from verified code to the executed patch, and the audit panel itself uses language models.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report that hidden tests miss about one quarter of defects caught by verification, and that a correct supplied formal specification raises SWE-bench Verified resolution from an approximately 85% unaided baseline to approximately 95%. End-to-end agents writing their own specifications do not improve the baseline; the specification-synthesis setting reports 56% of specifications passing the five-property audit.
technical.compute_or_cost: 500 issues are benchmarked; specifications use several verification backends. Reconstructing the entire corpus is reported as expensive; per-instance artifacts and recorded gate outcomes are intended to support rechecking.
technical.demonstrated_result: The v2 arXiv paper describes its 500-instance benchmark, verification pipeline, evaluation settings, audit procedures, reported outcomes and limitations. No independent rerun of the benchmark or inspection of the released proof bundles has been completed; all performance and trustworthiness results remain author-reported.
technical.implementation_status: Authors report a pipeline that checks proof obligations, execution/refinement equivalence, axioms, specification soundness/completeness/faithfulness, and leakage. Each instance includes a proof bundle and gate outcomes in the announced release.
technical.mechanism: Benchproofer constructs formal specifications, axiomatizes unchanged repository behavior, and admits benchmark instances only after mechanical checks and adversarial language-model audits. A candidate patch must refine an implementation that verifies against the specification.
technical.novelty: Applies machine-checked formal specifications to real repository issues with a paired pre-fix implementation, reference patch and audited proof bundle, while measuring the gap between supplied and self-synthesized specifications.
technical.regime: Repository issue resolution on SWE-bench Verified (500 issues) and the Python fragment of SWE-bench Pro. Evaluated models/verifiers and budgets vary by formal backend; headline 85-to-95 comparison is on SWE-bench Verified.
technical.reproducibility: Paper says the construction pipeline and all instance artifacts will be released. The release has not been independently downloaded or audited.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within-paper SWE-bench Verified comparisons include an unaided baseline, an end-to-end setting where the agent writes a specification and patch, and a verified-from-spec setting where the specification is supplied. Appendix reports repeated runs for major settings.

title: SWE-Proof reports that machine-checkable specifications improve issue resolution, while specification faithfulness limits autonomous gains
why_it_matters: The paper separates proof checking from the harder task of expressing the intended behavior faithfully. Its reported gap suggests formal verification can catch defects missed by tests when the specification is sound, while an agent that writes its own incomplete specification can gain little. This is consequential for software-agent evaluation and tool design, but does not show that general coding agents can autonomously produce correct proofs or specifications in ordinary repositories.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports replaying 4,371 human-authored attacks from a public payment-agent CTF against 14 models from eight labs, with 225,964 completed evaluations across policy levels, replay tracks and architectures.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: At restricted Levels 2–4, authors report 140 disallowed-recipient transfers among 76,842 model-only evaluations and zero among 69,297 evaluations behind a deterministic authorization layer; the matched subset reports 105 versus zero on 68,970 triples.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Authors bound the zero across 790 source sessions with a session-level rule-of-three upper bound of 0.38%; they also report 25,370 successful payments behind the layer, so the result was not produced by refusing all transfers.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper discloses that its local Level 4 engine additionally required a confirmation code not required by the published policy pack; therefore the Level 4 zero does not alone establish behavior under the published pack.

claims.label: INFERRED
claims.text: No live-deployment rate, cross-tool transfer rate, representative attacker-population estimate or benign-traffic false-positive rate is established by this benchmark.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the replay counts, session-clustered bounds or matched comparisons has been completed.
The local engine’s parity against the hosted verifier is reported on 100 cases only, and a disclosed Level 4 rule differs from the published policy pack.
The corpus has no benign traffic, so the practical trade-off between rejecting unauthorized actions and blocking legitimate requests is unmeasured.
Transfer beyond the simulated payment tool and attacker population is not established.

importance_rationale: If the bounded simulated-payment result is true and the same tool-boundary property transfers to real agents, an independently enforced authorization layer could materially reduce unauthorized financial actions even when models still issue payment requests. The claim affects design and evaluation choices across consequential tool use, but one author-reported payment benchmark does not establish transfer to other tools or deployed systems.
limitations: The tested system is one simulated bank and one payment tool; the paper explicitly does not claim transfer to code execution, data access or agent-to-agent delegation.
The attacks are self-selected CTF submissions, not a representative user or state-grade attacker sample; no population risk rate follows.

The local policy engine is stricter than the published Level 4 policy pack because it required an extra confirmation code, so the Level 4 zero is not evidence about the published pack’s Level 4 behavior.
The policy engine was checked against its hosted verifier on a reported 100-case parity sample; the research desk did not inspect or rerun that test.
The corpus contains no benign-task evaluation, so false-positive or legitimate-traffic overblocking rates cannot be inferred.
18,812 planned evaluations did not complete; multi-turn coverage is incomplete for some models and cells.
Cross-provider API defaults such as top_p and penalties were not normalized.
summary: In arXiv:2609.22076v1, APort’s author replays 4,371 human-written attacks from a live payment-agent capture-the-flag event against 14 models from eight labs, comparing model-only execution with a deterministic pre-action authorization check. Across restricted Levels 2–4, the paper reports 140 transfers to disallowed recipients in 76,842 model-only evaluations and none in 69,297 evaluations behind the layer; 105 versus zero also occurs on 68,970 matched model, prompt and track triples. The zero is bounded by 790 source sessions (session-clustered rule-of-three upper bound 0.38%). The result concerns one simulated payment tool and a locally implemented policy engine; the paper discloses a Level 4 confirmation-code mismatch that makes its measured layer stricter than the published policy pack. No inference to other tool domains, live deployment rates, or benign-task overblocking is supported.

technical.claimed_result: Across Levels 2–4, authors report 140 disallowed-recipient transfers in 76,842 model-only evaluations versus zero in 69,297 behind the layer, and 105 versus zero on 68,970 matched model-prompt-track triples. The session-clustered upper bound for the zero is 0.38% across 790 source sessions.
technical.compute_or_cost: 225,964 of 244,776 planned evaluations completed; authors release evaluations, policy passports, scoring code and analysis script.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv paper and released HTML report a 4,371-attack replay design and disclose counts, methods, limitations and artifact links. No independent rerun of the data or policy engine has been completed; all performance and security-effect claims remain author-reported.
technical.implementation_status: Paper reports a local deterministic implementation ported from the CTF server. It matched the hosted verifier on a 100-case parity sample; Level 4 additionally required a confirmation code beyond the published pack, making that measured layer stricter.
technical.mechanism: A deterministic policy engine evaluates each transfer request against a structured capability/passport before tool execution; denied calls do not execute, while allowed payments remain available.
technical.novelty: Combines human-authored real-CFT attacks, multi-model replay, matched layer/no-layer comparison and state-change outcomes at the authorization boundary.
technical.regime: Fourteen API-served models from eight labs; five simulated payment-policy levels; two replay tracks; attacks from a 2026 public CTF, 97.7% of which arrived in its March 6–12 launch window. Restricted Levels 2–4 are the primary authorization comparison.
technical.reproducibility: Authors link a CC BY 4.0 dataset and analysis artifacts. The released corpus requires accepting its research-use conditions; independent artifact integrity, rerun and policy-engine parity beyond the reported 100-case sample have not been checked.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within-paper matched comparison holds model, prompt and replay track constant while changing whether the deterministic pre-action layer is present. Aggregate comparisons also include unequal coverage and are not used as causal estimates.

title: APort Vault reports zero unauthorized transfers behind a deterministic payment authorization layer in a human-attack replay benchmark
why_it_matters: If the reported comparison generalizes, a deterministic authorization check at the tool boundary can prevent some disallowed high-consequence actions without relying on the model to refuse requests. The paper provides an unusually detailed, released replay corpus and separates requests, payments, decisions and unauthorized transfers. Its single simulated payment domain, attack-selected corpus and disclosed policy mismatch sharply limit transfer claims.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors derive that, under their retention model r(b)=Cb^-δ, a depth-k tree over N findings yields C^k N^(1-δ), and report that flat organization is optimal for yield under the model.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across 600 production deep-research traces, the authors report δ=0.34 (95% CI 0.30–0.38); across 16,082 tool-result handoffs, they report C=0.571 (95% CI 0.527–0.615). They report that each additional tier costs roughly 45% of yield in that measured setting.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent execution of the released scripts/corpora or replication of the reported constants was performed.
The empirical constants come from one research-agent scaffold; stability across other agents, task classes and tool boundaries is unmeasured.

importance_rationale: If the reported retention losses generalize, adding agent tiers could materially reduce how much useful research reaches decision makers, changing the expected value of multi-agent decomposition. The evidence is one author-reported paper and one research scaffold, so the consequence is conditional.
limitations: All empirical findings are reported by the paper authors and were not independently reproduced in this activation.
The main trace corpus uses one research-agent scaffold; transfer to other systems or tasks is not established.
The analytical conclusion depends on the paper’s retention model and assumptions; it does not establish that flat systems are generally superior on total task quality, cost or latency.
summary: A September 15 preprint models how multi-agent decomposition affects the findings that survive to a root agent. It derives a yield relationship under a stated retention model and reports measurements from 600 production deep-research traces and 16,082 tool-result handoffs. The empirical estimates are author-reported and tied to one research scaffold.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report δ=0.34 (95% CI 0.30–0.38) from 600 production deep-research traces and C=0.571 (95% CI 0.527–0.615) across 16,082 tool-result hops; under their model, each added tier reduces yield.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper and its method, reported measurements and limitations are publicly accessible. This activation did not reproduce the empirical measurements.
technical.mechanism: The paper models an agent handed b items as retaining each with probability r(b), composes this retention across a decomposition tree, and measures retention using production traces plus tool outputs with explicit item boundaries.
technical.regime: The empirical work covers the authors’ production deep-research traces and tool calls. The formal derivation applies under the paper’s stated retention assumptions.
technical.strongest_baseline: Flat processing is the comparison for yield under the stated retention model; empirical C is measured at tool-result handoffs with explicit item boundaries.

title: A preprint reports measurable retention loss across multi-agent research handoffs
why_it_matters: If the measured loss generalizes, adding agent tiers can reduce the information that reaches a final decision maker, even when parallel agents surface more sources. The paper identifies a tradeoff between smaller working contexts and end-to-end retention that system designers can measure.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that on an NVIDIA H100, RBS-Attention reached 20.65× standalone prefill-attention speedup, 11.92× vLLM prefill-attention speedup and 5.97× end-to-end time-to-first-token speedup at 128K context for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8, relative to dense execution in the same reported setup.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On Qwen3-32B, the authors report 88.65 overall RULER accuracy for RBS-Attention versus 89.52 for dense attention; the paper also reports LongBench-v2, InfiniteBench and Video-MME evaluations.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The v1 preprint describes a training-free selector that combines centroid relevance with radius-adaptive rescue using independently thresholded masks. Its attenuated rescue score is explicitly not a universal upper bound, and the paper reports substantial temporary selector workspace in its A100 measurements.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent run has confirmed the reported H100/A100 latency, quality, memory or selector-workspace values.
Transfer beyond the specified Qwen models and benchmark prompts is unknown.

importance_rationale: If independently sustained, several-fold lower time-to-first-token at 128K could materially change long-context serving choices and cost budgets. The result is limited to specified Qwen models, GPU configurations and author-run workloads; it does not establish general production economics.
limitations: The results are author-reported in one arXiv v1 preprint and have not been independently reproduced.
